profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-05T09:41:42.099+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
edited by imperial command.
Later
Tāi.
Emperor Wǔ [of Chén] already had merit towards the Liáng dynasty;
he considered himself to be surnamed Chén,
and was promoted from Duke of Wúxìng Commandery to Duke of Chén.
When he received the Mandate,
his state was consequently named Chén.
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì
Yǒngdìng 1st year (Dīngchǒu, 557)
In the tenth month of this year, he received the abdication,
and began to change the era name to Yǒngdìng.
Before the tenth month,
it was still Liáng Tàipíng 2nd year.
1 Spring,
first month,
xīnchǒu,
the Duke of Zhōu assumed the throne of Heavenly King.
His taboo name was Jué,
courtesy name Tuóluóní.
He was the third son of Yǔwén Tài.
When Yǔwén [Tài] assisted in government,
he admired and imitated the rites of Zhōu.
When Tài died,
Jué succeeded him,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhōu.
Having received the Mandate,
the state was named Zhōu.
He held court with all officials at the Lùmén.
The Lùmén
is the ancient Lù Mén.
Lù
means "great."
Yǔwén established the state,
and generally imitated ancient systems,
hence the outer court was called Lùmén.
Zhèng Xuán said: "The outer gate is called Gāomén,
the court gate is called Yìngmén,
and within is the Lùmén."
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "The Èryǎ says: 'The space between the gate and the screen is called níng (宁).'"
Guō [Pú] said: "The place where the lord stands to preside over court."
Lǐ Xún said: "The space between the two gatehouses outside the main gate is called níng."
It means the Son of Heaven holds court outside the Lùmén,
standing at the níng outside the gate
to await the arrival of the feudal lords,
hence it is said "standing at the níng."
However, the presence of a screen outside the gate
refers to the shù (樹) that blocks the gate.
The Èryǎ says: "The main gate is called Yìngmén."
It also says: "The screen
is called shù."
Lǐ Xún said: "It regularly stands before the gate to conceal it,
and is named shù."
Guō [Pú] said: "A small wall in the middle of the gate."
According to the annotations of Lǐ [Xún] and Guō [Pú], in inferring the ritual texts,
the inner screen for feudal lords was inside the Lùmén,
while the outer screen for the Son of Heaven was outside the Lùmén,
and near the Yìngmén.
Under the Zhōu system,
the Son of Heaven held three courts.
One was inside the Lùmén,
called the Yàncháo (燕朝),
and was managed by the Tàipú.
Thus, the Tàipú said,
"When the King holds the Yàncháo,
he rectifies his position."
The Wénwáng Shìzǐ says: "The ducal clan holds court in the inner court,
to show their closeness."
This was when the King and his clan members discussed auspicious matters,
and when the King retired, the marquises and grandees held court.
The second was the court outside the Lùmén,
called the Zhìcháo (治朝),
managed by the Sīshì.
Thus, the Sīshì said,
"Rectify the positions for the court ceremonies."
This was the daily court position.
When the King and the feudal lords engaged in guest archery,
it was also the same as the Zhìcháo.
The third was inside the Gāomén,
outside the Kùmén,
called the Wàicháo (外朝),
managed by the Cháoshì.
This was the court for inquiring of the common people.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
His deceased mother was made Empress Wén.
A general amnesty was issued.
Emperor Gōng of Wèi was enfeoffed as Duke of Sòng.
As wood succeeds Wèi's water virtue,
they followed the season of Xià,
and favored black for their attire.
Following the season of Xià
means using yínzhèng.
Favoring black for attire
followed the water element.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ fān.
Zhào Guì was made Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Dúgū Xìn, the Grand Minister of State (Dàzhǒngzǎi), was made Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo).
Yǔwén Hù, the Duke of Zhōngshān and Grand Minister of Rites (Dàzōngbó), was made Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ).
In the early days of the Later Zhōu dynasty, when Grand Ancestor [Yǔwén Tài] first controlled Guānyòu,
official titles had not yet been changed from the Wèi designations.
When the realm was generally pacified,
and new regulations were established,
he ordered the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) Lú Biàn to draw remotely from the Zhōu system,
establishing the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) and Three Solitaries (Sāngū)
as officials for expounding the Way;
next, he established the Six Ministers (Liùqīng)
to divide the various governmental duties.
When Emperor Mǐn received the abdication,
the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) commanded the military,
and Yǔwén Hù held this position
to control vital military power.
2 An edict appointed Wáng Lín as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn),
and Wáng Tōng, the Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè), as Left Assistant (Zuǒpúyè).
3 The King of Zhōu sacrificed at the Yuánqiū,
claiming his ancestors descended from Shénnóng,
and offered Shénnóng sacrifices at the two mounds.
The Yǔwén clan claimed their ancestors descended from Yándì.
Yándì was destroyed by Huángdì,
and his descendants fled to the northern wilderness (Shuòyě).
Later, there was Gěwūtù,
who was heroic and had many strategies.
The Xiānbēi people honored him as their leader.
His descendant, Pǔhuí,
obtained three jade seals while hunting.
The inscription read
"Huángdì Xǐ" (Emperor's Seal),
believing it to be bestowed by Heaven.
Their custom was to call the Son of Heaven Yǔwén,
so they adopted it as their surname and dynastic name.
The two mounds
are the Yuánqiū (round mound) and Fāngqiū (square mound).
Pǔhuí's son, Mònà, migrated south from Yīnshān,
and first resided in Liáoxī.
He was posthumously honored as Xiàn Hóu.
His temple name was Tàizǔ.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
sacrifices were offered at the Fāngqiū.
On the day Jiǎchén,
sacrifices were made to the Dàshè.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: The Later Zhōu emulated Jī Zhōu,
and many of their sacrificial rites
followed the Yílǐ.
The Sīliáng
was in charge of the regulations for constructing altars.
The Yuánqiū had three tiers,
one *zhàng* and two *chǐ* high,
two *zhàng* deep,
with an upper diameter of six *zhàng*.
It had twelve steps,
each tier having twelve sections,
located seven *lǐ* to the south of the capital.
The outer sacred enclosure (yuán wěi) had a diameter of three hundred *bù*,
the inner enclosure was half that.
It was one tier square,
one *zhàng* high at the bottom,
with a diameter of six *zhàng* and eight *chǐ*,
and five *chǐ* high at the top,
four *zhàng* square.
It had eight sides,
one step per side,
ten steps per tier,
each step one *chǐ*.
The Fāngqiū was located ten *lǐ* to the north of the capital,
the mound had one tier and eight sides,
one *zhàng* high at the bottom,
six *zhàng* and eight *chǐ* square,
and five *chǐ* high at the top,
four *zhàng* square.
Each of the eight sides had one step,
each step one *chǐ*.
Its sacred enclosure had eight faces,
a diameter of one hundred and twenty *bù*,
the inner enclosure was half that.
A square altar was built in the southern suburb five *lǐ* south of the capital,
it was one *zhàng* and two *chǐ* high,
and two *zhàng* wide.
Its sacred enclosure was one hundred and twenty *bù* square,
the inner enclosure was half that.
The altar of Shénzhōu
was one *zhàng* high,
four *zhàng* square,
located to the right of the Fāngqiū in the northern suburb,
its sacred enclosure was like that of the Fāngqiū.
The sacrifices at the Yuánqiū and the southern suburb
both took place on the *shàngxīn* day of the first month.
The ancestral temple (zōngmiào) was on the right, and the altars of land and grain (shèjì) on the left.
The Emperor personally sacrificed to the Shèjì,
the Zhǒngzǎi performed the secondary offering,
and the Zōngbó the final offering.
At the end of Wèi, bandits rose everywhere,
and the state's resources were insufficient.
A tax of one coin per person was levied on those entering the market gate,
which is now abolished.
On the day Yǐsì,
offerings were made to the Tàimiào,
still following Zhèng Xuán's interpretation,
establishing Tàizǔ and the two Zhāo and two Mù as the five ancestral temples.
Those with virtue were separately established as Tiāomiào,
which were not destroyed.
The Jì Wángzhì says: The Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples,
three Zhāo and three Mù,
together with the temple of the Tàizǔ makes seven.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: This Zhōu system of seven refers to
Tàizǔ, and the Tiāo temples of Wénwáng and Wǔwáng, plus four close ancestral temples.
The Juéyí Yàozhù says: Regarding Zhāo and Mù,
the father faces south,
hence called Zhāo (bright);
Zhāo
means brightness.
The son faces north,
hence called Mù (solemn);
Mù
means solemnity/accordance.
Lǐ Fú said: Zhāo
was originally written as it is,
but to avoid the taboo name of Hàn Zhāo,
it was changed to Sháo.
Another explanation says: Jìn Wéndì's name was Zhāo,
hence it was read as Sháo.
On the day Xīnhài,
sacrifices were offered at the southern suburb.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Empress Yuán was established.
The Empress
was the Princess Jìn'ān, daughter of Wèi Wéndì.
4 Féng Xiǎn, the lord of Qí's Nán'ān city, requested to surrender to Zhōu.
Zhōu's Zhùguó Yǔwén Guì dispatched Guō Yàn, the Cìshǐ of Fēngzhōu from Tàiyuán, to lead troops to receive him.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Huánggāng County of Yǒng'ān Commandery
was called Nán'ān by Qí.
Also, Wèi Shōu's Zhì states: In the early Tiānpíng era,
Nán'ān Commandery was established,
belonging to Xiāngzhōu,
but later fell.
Considering its location,
it should be within the bounds of Yè County, Yǐngchuān Commandery, as mentioned in the Wǔdài Zhì.
Also, the Wǔdài Zhì states: Wǔdāng County of Xīyáng Commandery,
formerly had Wǔdāng Commandery and Shǐpíng Commandery established,
later changed to Qíxīng Commandery.
Liáng established Xīngzhōu,
Later Zhōu changed it to Fēngzhōu,
and Suí called it Jūnzhōu.
Jiàng
is pronounced as *liàng*.
5 The Tǔyùhùn raided Zhōu,
attacking the three prefectures of Liáng, Shàn, and Hé.
Wǔwēi Commandery was
Liángzhōu.
Xīpíng Commandery was
Shànzhōu.
Bàohǎn Commandery was
Hézhōu.
Tǔ
has the entering tone of *tūn*.
Gǔ
is pronounced *yù*.
Shàn
is pronounced *shízhàn*.
In the third year of Wèi Huángchū,
the position of Dūdū Zhūzhōu Jūnshì (Commander-in-chief of military affairs of all prefectures) was first established.
There was also the Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn (Commander-in-chief of all military forces, internal and external),
whose responsibilities were particularly heavy.
The Southern and Northern Dynasties both followed this system.
Moreover, for military campaigns, there were Dūdū Zhūjūn,
and the Grand Dūdū of the Left, Right, Front, Rear, and Central armies.
Internally, for palace guards, there were Zhèng-fù Dūdū (chief and deputy commanders), Sǎn Dūdū (dispersed commanders), Shuài Dūdū (marshal commanders), Lǚ Dūdū (regimental commanders).
Externally, for prefectures and commanderies, there were Fángchéng Dūdū (city defense commanders), Zhàngnèi Dūdū (tent interior commanders).
Although the name Dūdū was the same,
their ranks and responsibilities were vastly different.
This Qínzhōu Dūdū
likely commanded the prefectures of Hé, Wèi, Liáng, and Shàn.
In the Later Zhōu's nine ranks system,
a Dūdū held the eighth rank.
Those granted the titles Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn or Kāifǔ Yítóng
were also given the additional titles of Shǐchíjié and Dà Dūdū,
which was the ninth rank.
His subordinates all expressed their concerns,
but Yì said:
"The art of attack and conquest
is not a strength of the barbarians.
This raid
is nothing more than plundering border herds.
If they plunder but gain nothing,
they will naturally retreat.
To send a weary army
will surely achieve nothing."
Yì had already figured it out completely.
Liǎo
means clear.
Chāo
is pronounced *chǔjiāo*.
Chuǎi
is pronounced *chūwěi*.
After several days,
a report arrived,
which was indeed as Yì had predicted.
6 At first,
Liáng Shìzǔ made Shǐxīng Commandery into Dōnghéng Prefecture,
and appointed Ōuyáng Wěi as its governor.
After a long time,
Wěi was transferred to be the governor of Yǐng Prefecture,
but Xiāo Bó kept Wěi and would not let him go.
Shìzǔ replaced Bó with Wáng Lín as the governor of Guǎngzhōu,
but Bó sent his general Sūn Dàng to oversee Guǎngzhōu,
and led all his forces to garrison Shǐxīng to avoid him.
See volume 165, the third year of Chéngshèng of Liáng Yuándì.
將 (jiàng),
pronunciation is liàng;
same below.
監 (jiān),
pronunciation is gōng xián.
帥 (shuài),
read as 率 (shuài).
He did not go to pay respects,
but closed his gates and defended himself.
Bó was enraged,
and sent troops to attack him,
seizing all his goods, wealth, horses, and weapons;
soon after, he pardoned him,
allowed him to return to his place,
and formed an alliance with him.
When Jiānglíng fell,
Wěi then served Bó.
In the second month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Bó raised an army in Guǎngzhōu,
and sent Wěi, along with his generals Fù Tài and Xiāo Zī, to be the vanguard.
Zī
was Bó's nephew from his father's side.
Yú Xiàoqǐng, the governor of Nánjiāng Prefecture, joined him with his troops.
Xiàoqǐng was stationed at Xīnwú,
which was probably where Nánjiāng Prefecture was established,
and he was appointed its governor.
The text Kǎoyì says: Diǎnlǜe records
"governor of Nánkāng Prefecture."
We follow the Liángshū here.
7 On the day Guǐyǒu,
the Zhōu royal court held a morning audience in the eastern suburbs;
on the day Wùyín,
sacrifices were made to the Great Altar of Soil.
8 Zhōu Chǔgōng Zhào Guì and Wèigōng Dúgū Xìn had both originally been peers of Tàizǔ.
Yǔwén Tài's temple name was Tàizǔ.
Yǔwén Hù was promoted from Zhōngshān Gōng to Jìn Gōng.
Guì plotted to kill Hù,
but Xìn stopped him;
Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Yǔwén Shèng reported this.
On the day Dīnghài,
Guì entered the court,
and Hù seized and killed him,
and dismissed Xìn from office.
This was the so-called time when "the lord is young and the state is in doubt,
and the high officials have not yet pledged allegiance."
After killing Zhào Guì,
Hù's power and authority were established.
9 Xú Dù, the leader of the army, went out of Dōngguān to invade Qí,
and on the day Wùzǐ,
arrived at Héféi,
and burned three thousand Qí ships.
10 Ōuyáng Wěi and others advanced out of Nánkāng.
Wěi garrisoned Kǔzhútān in Yùzhāng,
Fù Tài occupied Zhíkǒucheng,
Yú Xiàoqǐng sent his younger brother Xiào Mài to guard the commandery city,
and he himself went out of Yùzhāng to occupy Shítou.
The Shuǐjīngzhù says: The Gànshǔi flows past the north of Yùzhāng Commandery,
on the west bank of the river there is a rocky outcrop,
called Shítou,
a ferry crossing point.
Wāng Zǎo says: From Yùzhāng, crossing the river to the west,
there is a mountain that stands majestically,
extending along the river,
that is Shítou Zhǔ;
it blocks the river and backs onto the city,
nearly ten lǐ away,
it is the place where Yīn Xiàn threw his letter.
勱 (mài),
pronunciation is mài.
He also made an agreement,
to jointly defeat Wěi,
and said:
"If the matter succeeds,
give me the horses and weapons."
Then he sent out his army,
advancing together with Wěi.
When they reached the foot of Fǎchéng,
Tán Láng feigned defeat and fled,
Fǎ took advantage of this,
Wěi lost his support and fled,
Tán Láng took his horses and weapons,
and returned to Bāshān.
Zhōu Wényù's army had few boats,
Yú Xiàoqǐng had boats at Shàngláo,
Wényù sent his army commander Jiāo Sēngdù to attack them,
seized all of them and returned,
and then set up a stockade in Yùzhāng.
Food ran out in the army,
and the generals wanted to retreat,
but Wényù did not allow it,
and sent someone to secretly deliver a letter to Zhōu Dí,
proposing to become sworn brothers.
Dí was very pleased upon receiving the letter,
and promised to supply provisions.
Thereupon Wényù divided his forces, sending the old and weak to go downstream in the old boats,
and burned the Yùzhāng stockade,
pretending to be in flight.
Xiàoqǐng saw this,
was greatly pleased,
and no longer took precautions.
Wényù marched quickly along secret paths,
occupying Qiānsháo,
upstream of Qiānsháo were Ōuyáng Wěi and Xiāo Zī,
downstream were Fù Tài and Yú Xiàoqǐng's camps,
Wényù occupied the middle,
built a city and entertained his soldiers,
Wěi and the others were greatly alarmed.
Wěi retreated into Níxī,
Wényù sent Yánwēi Jiāngjūn Zhōu Tiěhǔ and others to attack Wěi,
and on the day Guǐsì,
captured him.
Wényù arrayed his forces grandly,
and feasted with Wěi on a boat,
cruising beneath Zhíkǒucheng,
he sent his general Dīng Fǎhóng to attack Tài,
and captured him.
Zī and Xiàoqǐng retreated and fled.
11 On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Zhōu appointed Yú Jǐn as Tàifù,
Dàzōngbó Hóumòchén Chóng as Tàibǎo,
Jìn Gōng Hù as Dàzǒngzǎi.
As Yú Jǐn and Hóumòchén Chóng had already reached the rank of Gōng,
Yǔwén Hù, if he were promoted by seniority to Dàzǒngzǎi,
would actually be the prime minister of Zhōu.
Gāoyáng Gōng Dáxī Wǔ was Dàsīkòu.
12 The Zhōu people killed Wèi Gōngdì.
13 In the third month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Zhōu Wényù sent Ōuyáng Wěi and Fù Tài to Jiànkāng.
Chéngxiàng Bàxiān had old ties with Wěi,
released him and treated him generously.
Bàxiān rose from Lǐngnán,
hence he had old ties with Wěi.
14 Zhōu Jìn Gōng Hù considered Zhào Jǐng Gōng Dúgū Xìn's reputation too great,
and did not wish to execute him openly,
so on the day Jǐyǒu,
he forced him to commit suicide.
15 On the day Jiǎchén,
Sīkōng Wáng Lín was appointed governor of Xiāng and Yǐng Prefectures.
16 Qújiāng Hóu Bó was in Nánkāng,
and when he heard that Ōuyáng Wěi and others had been defeated,
fear spread in his army.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Chén Fǎwǔ, the governor of Dé Prefecture,
The Wǔdàizhì says: Rìnán Commandery,
Liáng established Dé Prefecture.
killed him.
17 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
four-column coins were minted,
one being equivalent to twenty.
At the end of Liáng, there were two-column coins and goose-eye coins,
people at the time used them interchangeably,
their value was the same,
but the two-column coins were heavier,
and the goose-eye coins were lighter.
Now, four-column coins were minted,
one being equivalent to twenty fine coins.
18 Qí sent an envoy to request peace.
19 On the day Rénwǔ,
the Zhōu King visited Chénglíng;
the tomb of Zhōu Tàizǔ was called Chénglíng.
On the day Yǐyǒu
he returned to the palace.
20 Qí appointed Tài-shī Hú-lǜ Jīn as Yòu-chéng-xiàng,
former Dà-jiàng-jūn Kě-zhū-hún Dào-yuán as Tài-fù.
Kě-zhū-hún Dào-yuán was formerly Chē-qí Dà-jiàng-jūn.
Later, Qí established the positions of Tài-shī, Tài-fù, and Tài-bǎo,
which were known as the Sān-shī.
These were modeled after the ancient Shàng-gōng,
and only those with exceptional merit and virtue could hold them.
Next were Dà-sī-mǎ and Dà-jiàng-jūn,
known as the Èr-dà,
both responsible for military affairs.
Next were Tài-wèi, Sī-tú, and Sī-kōng,
known as the Sān-gōng.
All were of the first rank.
The two generals, Piáo-qí and Chē-qí, when granted additional titles,
ranked below Kāi-guó Jùn-gōng.
Kāi-guó Jùn-gōng
was of the first sub-rank.
Shàng-shū-lìng Cháng-shān-wáng Yǎn was made Sī-kōng,
Lù Shàng-shū-shì Cháng-guǎng-wáng Zhàn was made Shàng-shū-lìng,
Yòu Pú-shè Yáng Yīn was made Zuǒ Pú-shè,
and was also granted the title of Kāi-fǔ Yí-tóng Sān-sī.
Furthermore, Bìng-shěng Shàng-shū Yòu Pú-shè Cuī Xiān was made Zuǒ Pú-shè,
and Shàng-dǎng-wáng Huàn was appointed Lù Shàng-shū-shì.
Since Gāo Huān resided in Jìn-yáng,
Bìng-zhōu had officials such as Xíng-tái Shàng-shū-lìng and Pú-shè.
When Qí Xiǎn-zǔ received the abdication of Wèi,
the Bìng-zhōu Xíng-tái was made Bìng-shěng,
and its rank and responsibilities were second only to Yè-shěng.
21 On the day Dīng-hài,
the King of Zhōu offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
22 On the day Rén-chén,
the four-column cash was changed to be worth ten;
on the day Bǐng-shēn,
the circulation of small cash was again halted.
"Halted" (bì) means
stopped and prevented from circulating.
Small cash (xì-qián) were
those privately minted by the populace.
At that time, private cash was small,
and transactions involved cartloads of cash,
no longer bothering to count.
Fù,
pronounced like "fú yòu";
the other instance of fù below is the same.
23 Bó, the former Marquis of Qǔ-jiāng, whose chief commander Lán Yī attacked and killed Tán Shì-yuǎn,
and his military commander Xià-hóu Míng-chè killed Yī,
and surrendered with Bó's head.
Bó's former secretary Lǐ Bǎo-zàng, acting on behalf of the Marquis of Huái-ān, Rèn, occupied Guǎng-zhōu.
Rèn was also a son of the Xiāo clan,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Huái-ān.
Hé Chéng-tiān's record states: Yù-lín Commandery has Huái-ān County.
They built two cities,
each occupying one, and deployed many ships and vessels,

is pronounced *shuài*;
all subsequent instances of 帥 are the same.
Zhōu sent Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Hèruò Dūn, Chìluó Huī, and others to attack them.
They beheaded Yān
and captured all his troops.
45 That year,
an imperial edict commanded Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng Xiāo Gān to persuade and pacify the people of Mǐnzhōng.
At that time, Xióng Tánlǎng was in Yùzhāng,
Zhōu Dí in Línchuān,
Líu Yì in Dōngyáng,
and Chén Bǎo Yìng in Jìn'ān.
They were all connected,
and the powerful chieftains in Mǐnzhōng often built fortresses to protect themselves.
The Emperor was concerned about this,
so he sent Gān to explain the consequences of misfortune and fortune.
The chieftains all led their troops to surrender.
Gān was then appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān.
According to the *Wǔdàizhì*: Jiàn'ān County in Mǐnzhōu
was formerly Jiàn'ān Commandery,
and Nán'ān County was formerly Jìn'ān.
The territory of Jiàn'ān
became Jiànzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The territory of Jìn'ān
became Quánzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
He was the son of Zǐfàn.
Xiāo Zǐfàn was
the son of Qí Yùzhāngwáng Yì.
46 Earlier,
Xi Kè, the governor of Xìngzhōu under the Liáng dynasty, surrendered his prefecture to Wèi.
The Grand Ancestor of Zhōu appointed Xi Kè as the governor of Fēngzhōu.
The *Wǔdàizhì*: Wǔdāng County in Xīyáng Commandery
was formerly Wǔdāng Commandery and Shǐpíng Commandery,
later renamed Qíxīng Commandery.
Liáng established Xìngzhōu,
later Zhōuhòu changed it to Fēngzhōu,
and Suí changed it to Jūnzhōu.
The character 降,
is pronounced *hùjiāng*.
Xi Kè still followed the Liáng laws
and did not comply with the northern system.
The Zhōu people secretly wished to replace him,
but found it difficult to find a suitable person.
So they appointed Sìxiàn Zhōngdàfū Línghú Zhěng as acting administrator of Fēngzhōu.
The *Tángliùdiǎn* states: Later Zhōu's Qiūguān office had two Sìxiàn Zhōngdàfū,
who were responsible for assisting the judicial administration of the Sīkòu,
to rectify punishments.
This position was comparable to that of the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Zhěng extensively spread his benevolent authority,
engaging wholeheartedly in administration and reception.
Within a few months,
his influence permeated the prefecture.
Consequently, Zhěng was appointed as the governor of Fēngzhōu,
and Xi Kè was made the governor of Húzhōu.
The *Wǔdàizhì*: Húyáng County in Chōnglíng Commandery
was formerly Huái'ān Commandery and Nánxiāngzhōu under Hòuwèi,
later renamed Nánpíngzhōu.
Xīwèi changed it to Shēngzhōu,
and later again to Húzhōu.
Within ten days,
the city and administration were completely set up,
and those who relocated felt at home.
When Xi Kè departed,
many of his subordinates wished to stay and serve Zhěng as his aides.
Zhěng explained the court regulations
and did not permit it.
"Court regulations" refers to
the laws and regulations of the Zhōu court.
The character 朝,
is pronounced *zhíyáo*.
47 The Qí people built a double wall inside the Great Wall,
extending from Kùluòzhī eastward to Wūgēshù.
The *Běishǐ* writes it as
"Kùluòbá, Wūgēshù."
The character 重,
is pronounced *zhílóng*.
48 Initially,
a diviner in Qí said,
"Those who destroy Gāo wear black clothes."
Therefore, when Gāozǔ went out,
he disliked seeing Buddhist monks.
Xiǎnzǔ was in Jìnyáng
and asked his attendants,
"What is the blackest thing?"
They replied,
"Nothing is blacker than lacquer."
The Emperor, considering Shàngdǎngwáng Huàn to be the seventh among his brothers,
ordered Kùzhí Dūdū Pòliùhán Bóshēng to go to Yè to summon Huàn.
When Huàn reached Zǐmòqiáo,
he killed Bóshēng and escaped,
floating across the Yellow River to the south.
When he arrived at Jìzhōu,
he was captured by someone
and sent to Yè.
The "black ones"
referred to the military uniforms of the Yǔwén.
Qí Xiǎnzǔ then used this as a pretext to kill his younger brother.
How is this different from Qín attacking the Xiongnu because the saying was "those who destroy Qín are Hú,"
or Táng Tàizōng killing Lǐ Jūnxiàn because "those who replace Táng are the Wǔ clan"?
The character 濟,
is pronounced *zǐlǐ*.
When the Emperor was the Duke of Tàiyuán,
he and Yǒng'ān Wáng Jùn both met Shìzōng.
The Emperor sometimes had mucus flowing from his nose.
Nasal discharge is called 'tì'.
"[Why don't you] wipe the nose of your second elder brother!"
Xiǎnzǔ was second in age among his brothers.
'Wéi',
pronounced yú wěi.
When he ascended the throne,
Jùn was the Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
He was intelligent and compassionate,
and officials and common people rejoiced in him.
Jùn, seeing that the Emperor was addicted to alcohol,
privately said to his close attendants:
"My second elder brother has damaged his virtue due to alcohol,
and no court official dares to admonish him.
The great enemy has not yet been eliminated."
'Great enemy',
refers to Zhōu.
"I wish to travel by post-horse to Yè to remonstrate with him face-to-face,
but I do not know if he will listen to me."
Someone secretly reported this to the Emperor,
and the Emperor became even more resentful.
When Jùn came to court,
he accompanied the Emperor on an outing to Dōngshān.
The Emperor amused himself by stripping naked.
'Luǒchéng',
means to expose one's body.
'Luǒ',
pronounced láng guǒ.
'Chéng',
pronounced chí chéng.
'Lè',
pronounced luò.
"[This is] not proper for a ruler of men!"
The Emperor was displeased.
Jùn also summoned Yáng Yīn to a secluded place
and criticized him for not remonstrating.
At that time, the Emperor did not want high-ranking officials to communicate with the various princes.
Yīn, in fear,
reported this.
The Emperor was greatly enraged and said:
"Small men are always hard to tolerate!"
'Yóulái',
is like what people now say 'cónglái' (always, from ancient times).
He returned to the palace.
Jùn soon returned to his province,
and again submitted a strongly worded memorial of remonstrance.
An imperial edict summoned Jùn.
Jùn feared misfortune,
and declined, citing illness, so he did not come.
The Emperor dispatched a swift messenger to arrest Jùn.
Several thousand old and young wept as they saw him off.
Upon arriving in Yè,
he and Shàngdǎng Wáng Huàn were both put into iron cages,
and placed in the dungeon of the northern city,
where they ate, drank, and relieved themselves
all in one place.
1. In spring,
the first month,
Wáng Lín led his troops down,
reaching Pénchéng,
and encamped at Báishuǐpǔ,
with a hundred thousand armored soldiers.
Lín appointed Lǔ Xīdá, the Cìshǐ of Běi Jiāngzhōu, as Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn.
The Emperor also appointed Xīdá as Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn,
and each sent drummers, wind musicians, and female entertainers.
Xīdá accepted both,
procrastinated and observed,
but did not assume either post.
The Emperor sent Ānxī Jiāngjūn Shěn Tài to attack him,
but did not succeed.
Lín wanted to lead his army eastward,
but Xīdá controlled the middle stream.
Lín sent envoys to persuade and entice him,
but he ultimately did not comply.
On the day Jǐhài,
Lín sent his Jìshì Zōng Xì to seek aid from Qí,
and also requested to accept Liáng Yǒngjiā Wáng Zhuāng to preside over the Liáng sacrifices.
Zhuāng was a hostage in Qí;
see volume Shang, Liáng Jìngdì Shàotài Yuánnián.
The land from Nánkāng to Yùzhāng
was called Nánchuān,
named after the course of the southern river.
Qí stated that they would come to assist.
The eight commanderies under Dí's jurisdiction
were Nánkāng, Yíchūn, Ānchéng, Lúlíng, Línchuān, Bāshān, Yùzhāng, and Yùníng.
Yáo Sīlián's Chén Shū records
"proclaimed loudly that they would come to assist."
'Shǒu',
pronounced shì yòu.
He generously comforted and pacified them.
Yú Xiàoqǐng, the cave chieftain of Xīnwú, sent the Buddhist monk Dàolín to persuade Lín, saying:
"Zhōu Dí and Huáng Fǎ both rely on Jīnlíng,
secretly watching for opportunities.
If the great army advances,
they will surely become a future problem.
It is better to first pacify Nánchuān,
and then advance eastward.
Xiàoqǐng requests to lead all his subordinates to follow your subordinates."
Lín then dispatched Qīngchē Jiāngjūn Fán Měng, Píngnán Jiāngjūn Lǐ Xiàoqīn, and Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Liú Guǎngdé with eight thousand soldiers to proceed there,
making Xiàoqǐng the supreme commander of the three generals,
to encamp at the former commandery of Línchuān.
The former commandery of Línchuān
was where Zhōu Fū was stationed.
Lín sent troops to attack Dí,
and also to threaten Fū.
This was to observe their actions.
2. Hóu Zhèn was appointed Sīkōng, with the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Ōuyáng Wěi, the Cìshǐ of Héngzhōu, was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Jiāo, Guǎng, and other nineteen prefectures, and Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu.
3. Zhōu appointed Jìn Gōng Hù as Tàishī.
4. On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Emperor performed the southern suburban sacrifice and granted a general amnesty.
On the day Yǐsì,
he performed the northern suburban sacrifice.
5. On the day Xīnhài,
Zhōu Wáng Gēng performed the ceremonial plowing of the field.
6. On the day Guǐchǒu,
Zhōu established Wáng Hòu Dúgū Shì as empress.
The Empress
was the daughter of Dúgū Xìn.
7. On the day Wùwǔ,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the Míngtáng.
8. In the second month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Shěn Tài, the Cìshǐ of Nán Yùzhōu, fled to Qí.
Tài was unable to save Hóu Āndū from defeat when advancing,
nor could he control Lǔ Xīdá's stubbornness when retreating.
He probably feared punishment and fled north.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: the Běi Qí Dìjì places this in the eighth month.
Now it follows the Chén Dìjì.
9. Sīmǎ Xiāonán, the Cìshǐ of Běi Yùzhōu in Qí,
seeing that the Qí ruler's cruelty was intensifying,
secretly planned for his own safety,
and deliberately showed kindness to the people under his jurisdiction.
Xiāonán was married to the daughter of Gāozǔ,
but their relationship was not harmonious,
and the princess complained about him.
When Shàngdǎng Wáng Huàn fled,
there was great chaos in Yè,
and it was suspected that he was heading to Chénggāo.
Běi Yùzhōu in Qí was governed from Hǔláo,
which was the territory of Chénggāo.
He had a grudge against Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Bì Yìyún.
Yìyún sent Yùshǐ Zhāng Zǐjiē to Běi Yùzhōu to gather rumors,
first prohibiting Xiāonán's diǎnqiān, household retainers, and others.
Xiāonán, in fear,
secretly ordered his trusted Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Péi Zǎo to use a private leave of absence as a pretext,
travel secretly into the pass,
and request to surrender to Zhōu.
In the third month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Zhōu sent *Zhùguó* Dáxī Wǔ and *Dà Jiāngjūn* Yáng Zhōng with five thousand cavalry to welcome Xiāonán.
They galloped five hundred *lǐ* into Qí territory via a secret path.
They sent three messengers to report to Xiāonán,
but received no reply.
Thirty *lǐ* from Hǔláo,
Wǔ suspected trouble
and wanted to return.
Zhōng said,
"There is death if we advance,
but no life if we retreat!"
He alone led a thousand cavalry at night to the foot of the city.
The city was steep and precipitous on all four sides;
only the sound of watchman's clappers could be heard.
Wǔ personally came
and waved several hundred cavalry to go west.
Zhōng ordered the remaining cavalry to stand firm,
awaiting the opening of the gate to enter,
and then dispatched someone to summon Wǔ.
Qí's town commander Fú Jìngyuǎn led two thousand armored soldiers to occupy the eastern part of the city.
The town commander
held the office of *Fángchéng Dà Dūdū*.
The eastern part of the city
was the eastern side of Hǔláo City.
*Běi Shǐ* records it as
"eastern battlements."
Wǔ was apprehensive of it
and did not wish to hold the city,
so he took many valuables
and returned first with Xiāonán and his subordinates.
Zhōng with three thousand cavalry formed the rearguard.
Upon reaching the south of Luò,
they all dismounted and lay down.
Qí's forces came in pursuit,
reaching the north of Luò.
Zhōng said to his officers and soldiers,
"Just eat your fill.
We are now in a place of death,
and the enemy will surely not dare to cross the water!"
It turned out to be so,
and they slowly withdrew.
Wǔ sighed and said,
"Dáxī Wǔ considered himself the strongest warrior in the world,
but today I am convinced [of your superiority]!"
Zhōu appointed Xiāonán as *Xiǎo Sītú*.
*Táng Liù Diǎn* says: Zhōu's *Dìguān Xiǎo Sītú*
was a *Zhōng Dàfū*.
The Later Zhōu followed the Zhōu official system.
Dù Yòu's *Tōngdiǎn*: Later Zhōu's *Dìguān Xiǎo Sītú*
was an *Shàng Dàfū*,
of the sixth rank.
*Kǎo Yì* says: *Běi Qí Dìjì*:
"In the fourth month,
Xiāonán rebelled."
We follow *Zhōu Shū* and *Diǎnlüè* here.
On the 10th *Dīngyǒu* day,
the Qí ruler returned to Yè from Jìnyáng.
*Kǎo Yì* says: *Běi Qí Dìjì*:
"In the eighth month of Tiānbǎo's seventh year,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng."
It does not mention his return.
In the eighth year,
in the fourth month,
the Emperor was at an archery range east of the city,
ordering all women in the capital to come and watch.
This means he was in Yè.
This month also says
"returned from Jìnyáng."
In the sixth month,
on the *Yǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor toured north from Jìnyáng,
so he was again in Jìnyáng.
There must be discrepancies;
we do not dare to add or subtract from it now.
Qí dispatched troops to escort Liáng's Prince Yǒngjiā, Zhuāng, to Jiāngnán,
and formally appointed Wáng Lín as *Liáng Chéngxiàng*, *Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn*, and *Lù Shàngshū Shì*.
Lín sent his nephew Shūbǎo to lead the sons of the *Cǐshǐ* of his ten prefectures to Yè.
Lín enthroned Zhuāng as Emperor.
*Kǎo Yì* says: *Běi Qí Dìjì*:
"In the eleventh month,
on the *Dīngsì* day,
Lín sent an envoy to request the enthronement of Zhuāng,
and still had Jiāngzhōu subordinate itself,
letting Zhuāng reside there.
In the twelfth month,
on the *Guǐyǒu* day,
an edict made Zhuāng the Liáng ruler,
moving his residence to Jiǔpā."
We follow *Chén Shū* and *Diǎnlüè* here.
However, *Chén Shū* and *Diǎnlüè* both say Zhuāng was enthroned in Yǐngzhōu.
According to Lín's location at Pénchéng at that time,
it is likely he initially resided in Jiāngzhōu and later moved to Yǐngzhōu.
He posthumously honored Jiàn'ān Gōng Yuānmíng as Mǐn Emperor.
Yuānmíng's deposition is seen in the previous volume under Liáng Jìngdì's Shàotài first year.
His death is seen in Tàipíng first year.
The rest followed the Qí court's commands.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the
*Yǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor had someone harm Liáng Jìngdì,
and established Jìqīng, son of Liáng Wǔlín Hóu Zī, as Prince of Jiāngyīn.
On the *Jǐsì* day,
Zhōu appointed *Tàishī* Hù as *Yōngzhōu Mù*.
Later Zhōu's *Yōngzhōu Mù*
was of the ninth rank.
*Yōng* is pronounced *yúyòng fān*.
On the *Jiǎxū* day,
Zhōu's Empress Dúgū died.
On the *Xīnsì* day,
Qí granted a general amnesty.
The Qí ruler prayed for rain at the temple of Xīmén Bào due to drought,
but it did not respond.
He destroyed it
and also excavated his tomb.
During the Warring States period,
Wèi appointed Xīmén Bào as the magistrate of Yè,
who dug twelve canals to benefit the people,
thus both the temple and tomb were in Yè.
In the fifth month,
on the *Guǐsì* day,
Yú Xiàokǒng and others encamped two thousand troops at Gōngtáng,
connecting eight fortified cities to pressure Zhōu Dí.
After "and others"
there should be the character "multitude"
for the sentence to flow smoothly.
They requested peace
and also sent military provisions.
Fán Měng and others wanted to accept the alliance and return;
Xiàokǒng was greedy for their gains
and did not allow it,
instead building fences to surround them.
Because of this,
Měng and others became discordant with Xiàokǒng.
Zhōu appointed *Dà Sīkōng* Hóumòchén Chóng as *Dà Zōngbó*.
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
Zhāng Xiǎnhé, Qí's southern city commander of Guǎnglíng, and *Chángshǐ* Zhāng Sēngnà each led their respective units to surrender.
On the
*Xīnchǒu* day,
Qí appointed *Shàngshū Lìng* Chángguǎng Wáng Zhàn as *Lù Shàngshū Shì*,
and *Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn* Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn as *Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè*.
On the *Jiǎchén* day,
former *Zuǒ Púyè* Yáng Yīn was appointed *Shàngshū Lìng*.
On the *Xīnyǒu* day,
the Emperor went to Dàzhuāngyán Temple to give up his body (renounce worldly life);
the former cart overturned,
but the latter cart did not learn from the warning.
Their ears and eyes were accustomed to worshipping Buddha,
not knowing its error.
On the *Rénxū* day,
the various ministers presented a memorial requesting his return to the palace.
In the sixth month,
on the *Yǐchǒu* day,
the Qí ruler toured north,
appointing Crown Prince Yīn as regent,
and thereupon established the *Dà Dūdū Fǔ* to manage various affairs separately from the *Shàngshū Shěng*,
and also opened offices and appointed aides.
The Qí ruler particularly emphasized their selection,
appointing Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì as *Shìzhōng* and acting *Dà Dūdū Fǔ Chángshǐ*.
On the *Jǐsì* day,
an edict commanded *Sīkōng* Hóu Tián and *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn* Xú Dù to lead a naval force as the vanguard to attack Wáng Lín.
The Qí ruler arrived at Qílián Pond;
Qílián Pond is Fényáng's Tiānchí (Heavenly Pond);
northerners called heaven *Qílián*.
On the *Wùyín* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
In autumn,
on the *Wùxū* day,
the Emperor went to Shítou
to see off Hóu Tián and others.
This was the *Wùxū* day of the seventh month of autumn.
[Commentary: The twelve-line edition correctly has the two characters
"seventh month";
the *Yǐ* eleven-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same.]
Gāozhōu *Cǐshǐ* Huáng Fǎ, Wúxīng *Tàishǒu* Shěn Kè, and Níngzhōu *Cǐshǐ* Zhōu Fū.
At that time, Níngzhōu was probably established at the former prefecture of Línchuān,
with Fū appointed as *Cǐshǐ*.
Fū blocked the river mouth from the former prefecture of Línchuān,
and divided his troops to attack Yú Xiàokǒng's other city.
Fán Měng and others failed to rescue it and perished;
Liú Guǎngdé moved downstream first,
thus surviving.
Xiàokǒng and others all abandoned their boats and led their troops to flee on foot.
Dí pursued and attacked them,
capturing all of them,
sending Xiàokǒng and Lǐ Xiàqīn to Jiànkāng,
and returning Fán Měng to Wáng Lín.
On the 28th, *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor sent Shàngshū of the Lìbù, Xiè Zhé, to issue an imperial decree to Wáng Lín.
Zhé
was the grandson of Fěi.
Xiè Fěi
was the son of Zhuāng,
and served successively the Sòng, Qí, and Liáng dynasties.
Fěi,
pronounced *fū wěi*.
In the 8th month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Zhōu dynasty granted a general amnesty.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Qí Lord returned to Yè.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict commanded Línchuān Wáng Qiàn to march west,
departing from Jiànkāng with a fleet of 50,000 troops.
The Emperor went to Yěchéng Sì to see him off.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Qí Lord went to Jìnyáng.
While Wáng Lín was at Báishuǐ Pǔ,
Zhōu Wényù, Hóu Āndū, and Xú Jìngchéng promised Wáng Zǐjìn a hefty bribe.
Zǐjìn then pretended to fish from a small boat near the shore.
At night,
he carried Wényù and Āndū ashore,
hid them in deep grass,
and personally surrendered to the Chén army.
He returned to Jiànkāng and impeached himself;
the Emperor granted him an audience
and pardoned them both.
On the *wùyín* day,
they were reinstated to their original posts.
Wényù and Āndū were not punished despite their army's defeat,
and were quickly restored to their positions.
Why was this?
The two were renowned generals at the time,
and punishing them would mean having no one to utilize.
Xiè Zhé returned to report,
and Wáng Lín requested to return to Xiāngzhōu.
An imperial edict recalled all the armies.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the armies arrived back from Dàléi.
In the 9th month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Zhōu dynasty enfeoffed the Grand Tutor (Shàoshī) Yuán Luó as Hánguó Gōng to continue the lineage of Wèi.
After the fall of Jiānglíng,
Yuán Luó returned to Wèi.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
King Wǔ of Zhōu went to Tóngzhōu;
in winter,
the 10th month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
he returned to Cháng’ān.
Yú Xiàokǒng’s younger brother Xiàomài and his son Gōngyáng still held their old stockade and refused to submit;
this was the old stockade of Xīnwú.
Mài,
pronounced *mài*.
Yáng,
pronounced *yú zhāng*.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
an imperial edict ordered Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Zhōu Wényù to command all armies to depart from Yùzhāng and suppress them.
The three terraces of Qí were completed,
and they were renamed: Tóngjué to Jīnfèng,
Jīnhǔ to Shèngyìng,
and Bīngjǐng to Chóngguāng.
Wèi Wǔ built three terraces in the northwest of Yèchéng,
all using the city wall as their foundation;
the central one was called Tóngjuétái,
ten *zhàng* high,
which Shí Hǔ later increased by two *zhàng*;
the southern one was Jīnhǔtái,
and the northern one Bīngjǐngtái,
both eight *zhàng* high.
Gēng,
pronounced *gōng héng*.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Qí Lord arrived at Yè
and granted a great amnesty.
The Qí Lord toured the three terraces,
and playfully stabbed Dūdū Wèi Zǐhuī with a spear,
who died instantly.
Chángshān Wáng Yǎn, seeing that the emperor was
sunken in debauchery, displayed his sorrow and indignation in his expression.
The emperor noticed it
and said:
"As long as you are around,
why should I not indulge in pleasure!"
Yǎn could only weep and prostrate himself,
ultimately saying nothing.
The emperor also became greatly saddened,
throwing his cup to the ground, saying:
"You seem to despise me for being like this.
From now on, anyone who dares to offer me wine will be beheaded!"
He then took all the cups he used and broke and discarded them.
Not long after,
his debauchery worsened.

The Zhōu (周) people, hearing that Lín (琳) had moved east,
dispatched Shǐ Níng (史寧), Dūdū Jīng‧Xiāng Děng Wǔshí'èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督荊‧襄等五十二州諸軍事) and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史), with tens of thousands of soldiers to raid Yǐngzhōu (郢州) while it was undefended.
Sūn Yáng (孫瑒) defended the city from within.
Last year, when Wáng Lín (王琳) marched east,
he left Sūn Yáng (孫瑒) to guard Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced *liàng*.
Yáng (瑒)
is pronounced *zhìxìng*,

Fearing that his forces would collapse,
he led his naval forces eastward,

The sound of their watchman's clapper was heard by the Chén (陳) army.
Liú Bóqiú (劉伯球), Qí Yítóng Sānsī (齊儀同三司), led over ten thousand soldiers to assist Lín (琳) in naval combat.
Mùróng Zǐhuì (慕容子會), son of Xíngtái Mùróng Shìdé (行臺慕容恃德), led two thousand iron cavalry to encamp on the west bank of Wúhú (蕪湖),
creating a show of force.
On *Bǐngshēn* (丙申),
Zhèn (瑱) ordered his army to cook their morning meal and eat in their beds (i.e., be ready early) to await them.
At that time, the southwest wind was strong.
Lín (琳) believed he had divine assistance

Zhèn (瑱) and the others slowly emerged from Wúhú (蕪湖) to pursue them from behind,
and the southwest wind turned to Zhèn's (瑱) advantage.
Lín (琳) threw flaming torches to burn the Chén (陳) ships,
but they all turned back and burned his own ships.
Using fire attack against the wind,
this was why Wáng Lín (王琳) was defeated.
Battle ships were equipped with ramming poles at the front and back to strike enemy ships.
Molten iron was also sprinkled.
Lín's (琳) army was greatly defeated.
Two or three tenths of his soldiers drowned,
the rest abandoned their ships and went ashore,
nearly all of them being killed by the Chén (陳) army.
The Qí (齊) infantry on the west bank
trampled each other,
and all became stuck in the mud of the reeds;
the cavalry all abandoned their horses and fled,
only two or three tenths escaping.
Liú Bóqiú (劉伯球) and Mùróng Zǐhuì (慕容子會) were captured.
Tens of thousands were slain or captured.
All the military supplies and equipment of the Liáng (梁) and Qí (齊) armies were seized.
Lín (琳), in a *zé měng* (舴艋) (small boat), risked passing through the Chén (陳) forces and escaped.
Upon reaching Péngchéng (湓城),
he wanted to rally his scattered forces,

So, he fled to Qí (齊) with his wives, concubines, and about ten attendants.
Before this,
Lín (琳) had sent Shìzhōng Yuán Mì (侍中袁泌)

After the defeat,
all their attendants scattered.
Mì (泌) used a light boat to transport Zhuāng (莊) to the Qí (齊) border,

Zhòngwēi (仲威) escorted Zhuāng (莊) and fled to Qí (齊).
Mì (泌)
was the son of Áng (昂).
Yuán Áng (袁昂) was famous for his integrity between Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁).
From this point, all of Jiāngnán (江南) belonged to Chén (陳).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced *shuài*.

Jìnyáng (晉陽)

Bìng (幷)

Last year, Qí Xiǎnzǔ (齊顯祖) exterminated the Yuán (元) clan

Now, only the commoners (良口) are released;

11 On *Yǐsì* (乙巳),

12 During the mourning period for Qí Xiǎnzǔ (齊顯祖),

Empress Dowager Lóu (婁太后) wanted to enthrone him, but did not succeed.
When the crown prince ascended the throne,
he (Yǎn) then joined the court ranks.
As the Son of Heaven was in mourning (諒陰),

The East Lodge
was likely to the east of the Zhāoyáng Diàn (昭陽殿) in the Yè (鄴) Palace.
All matters were first submitted to him for decision.
Yáng Yīn (楊愔) and others believed that Yǎn (演) and Chángguǎng Wáng Zhàn (長廣王湛) held positions too close in proximity (to the new emperor)

After some time,
Yǎn (演) returned to his residence.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: *Běi Qí Shū Xiàozhāo Jì* (北齊書孝昭紀) says:

Now we follow the *Yáng Yīn Zhuàn* (楊愔傳).
The princely mansion (藩邸)
was the Chángshān (常山) residence.
Someone said to Yǎn (演):
"A raptor leaving its nest
will surely suffer the misfortune of having its eggs discovered.
Why should the King frequently go out now?"
Zhōngshān Tàishǒu Yáng Xiūzhī (中山太守陽休之) went to visit Yǎn (演),
but Yǎn (演) did not see him.
Xiūzhī (休之) said to Wáng Xī (王晞), the King's attendant:
"In the past, the Duke of Zhōu (周公) read a hundred chapters in the morning
and met seventy scholars in the evening,

What does the Lù Wáng (錄王) suspect or fear, that he so refuses guests?"
Yǎn (演) was Lù Shàngshūshì (錄尚書事) as Chángshān Wáng (常山王),
hence he was called Lù Wáng (錄王).
Before this,
during Xiǎnzǔ's (顯祖) reign,
officials were not secure.
When Jìnán Wáng (濟南王) ascended the throne,
Yǎn (演) said to Wáng Xī (王晞):
"If one person can rule by merely folding his hands,

He then said:
"The court is lenient and benevolent,
truly a good ruler who adheres to the established ways."
Xī (晞) said:
"During the late emperor's time,
the Eastern Palace entrusted a barbarian

Now, though he is still young (春秋尚富),

Your Highness should be the first and last to attend him morning and evening,
personally receiving his commands,
instead of letting others handle the issuance of edicts.
Great power will inevitably fall elsewhere.
Even if Your Highness wishes to remain a prince,
how can that be possible?
Even if you could achieve a reclusive life (沖退),
do you believe your family's fortune (家祚) can be preserved for a long time?"
Jiāzuò (家祚)
is synonymous with guózòu (國祚, national fortune).
As Yǎn (演) was a paternal uncle and held the same close relation to the state's prosperity,
he spoke of *jiāzuò*.
Wáng Xī (王晞) had long advised Chángshān (常山) to supplant the main imperial line.
He said:
"How should I handle myself?"
Xī (晞) said:
"The Duke of Zhōu (周公) embraced King Chéng (成王) and acted as regent for seven years

Your Highness, please consider this!"
Yǎn (演) said:
"How dare I compare myself to the Duke of Zhōu (周公)!"
Xī (晞) said:
"Given Your Highness's current position and prestige,

Yǎn (演) did not respond.
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) had often sent the barbarian Kāng Hǔ'ér (康虎兒)

The Qi 主 was about to depart from Jìnyáng.
The one departing from Jìnyáng

Gāo Huān had established the Grand Chancellor's office in Jìnyáng,

The Chángguǎng Wáng was left to guard Jìnyáng;

When the outer court heard of this,

He also ordered Wáng Xī to be the Jìngzhōu Chief Clerk.
When Yǎn was about to leave,

Yǎn, fearing that there might be spies,

"Strive and be careful!"
He then spurred his horse and left.
Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn was in overall charge of the imperial guards.
Yáng Yīn announced an edict to leave five thousand escorting soldiers in Xīzhōng.
Jìnyáng was west of Yè,
hence it was called Xīzhōng.
從 (cóng),
pronounced cái yòng.
A few days after arriving at Yè,
Guīyàn only then learned of it,

The Lǐngjūn Dàjiàngjūn Kězhūhún Tiānhé
was the son of Dàoyuán.
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán returned to Gāo Huān from Lǒngyòu.

The Qi 主's aunt

"If the two Wáng are not executed,

少 (shǎo),

He wanted to return governance to the Empress Dowager.

The Shìzhōng Sòng Qīndào,

Sòng Biàn was employed by Wèi Xiàowén Dì.
taught the crown prince about official matters.

The palace lady Lǐ Chāngyí,

was very close to them,

in the morning,

The rear room of the Lù Shàngshū office

"When serving wine to Yīn and others,

I will say 'Seize the wine' once,

At the banquet,

Yīn loudly declared:

We honor the Son of Heaven,

Chángshān Wáng Yǎn wanted to slow things down.
Zhàn said:

Thereupon, fists and staffs struck wildly,

Each was held by ten men.
Yàn Zǐxiàn was very strong,

Zǐxiàn sighed, saying:

He had the Tàizǐ Tàibǎo Xuēgū Yán and others seize Yí at the Shàngyào Jú.
Wǔdài Zhì: The Shàngyào Jú

a system of the Later Qí.
"Not listening to the words of the wise has led to this;

The two Wáng, together with Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn, Hèbá Rén, and Húlà Jīn, pushed Yīn and others rudely into the Yúnlóng Mén.
"Tángtú" (唐突),
Guǎngyùn writes it as

He beckoned,

Chìlì

Yǎn had Guīyàn persuade him,

Yǎn entered,

Imperial guard officials, patrol guard officials, defense guard officials, assault guard officials, and gate guard officials were all subordinate,

After "Grand Empress Dowager"
it is suspected that the three characters
"Empress Dowager"

The Empress Dowager and the Emperor stood at the side.

Yáng Yīn,
courtesy name Zūnyàn.
Cháo (朝),
pronounced zhí yáo.
From princes and dukes downwards, everyone holds their breath in fear.

Wǔwèi É Yǒnglè,

Lè,

Now we follow the Běi Shǐ.
The Emperor was naturally slow-witted and tonguetied,

The Grand Empress Dowager ordered the guards to retreat,

She then sternly said,

All the armored guards withdrew.

Yáng Yīn

Chuàng,
pronounced chuàng.
"These people harbor rebellion,

The Emperor still could not speak.

Empress Dowager Lóu

Yù,

Qù,

The Empress Dowager said to the Emperor,

Thereupon, all of them were executed.
Yáng Yīn, entrusted with the care of the young sovereign,

Chángguǎng Wáng Zhàn, because Zhèng Yí had once slandered him,

Yáng Yīn, Kězhūhún Tiānhé, Yān Zǐxiàn, Sòng Qīndào, and Zhèng Yí,

Fù,
pronounced fù.

After Wèi was divided into East and West,
in the early Tiān-píng period of Eastern Wèi,
Qín-zhōu was re-established in Hé-dōng;
after the defeat at Shā-yuàn,
the territory of Hé-dōng fell to Western Wèi,
and later Zhōu established Pú-zhōu based on the old name of Pú-bàn.
We should transport provisions and stockpile weapons.
If they close their passes and do not come out,
we will gradually 'silkworm-eat' their Hé-dōng territory,
making them increasingly desperate day by day.
If they send out troops,
unless it's more than a hundred thousand,
they will not be a match for us.
The provisions consumed by our army
"損" (*sǔn*)
should be written as
Our soldiers should be replaced generation by generation annually,
with a new garrison each year.
If they come seeking battle,
we will not engage;
if they retreat,
we will capitalize on their weakness.
West of Cháng-ān,
the population is sparse and cities are distant,
making it truly difficult for enemy troops to move back and forth.
If they contend with us,
their agriculture will be abandoned,
and in no more than three years,
they will collapse on their own."
The Emperor deeply approved of this.
30 The Qí Lord personally led an attack on the Kù-mò-xī.
When they reached Tiān-chí,
the Kù-mò-xī fled north of the Great Wall.
(This is the Great Wall built by Emperor Wén-xuān.)
They captured seventy thousand cattle and sheep and returned.
31 In the twelfth month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, from early spring until the beginning of summer,
for capital offenses where the prisoner has confessed,
'已款' means the prisoner has confessed and submitted.
Modern people call a prison statement '獄款'.
'辟' (*pì*) is pronounced *pì*.
executions shall only be carried out in autumn and winter."
32 On the *jǐhài* day,
Wèi-chí Xiàn, the lord of Zhōu's Bā-líng City, surrendered.
Hóu Ān-dǐng, the Inspector of Bā-zhōu, was sent to guard it.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Dú-gū Shèng led his remaining troops to secretly escape from Yáng-yè-zhōu.
Hè-ruò Dūn's position became increasingly isolated.
33 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the Qí Lord returned to Jìn-yáng.
The Qí Lord executed a man in front of Wáng Xī and asked:
"Should this man die?"
Xī replied:
"He should die,
but I only regret that he did not die in the proper place.
I have heard 'Execute criminals in the marketplace,
and abandon them with the masses.'"
(Records the words of the Royal System.)
The Emperor's expression changed, and he apologized, saying:
"From now on, I will change it for you, Duke Wáng."
The Emperor wanted to make Xī a Shì-láng.
According to the biography of Wáng Xī in the *Běi Shǐ*,
"侍郎" (*shìláng*)
should be "侍中" (*shìzhōng*).
Someone advised Xī not to alienate himself.
Xī said:
"Since my youth,
I have seen many important people.
Those who achieved their ambitions for a short time
rarely avoided downfall.
'少時' (*shǎoshí*) means 'not for long'.
'少' (*shǎo*) is pronounced *shǎo*.
'鮮' (*xiǎn*) is pronounced *xiǎn*.
If one is not capable of handling current affairs,
how can the ruler's personal favor
be preserved?
Should one once lose control,
there would be no place to retreat.
It's not that I don't like holding important positions,
but I have considered it thoroughly."
34 Initially,
at the end of Qí Xiǎn-zǔ's reign,
grain prices soared.
When the King of Jì-nán ascended the throne,
Sū Zhēn-zhī, the Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, suggested
repairing the Tún at Shí-biē and other places.
From then on, the Huái-nán garrisons had sufficient food.
Dù Yòu said: Shí-biē
is eighty *lǐ* west of Ān-yí County in Chǔ-zhōu.
Dèng Ài built a city here
and constructed the Bái-shuǐ Pond,
which connected north to Hóng-zé,
for garrison agriculture covering thirteen thousand *qǐng*.
Ān-yí
was renamed Bǎo-yìng County in the first year of Táng Bǎo-yìng.
Jī Yè, the Inspector of Píng-zhōu, suggested
opening the Dū-kàng Pí
and establishing garrison agriculture.
Annually, hundreds of thousands of *shí* of rice and millet were harvested,
providing ample supplies for the northern border.
The Dū-kàng Pí
is in the area of Xīn-chéng County, Zhuó-zhōu, in the Táng dynasty.
Yān Jīng-kē presented a map to Qín from this very place.
'亢' (*kàng*) is pronounced *gāng*.
This was used to cover the expenses of Hé-nán.
Qí divided Hé-nèi and Jí Commandery into Yì-zhōu,
establishing the Huái-yì and other Tún.
This section is from the Five Dynasties' preface to the military provisions of Qí King Jì-nán until Emperor Xiào-zhāo;
the *Tōng-jiàn* extracted it
and attached it here.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *wùshēn* day,
Zhōu changed its era name to Bǎo-dìng.
Yǔ-wén Hù, the Grand Minister of the Interior, was made the Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs, both domestic and foreign.
The Five Administrations were placed under the jurisdiction of the Department of Heaven,
and all matters, great or small,
had to be decided by him first before being reported to the throne.
The Five Administrations are the Departments of Earth, Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter.
The historian states that Yǔ-wén Hù's power grew even greater.
'斷' (*duàn*) is pronounced *duàn*.
2 On the *gēngxū* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 The Zhōu Lord offered sacrifices at the Yuán-qiū.
4 On the *xīnhài* day,
the Qí Lord offered sacrifices at the Yuán-qiū;
on the *rénzǐ* day,
he performed the *dì* sacrifice at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
5 The Zhōu Lord offered sacrifices at the Fāng-qiū;
on the *jiǎyín* day,
he offered sacrifices to the Gǎn-shēng-dì at the southern suburb.
(Following Zhèng Xuán's theory,
sacrifices were offered to the Gǎn-shēng-dì Líng-wēi-yǎng in the southern suburb to pray for grain.)
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
he sacrificed to the Grand Altar of Soil.
6 The ruler of Qí sent Wáng Lín out from Héféi,
to recruit Cāng Chǔ people,
and plan further advances.
Péi Jǐnghuī, the Cìshǐ of Hézhōu,
(Kǎoyì says: The Běi Qí Shū writes
"Jǐnghuī."
We follow the Chén Shū here.)
requested to use his personal retainers as local guides.
The ruler of Qí dispatched Lín with Lú Qián, Zuǒ Chéng of the Xíngtái, to lead troops and join him.
Lín hesitated and was indecisive.
Jǐnghuī feared the matter would be exposed,
and personally fled to Qí.
(Note: Liáng established Hézhōu in Héféi.
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng,
it had already fallen to Qí.
Qí's territory
extended south to Lìyáng.
Chén likely established a relocated Hézhōu on the riverbank,
and appointed Jǐnghuī as its Cìshǐ.)
Shěn,
read 'chílín'.
Zhen Shòuyáng.
7 On the day Jǐsì,
the ruler of Zhōu offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào,
and promulgated the Six Officials' Regulations, authored by the Tàizǔ.
(Yǔwén Tài's temple name was Tàizǔ.)
(When Tài was chancellor of Wèi: he established the Six Officials,
based on the Six Canons of the Zhōu Lǐ, to form the Six Officials' Regulations.)
8 On the day Xīnwèi,
Yīn Liàng, the city lord of Xiāngzhōu for Zhōu, surrendered,
and Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
Hóu Tián and Hèruò Dūn had been locked in a standoff for a long time.
Tián could not subdue him,
so he offered to lend boats to send Dūn and others across the river.
(According to the Hèruò Dūn Zhuàn,
above "jièchuán"
is the character
"qiú".)
Dūn refused,
responding:
"Xiāngzhōu is my territory,
you are encroaching upon it.
If you insist on me returning,
you must withdraw a hundred lǐ from me."
Tián left the boats on the riverbank
and led his troops away.
Dūn then extricated himself and returned north;
five or six tenths of his soldiers died of illness.
Wǔlíng, Tiānmén, Nánpíng, Yìyáng, Hédōng, and Yídū Commandery were all pacified.
(The Wǔdài Zhì says: Lǐyáng Commandery, Cánlíng County,
formerly had Nánpíng Commandery established there.
Ānxiāng County
formerly had Yìyáng Commandery established there.
Nán Commandery, Sōngzī County,
formerly had Hédōng Commandery established there.
Sòng Bái says: Lǐyáng Commandery, Ānxiāng County,
was originally the land of Hàn Cánlíng County,
later in Later Hàn it was the land of Hànshòu County,
and Jìn once established Yìyáng Commandery there.)
Their names were removed, and they became commoners.
9 In the second month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the ruler of Zhōu offered sacrifices to the sun god in the eastern suburbs.
(According to the rites of the Three Dynasties,
in spring, one offers sacrifices to the rising sun,
and in autumn evenings, to the moon.
The people of Zhōu admired antiquity
and performed these rites.)
Cháo,
read 'zhíyáo'.
10 The people of Zhōu appointed Wéi Xiàokuān, the Xiǎo Sītú, as Cìshǐ,
because he had once achieved meritorious service at Yùbì.
(The event can be found in Volume 159, during the first year of Zhōngdàtóng of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.)
(According to the system of Later Zhōu,
a Xiǎo Sītú
held the sixth rank, equivalent to a Shàngdàfū.)
Xiàokuān possessed kindness and trustworthiness,
and was skilled at using spies.
Sometimes Qí people would accept gold and goods from Xiàokuān
and secretly send letters and reports,
so the people of Zhōu always knew Qí's movements beforehand.
There was a commander named Xǔ Pén,
who surrendered his garrisoned city to Qí.
Xiàokuān sent a spy to seize him,
and soon his head was brought back.
South of Líshí,
the uncivilized Hú frequently plundered.
(The Wǔdài Zhì says: Líshí Commandery,
Later Qí established Xīfénzhōu there.)
(The uncivilized Hú refers to the Jī Hú who were not affiliated with Zhōu.)
Shù,
read 'suǒjiǎo'.
Chāo,
read 'chǔjiāo'.
It was impossible to suppress them.
Xiàokuān wanted to build a city in a strategic location to control them.
So he mobilized one hundred thousand laborers from Héxī
and one hundred armored soldiers.
(Héxī refers to the west of Lóngmén River.)
Yuè, fearing the scarcity of soldiers,
dared not advance.
Xiàokuān said:
"This city can be completed in ten days.
The city is over four hundred lǐ from Jìnzhōu.
If we start building today,
the enemy territory will only know on the second day.
Even if Jìnzhōu mobilizes troops,
they will only gather on the third day.
During their deliberations,
it will naturally take another two days.
Counting their army's march,
they won't arrive for two more days.
By then, our city walls
will be finished."
He then ordered the construction.
The Qí people indeed reached the border,
but suspecting a large army,
they hesitated and did not advance.
That night,
Xiàokuān ordered villages south of the Fénshuǐ, near Mount Jiè and Mount Jì, to set fires.
The Qí people took these to be army camps
and withdrew their troops to secure themselves.
Yuè eventually completed the city and returned.
11 In the third month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Hóu Tián, the Tàiwèi Línglíng Zhuàngsù Gōng, passed away.
12 On the day Bǐngyín,
Zhōu changed the Eight-Dīng Army system to the Twelve-Dīng Army system,
requiring service for one month each year.
(The Eight-Dīng Army meant that
all able-bodied men in the territory were divided into eight shifts,
taking turns to serve.
The Twelve-Dīng Army meant that
they were divided into twelve shifts,
serving monthly,
in a continuous cycle.)
13 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the first day Bǐngzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
14 Zhōu appointed Wèichí Gāng, the Shǎofù, as Dà Sīkōng.
15 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Zhōu enfeoffed Kāng, son of Emperor Mǐn, as Jìguó Gōng,
and Yūn, the imperial prince, as Lǔ Gōng.
(Yūn was the son of Empress Lǐ.)
16 In the sixth month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
Zhōu sent Yīn Bùhài, the Yùzhèng, to visit as an envoy.
(The Zhōu Shū, in the biography of Shēn Huī, states: The Yùzhèng
was entrusted with important pronouncements,
essentially the duty of a Zhōngshū Shèrén.
The Běi Shǐ, in the biography of Lú Biàn, states: In the first year of Wǔchéng,
four Yùzhèng were added,
with the rank of Shàngdàfū.
Examining the Táng Liùdiǎn,
it says: Later Zhōu, following the Zhōu Guān,
placed a Nèishǐ Zhōngdàfū in the Chūn Guān Fǔ,
in charge of royal pronouncements.
This was comparable to the positions of Zhōngshū Jiān and Lìng;
later, they were increased to Shàngdàfū.
The Xiǎoshǐ Xiàdàfū
was comparable to the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng;
the Xiǎoshǐ Shàngshì
was comparable to the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Therefore, the Yùzhèng
also had the duty of speaking on behalf of the emperor,
near the emperor,
and even more intimately than the Zhōngshū.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn states: The Yùzhèng belonged to the Tiān Guān Fǔ.)
17 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zhōu re-minted coins,
inscribed "Bùquán,"
with a value of one equal to five,
circulating alongside Wǔzhū coins.
18 On the *jǐyǒu* day,
the Zhōu posthumously enfeoffed Imperial Uncle Hào as Duke of Shào,
with Huì, son of Hù, Duke of Jìn, as his heir.
Hào’s younger brother Lián was enfeoffed as Duke of Guó,
with Liàng, son of Dǎo, Duke of Zhāngwǔ, as his heir.
Lián’s younger brother Luòshēng was enfeoffed as Duke of Jǔ,
with Zhì, son of Hù, as his heir.
The Zhōu also posthumously enfeoffed Zhèn, Duke of Wǔyì and son of Tàizǔ, as Duke of Sòng,
with Shí, son of Shìzōng, as his heir.
Hào died in battle against Wèi Kěgū,
and had sons Shífèi, Dǎo, and Hù.
Shífèi and his uncle Lián were both killed by Gāo Huān,
leaving no descendants.
Therefore, Huì and Liàng were made their heirs.
Luòshēng was killed by Ěrzhū Róng,
and Zhèn died young.
Both had no descendants,
so heirs were also established for them.
19 When the Qí ruler executed Yáng and Yàn,
he promised to make Zhàn, Prince of Chángguǎng, the Crown Prince.
However, he later established Crown Prince Bǎinián,
which displeased Zhàn.
The Emperor was in Jìnyáng,
while Zhàn remained in Yè as its defender.
Yáng and Yàn
refer to Yáng Yīn and Yàn Zǐxiàn.
Shǒu
can also be pronounced shǒu.
Gāozǔ’s grand-nephew;
Gāo Huān’s temple name was Gāozǔ.
Yuánhǎi’s father, Sīzōng,
was a nephew of Huān.
Sàn,
pronounced sì dàn.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì.
Cóng,
pronounced cái yòng.
The Emperor appointed Kùdí Fúlián of Dàirén, the Commander-in-Chief, as Governor of Yōuzhōu,
and Xiàn, younger brother of Húlǜ Guāng, as Commander-in-Chief,
to divide Zhàn’s power.
Zhàn kept Fúlián,
and did not allow Xiàn to take up his duties.
The Qí ruler then appointed Fúlián to Yōuzhōu in place of Xiàn,
and Xiàn as Commander-in-Chief in place of Fúlián,
to divide the authority in Yè.
Zhàn knew the reason,
so he kept Fúlián and prevented him from going to Yōuzhōu.
When Xiàn arrived,
he also did not allow him to take up his duties in the Commander-in-Chief’s office.
Earlier,
Mǐndiào, Prince of Jìnán, Cháng, was in Yè.
The posthumous title of Yīn, Prince of Jìnán, was Mǐndiào.
Xiān,
pronounced xī jiàn.
Jì,
pronounced zǐ lǐ.
Guīyàn, Prince of Píngqín, feared that Jìnán would be re-established,
which would be disadvantageous to him.
The Qí ruler had relied on Guīyàn’s military power to kill Yáng and Yàn.
After Yáng and Yàn died, Jìnán was deposed.
Therefore, Guīyàn feared his re-establishment
would be disadvantageous to him.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
The Emperor then sent Guīyàn to Yè
to summon the Prince of Jìnán to Jìnyáng.
Zhàn felt uneasy,
and asked Gāo Yuánhǎi for advice.
Yuánhǎi said,
“The Empress Dowager is well.
His Majesty is exceptionally filial and fraternal.
Your Highness need not have any other worries.”
Zhàn said,
“Is this not my intention to be sincere?”
Yuánhǎi asked to return to his quarters,
to think it over for a night.
Zhàn immediately kept Yuánhǎi in the back hall.
Yuánhǎi did not sleep until dawn,
only pacing slowly around the bed.
Before the night watch ended,
Zhàn rushed out,
saying,
“What is your divine plan?”
Yuánhǎi replied,
“There are three plans,
but I fear they may not be usable.
I suggest Your Highness follow the precedent of Liáng Xiàowáng,
and with a few cavalry, enter Jìnyáng,
first see the Empress Dowager and beg for mercy.
The story of Liáng Xiàowáng
can be found in Volume 16, under the second year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn.
Request to relinquish military power,
vowing to do so until death,
and not interfere in court affairs.
This will surely guarantee the security of Mount Tài.
This is the best plan.
Otherwise,
you should submit a memorial stating
that your authority is too great,
and you fear slander from the masses.
Request to be appointed Governor of Qīng and Qí Prefectures,
and live in quiet seclusion.
This will surely avoid public criticism.
This is the middle plan.”
He was then asked for the lower plan.
He said,
“To speak of it would mean extermination of my clan.”
Zhàn pressed him firmly.
Yuánhǎi said,
“Jìnán is the legitimate heir.
The Emperor, falsely using the Empress Dowager’s order, deposed him.
Now, gather the civil and military officials,
show them the edict to summon Jìnán,
seize Húlǜ Fēnglè,
Húlǜ Xiàn,
courtesy name Fēnglè.
Lè
is pronounced luò.
Establish Jìnán as the sovereign,
issue orders to the realm,
and with righteousness, suppress injustice.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity!”
Zhàn was greatly pleased.
However, being timid by nature,
he was indecisive and could not act on it.
He had the diviner Zhèng Dàoqiān and others consult the omens,
and they all said,
“It is not favorable to initiate action;
stillness brings good fortune.”
There was Pān Zǐmì, Magistrate of Línlǜ,
who was skilled in divination.
Línlǜ County
belonged to Hénèi Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
to Jí Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
In the first year of Yǒng'ān under Wèi Jìngzōng, Línlǜ Commandery was established,
comprising Línlǜ County.
Lǜ
is pronounced lǘ.
“The imperial carriage will pass away late,
and Your Highness will be the ruler of the realm.”
Zhàn kept him confined within to await this.
He also had shamans divine,
most of whom said,
“There is no need to raise an army;
great fortune will come of its own accord.”
Zhàn then received an edict
to send several hundred cavalry to escort the Prince of Jìnán to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor sent someone to poison him.
The Prince of Jìnán refused,
so he was strangled to death.
The Emperor soon regretted it.
20 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *jiǎxū* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
21 On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Qí appointed Yǒu, Prince of Péngchéng, as Grand Protector,
and Wèi Càn, Prince of Chánglè, as Grand Commandant.
22 Qí Sùzōng went hunting,
a rabbit startled his horse,
causing him to fall and break his ribs.
Empress Dowager Lóu visited him,
and asked three times about the whereabouts of Jìnán.
The Qí ruler did not reply.
The Empress Dowager angrily said,
“Did you kill him?
You didn’t listen to my words,
so it serves you right to die!”
She then left,
without looking back.
In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎchén* day,
an edict declared that the heir, Chōng, was young and weak,
and ordered Zhào Jùnwáng Ruì, Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, to convey the imperial will,
summoning Zhàn, Prince of Chángguǎng, to assume the great treasure.
He also wrote a letter to Zhàn, saying,
“Bǎinián is innocent.
You may dispose of him as you please,
but do not imitate those who came before.”
On this day,
he died at the Jìnyáng Palace.
He was twenty-seven years old.
He said he regretted not seeing the Empress Dowager ascend the mountain tomb.
Yán Zhītuī commented: Xiàozhāo was naturally extremely filial,
yet he did not know taboos,
reaching such a point;
it was truly due to his lack of learning.
23 Zhào Jùn Wáng Ruì (趙郡王叡) first dispatched Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Wáng Sōngnián (王松年) to Yè (鄴),
to proclaim Sùzōng's (肅宗) dying wish.
Zhàn (湛) still suspected it was a trick,
so he sent his confidant to the coffin first
to open it and look.
The messenger returned,
and Zhàn (湛) was pleased.
He rushed to Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and sent Hénán Wáng Xiàoyú (河南王孝瑜) to enter the palace first
to change the imperial guards.
On guǐchǒu (癸丑) day,
Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the imperial throne in the Southern Palace.
His taboo name was Zhàn (湛).
He was Bóhǎi Wáng Huān's (勃海王歡) ninth son,
and Xiàozhāo Dì's (孝昭帝) maternal younger brother.
The Southern Palace
was the Jìnyáng (晉陽) Southern Palace.
The era name was changed to Tàiníng (太寧).
24 The Zhōu (周) people promised to return Ānchéng Wáng Xù (安成王頊),
and sent Sīhuì Shàngshì (司會上士) Dù
Gǎo (杲) as an envoy.
The Rites of Zhōu (周禮) in the section on Heavenly Officials (天官) include the Sīhuì (司會),
who oversees all the accounts of the administration of the various states, capitals, and villages, and their financial expenditures recorded in written contracts and cadastral maps.
They audited all their accounts
and examined their completion by year, month, and day.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said: Huì (會)
means a grand accounting.
The Sīhuì (司會) was in charge of the grand accounts of the realm,
the head of the accounting officials,
like today's Shàngshū (尚書).
I note that in the Later Zhōu (後周) Land Officials (地官),
which was the same as the Táng (唐) Hùbù Shàngshū (戶部尚書),
the Sīhuì (司會) would be like the Táng (唐) Dùzhī Lángzhōng (度支郎中),
but the Six Canons (六典) do not explain why.
Dù Yòu's (杜佑) Tōngdiǎn (通典) states that
the Later Zhōu (後周) Sīhuì (司會)
belonged to the Heavenly Officials' Bureau (天官府),
and had Zhōng Dàfū (中大夫),
Shàngshì (上士),
and Zhōngshì (中士) ranks.
Immediately, an envoy was dispatched to reply,
and bribes of the land of Qiánzhōng (黔中) and Lǔshān Jùn (魯山郡) were offered.
If Zhōu (周) obtained Qiánzhōng (黔中),
it would fully possess Bāshǔ (巴蜀); if it obtained Lǔshān (魯山),
it would fully possess Hànmiǎn (漢沔).
Therefore, they lured them with what they desired.
25 Qí (齊) appointed Péngchéng Wáng Yǒu (彭城王浟) as Tàishī (太師) and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事),
Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn (平秦王歸彥) as Tàifù (太傅),
Wèi Càn (尉粲) as Tàibǎo (太保),
Píngyáng Wáng Yān (平陽王淹) as Tàizǎi (太宰),

Its system of punishments: First, the cane (zhàngxíng),

Second, the whip (biānxíng),

Fourth, exile (liúxíng),

Fifth, capital punishment (sǐxíng): *qìng*, strangulation (jiǎo), beheading (zhǎn), public display of head (xiāo), dismemberment (liè).
*Qìng*, strangulation, beheading, public display of head, dismemberment.
In ancient times, if a member of the imperial clan committed a crime,

Zhèng Xuán (Zhèng Xuán) said: "To hang and strangle to death is called *qìng*."

Jiàng (Jiàng) is the primary flavoring for food.

After Jǐn (Jǐn) finished eating,

From the Three Dynasties (Sāndài) onward,

were only practiced by Hàn Míngdì (Hàn Míngdì) and Zhōu Wǔdì (Zhōu Wǔdì).
Sīkōng Hóu Āndū 侯安都, relying on his achievements, became arrogant and overbearing.
He frequently gathered civil and military officials for horse-riding, archery, and poetry composition.
Guests in his private residence [zhāi]
often numbered up to a thousand.
Many of his subordinate generals [jiàngshuài]
did not comply with laws and regulations.
When they were investigated and arrested [shōushè],
shè
means to record [lù] and
to capture [bǔ].
Jiàng
is pronounced as liàng.
Shuài
is pronounced as suǒlèi.
The Emperor's [Shàng] nature was strict and proper.
He resented this internally,
but Āndū 侯安都 did not perceive it.
Whenever there was a memorial [biǎo] or a petition [qǐ],
after it was sealed,
if there was something not fully expressed,
he would open it and add a note himself, saying:
"Further petitioning on a certain matter."
Also, during imperial banquets,
when he was flushed with wine,
he would sometimes sit with his legs spread [jī] or lean askew.
He once attended a xìyǐn 禊飲 (purification ritual banquet) in the Lèyóu 樂遊 Garden,
and said to the Emperor [Shàng]:
"How does this compare to when you were Prince of Línchuān 臨川?"
The Emperor [Shàng] did not respond.
Āndū 侯安都 repeated it three times.
The Emperor [Shàng] said:
"Though this is Heaven's mandate,
it is also due to your Lordship's [Mínggōng] strength."
After the banquet,
he requested to borrow the ceremonial tents [gōngzhàng] and water decorations [shuǐshì],
wanting to host his wives and concubines for a banquet in the imperial hall.
Although the Emperor [Shàng] granted permission,
he was very displeased.
The next day,
Āndū 侯安都 sat on the imperial throne,
and his guests occupied the positions of officials,
offering cups to wish him long life.
Coincidentally, the Chóngyún Diàn 重雲殿 suffered a disaster [fire],
and Āndū 侯安都 led his officers and soldiers, clad in armor, into the hall.
The Emperor [Shàng] greatly disliked this,
and secretly prepared for him.
These were all events from previous days,
which the historian [shǐ] recounts to explain the cause of Āndū's 侯安都's downfall.
Chóng
is pronounced as zhílóng.
Wù
is pronounced as wūlù.
Later, when Zhōu Dí 周迪 rebelled,
the court deliberated that Āndū 侯安都 should be sent to suppress him.
However, the Emperor [Shàng] instead sent Wú Míngchè 吳明徹.
He also repeatedly dispatched imperial envoys [táishǐ] to investigate Āndū's 侯安都's subordinates
and to check for deserters and rebels.
Āndū 侯安都 sent his别驾 [biéjià] Zhōu Hóngshí 周弘實 to seek favor with the Retainer [Shèrén] Cài Jǐnglì 蔡景歷.
Cài Jǐnglì 蔡景歷 was the Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人.
Since Emperor Wǔ 武帝,
he had enjoyed special trust and closeness,
for the power of the Chén 陳 dynasty largely resided in the Zhōngshū 中書 (Central Secretariat).
Jǐnglì 景歷 recorded his statement [zhuàng],
and fully presented it to the throne.
Consequently, to please the Emperor [xīzhǐ], he accused Āndū 侯安都 of plotting rebellion.
The Emperor [Shàng] feared he would not obey a summons,
so he appointed him as the governor of Jiāngzhōu 江州.
In the fifth month,
Āndū 侯安都 returned from Jīngkǒu 京口 to Jiànkāng 建康.
His troops entered Shítou 石頭.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor [Dì] invited Āndū 侯安都 to a banquet in Jiādé Diàn 嘉德殿.
He also gathered Āndū's 侯安都's subordinate generals [jiàngshuài] in the Shàngshū Cháotáng 尚書朝堂.
At the banquet, Āndū 侯安ū was arrested
and imprisoned in the west wing [Xīshěng] of Jiādé Diàn 嘉德殿.
His generals [jiàngshuài] were also arrested,
all their horses and weapons were confiscated, and then they were released.
Subsequently, Cài Jǐnglì's 蔡景歷's memorial [biǎo] was brought out
and shown to the court.
An imperial edict was then issued to publicly expose his crimes.
The next day,
he was granted death,
but his wife and children were pardoned,
and funds were provided for his funeral.
Earlier,
Gāozǔ 高祖 was in Jīngkǒu 京口.
After Gāozǔ 高祖 and Wáng Sēngbiàn 王僧辯 pacified Táichéng 臺城,
they garrisoned Jīngkǒu 京口.
Dù Sēngmíng 杜僧明, Zhōu Wényù 周文育, and Hóu Āndū 侯安都 came to offer felicitations [shòu],
offering cups to wish him long life.
Accumulating merits is called 'fá'.
"You are all good generals,"
he said, "but you each have your shortcomings.
Duke Dù 杜公 is ambitious but ignorant, familiar with subordinates but arrogant towards superiors;
Marquis Zhōu 周侯 is indiscriminate in his friendships and overly trusting;
Master Hóu 侯郎 is arrogant, extravagant, and insatiable, frivolous and unrestrained;
none of these are ways to preserve oneself."
In the end, all turned out as he had predicted.
"No one understands a minister better than his sovereign,"
truly this saying is correct.
Zú
is pronounced as zǐxù.
On the day of Yǐmǎo 乙卯,
the Qí Zhǔ 齊主 (Lord of Qí) sent the concurrent Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 Cuī Zǐwǔ 崔子武 to establish friendly relations.

is pronounced as xīdǎn.
Qí
