The Qí 齊 Shìzhōng 侍中 and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司 Hé Shìkāi 和士開 was favored by the Qí Zhǔ 齊主.
When the Qí Zhǔ 齊主 held court [shìshì] in the outer palace,
or was feasting and rewarding in the inner palace,
in a short while,
he could not help but meet with Shìkāi 士開.
Sometimes Shìkāi 士開 would not return home for several days,
entering the palace multiple times a day;
sometimes after being allowed to leave,
he would be summoned back shortly thereafter,
and before he arrived,
mounted messengers would be sent one after another to urge him on.
His cunning flattery was manifold,
and imperial favor grew daily.
The rewards and gifts he received throughout his time
were countless.
Whenever he attended the Emperor's [Dì] side,
his words, demeanor, and deportment
were utterly vulgar and profane;
night and day,
there was no longer any decorum between ruler and minister.
He often said to the Emperor [Dì]:
"From ancient times, emperors and kings,
all turn to dust.
What difference is there between Yáo Shùn 堯舜 and Jié Zhòu 桀紂!
Your Majesty should, while still young and strong,
indulge to the fullest in pleasure,
and act as you please.
One day of gratification
can be worth a thousand years.
Entrust all state affairs to your high officials;
why worry that they won't be handled?
There's no need to exert and restrict yourself!"
The Emperor [Dì] was greatly pleased.
Thus, he entrusted Zhào Yànshēn 趙彥深 with official appointments and noble ranks,
Yuán Wényáo 元文遙 with finances,
Táng Yōng 唐邕 with the outer forces [wàibīng] and cavalry [qíbīng].
Wàibīng 外兵 and Qíbīng 騎兵.
Bóhǎi Wáng Huān 勃海王歡 (Gāo Huān 高歡) was the Chancellor of Wèi 魏.
The Wàibīng Cáoshǐ 外兵曹 and Qíbīng Cáoshǐ 騎兵曹 of the Chancellor's [Chéngxiàng] office were separately in charge of military forces.
When Wénxuān 文宣 (Emperor Wenxuan of Northern Qi) received the abdication,
all departments were transferred to the Shàngshū 尚書 (Department of State Affairs),
but these two departments alone remained,
known as the Wàibīng Shěng 外兵省 and Qíbīng Shěng 騎兵省.
According to the biography of Hé Shìkāi 和士開,
at that time, Yōng 邕 was entrusted with the Wàibīng 外兵,
and Bái Jiàn 白建 with the Qíbīng 騎兵.
The Emperor [Dì] held court [shìcháo] once every three or four days,
merely writing a few characters,
saying almost nothing,
and then retired shortly thereafter.
Cháng Càn 長粲 was
the son of Sēng Jìng 僧敬.
For Sēng Jìng 僧敬, see volume 158, Emperor Wǔdì 武帝 of Liáng 梁, Dàtóng 大同 seventh year.
The Emperor ordered Shìkāi to play bóshuò with Empress Hú.
Hé'nán Kāngxiànwáng Xiàoyú remonstrated, saying:
"The Empress is the mother of the empire;
how can she hold hands with a subject! "
Xiàoyú further said:
"Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì,
his father died unnaturally.
Ruì's father, Chēn,
was Bóhǎi Wáng Huān's younger brother.
He caused trouble in Huān's inner court,
and consequently died by staff.
For this reason, Ruì and Shìkāi jointly slandered him.
Shìkāi said Xiàoyú was extravagant and presumptuous.
Ruì said,
'East of the mountains, only the King of Hé'nán is heard of;
His Majesty is not heard of.'
The Qí ruler mostly resided in Jìnyáng,
which is west of the mountains.
The lands of Sī, Jì, Dìng, Yīn, Yíng, and Cāng
were all east of the mountains.
Xiàoyú secretly conversed with the imperial woman Ěrzhū.
According to Qí regulations,
the eighty-one imperial women
ranked equivalent to a principal fourth-grade official,
the 'imperial concubines' of old.
Xiàoyú's biography states: Ěrzhū served the Empress Dowager,
and Xiàoyú had previously had an affair with her.
(The Emperor) was greatly enraged.
On the day Gēngshēn,
he forced Xiàoyú to drink thirty-seven cups of wine.
Xiàoyú was corpulent,
his waist measured ten spans.
The Emperor ordered his attendants, Lóu Zǐyàn, to carry him out,

Upon reaching Xīhuámén,
he became agitated, threw himself into the water, and died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Tàiwèi and Lù Shàngshūshì.
Among the princes in the palace,
none dared to utter a sound,
only Héjiān Wáng Xiàowǎn cried loudly and departed.
Xiàowǎn was
Xiàoyú's younger brother.

Duke of Yángshān Commandery.

Liáng established Yángshān Commandery.

On the day Xīnwèi,

21st year, on the day Bǐngxū,
the Zhōu ruler arrived at Tóngzhōu.
22nd year, initially,
the Zhōu people wanted to ally with the Tūjué Mùgǎn Kèhán to attack Qí,
promising to take his daughter as Empress,
and sent Yùbó Dàfū Yáng Jiàn.
Táng Liùdiǎn states: The Northern Zhōu Tiānguān newly established two Yùbó Zhōngdàfū.
When the Son of Heaven went out or entered, they attended at his left and right.
During great sacrifices, they offered towels for washing.
Emperor Wǔ changed Yùbó to Nàyán,
which was probably the office of Shìzhōng.
At the end of Emperor Xuān's reign,
another Shìzhōng was separately established as an honorary official.
Zuǒ Wǔbó was
probably a guard official;
see note later.
The Qí people, hearing of this, were afraid,
and also sent envoys to seek marriage with the Tūjué,
bestowing very generous bribes.
Mùgǎn, greedy for Qí's heavy gifts,
intended to seize Jiàn and others and send them to Qí.
Jiàn, aware of this,
reproached Mùgǎn, saying:
"Your Great Ancestor once fostered good neighborly relations with the Kèhán.
Several thousand Rúrú tribesmen came to surrender,
and the Great Ancestor handed them all over to the Kèhán's envoy
to please the Kèhán.
The event is recorded in volume 166, Liáng Jìngdì Shàotài 1st year.
Rúrú,
pronounced Rén-yǎn.
Jiàng,
pronounced Hù-jiāng.
Are you not ashamed before the spirits? "
Mùgǎn looked distressed for a long time, then said:
"Your words are true.
My decision is made.
We shall jointly pacify the eastern bandits,
and then I will send my daughter. "
Jiàn and the others returned with their report.
A textual comparison notes: Diǎnlüè places this in Bǎodìng 2nd year.
According to Wáng Qìng's biography,
that year was when the campaign to invade Bìng began.
Hence, it is placed here.
The high officials requested to dispatch 100,000 men to attack Qí.
Zhùguó Yáng Zhōng alone believed that 10,000 cavalry would be sufficient.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Zhōng was sent with 10,000 infantry and cavalry,
to attack Qí from the northern route with the Tūjué.
Dàjiāngjūn Dáxī Wǔ was also sent to lead 30,000 infantry and cavalry
from the southern route, emerging at Píngyáng,

23rd year, winter,
11th month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
Zhāng Zhāodá greatly defeated Zhōu Dí.
Dí escaped and hid in the mountains and valleys.
The people mutually concealed him;
even under threat of execution,
none would speak.
24th year, 12th month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Zhōu ruler returned to Cháng'ān.
Returned from Lǒngshàng.
25th year, on the day Bǐngshēn,
a general amnesty was issued.

crossed the ridge,
pressed towards Jiàn'ān,
to suppress Chén Bǎoyìng.
An edict appointed Yízhōu Cìshǐ Yú Xiàoqǐng.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán of Liáng,
the land of Yízhōu had already fallen to Zhōu.
Chén merely appointed Yú Xiàoqǐng to remotely hold the title of Yízhōu Cìshǐ.
27th year, that year,
the first sacrifice to Shǐxīng Zhāolièwáng was held in Jiànkāng,

The Emperor succeeded Gāozǔ, and had his son Bómào conduct the sacrifice to Shǐxīng Zhāolièwáng.
Now, for the first time, sacrifices were offered to him with imperial rites,
which was improper.
28th year, Zhōu Yáng Zhōng captured over twenty Qí cities.
The Qí people defended the narrow passes of Xínglǐng.
Táng records: Yànmén County, Dàizhōu, has Dōngxíng Pass and Xīxíng Pass.
Xíng,
pronounced xíng.
Ài,
pronounced Wū-xiè.
The three Tūjué Kèhán—Mùgǎn, Dìtóu, and Bùlí—converged with 100,000 cavalry.
Mùgǎn divided his state into three parts: Mùgǎn's royal camp was at Dūjīnshān;
Dìtóu Kèhán commanded the east;
Bùlí Kèhán commanded the west.
Jué,
pronounced Jiǔ-wù.
Gǎn,
pronounced Gōng-dàn.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
they entered from Héngzhōu via three routes simultaneously.
At that time, heavy snow fell for several tens of days,
covering over a thousand li north and south,
with several feet of snow on flat ground.
The Qí ruler hastened from Yè, doubling his speed to meet them.
On the day Wùwǔ,
he arrived at Jìnyáng.
Húlǜ Guāng led 30,000 infantry
and camped at Píngyáng.
To resist Dáxī Wǔ's army.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the Zhōu army and Tūjué pressed towards Jìnyáng.
The Qí ruler, fearing their strength, dressed in military attire and led his palace women, intending to flee east.
Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì and Héjiān Wáng Xiàowǎn intercepted his horse and remonstrated.
Xiàowǎn requested that the deployment be entrusted to Ruì,
promising strict order.
The Emperor agreed,
ordering that all movements of the six armies follow Ruì's instructions,
and appointed Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Sháo to take overall command.
The deployment was entrusted to Ruì, but Duàn Sháo oversaw the entire matter.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Gēngshēn, which was the first day of the month,
the Lord of Qí ascended the north city wall,
which was the north city wall of Jìnyáng.
The Tujue blamed the Zhou people, saying:
"You said Qí was in chaos,
and so we came to attack it.
But the Qí people also have iron in their eyes;
how can we withstand them?!"
The Zhou people used infantry as their vanguard,
descending from Xīshān to about two li from the city.
All the generals wanted to meet and attack them,
but Duàn Sháo said:
"The strength and momentum of infantry
are naturally limited.
Now that the accumulated snow is thick,
a counter-attack is not convenient.
It is better to array our forces and wait for them.
They will be exhausted while we are fresh;
we are certain to defeat them."
When they arrived,
Qí sent out all its elite troops with drums and shouts.
The Tujue were startled and dismayed,
and withdrew up Xīshān.
They refused to fight,
and the Zhou army was greatly defeated and returned.
The Tujue led their troops out of the pass,
allowing their soldiers to plunder extensively.
From Jìnyáng northward for over seven hundred li,
no people or animals were left.
This means seven hundred li north of Jìnyáng.
畜 (chù)
is read xǔjiù (許救).
They dared not approach.
When the Tujue returned to Jínglǐng,
it was frozen and slippery,
so they laid out felt to cross.
The Hu horses were cold and thin,
with no hair below their knees.
By the time they reached the Great Wall,
most of the horses had died,
and they cut their spears short to use as staffs to return.
Dáxī Wǔ reached Píngyáng,
not yet knowing that Zhōng (referring to Yúwén Zhōng, not to be confused with a character named Zhōng elsewhere) had retreated.
HúLǜ Guāng sent him a letter saying:
"The swan has already soared into the vast sky,
but the fowler still gazes at the marsh."
Hàn's Sīmǎ Xiāngrú in his 'Difficulty with the Elder of Shǔ' said: "The fire-bird has already soared into the vast sky,
but the fowler still gazes at the reedy marsh."
沮 (jù)
is read jiāngyù (將預).
He also returned.
Guāng pursued them,
entered Zhou territory,
captured over two thousand people, and returned.
Guāng met the Emperor in Jìnyáng.
The Emperor, having just suffered a great invasion,
embraced Guāng's head and wept.
Rènchéng Wáng Xié stepped forward and said:
"Why such distress!"
And so he stopped.
Originally,
during the reign of Qí Xiǎnzǔ,
the Zhou people were always afraid of Qí troops crossing west,
and every winter month,
they guarded the river and broke the ice.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
favored courtiers were in power,
and court governance gradually became chaotic.
The Qí people broke the ice to prepare against the threat of Zhou troops.
HúLǜ Guāng worried about this,
saying:
"The state has always had the ambition to annex Guān and Lǒng,
but now it has come to this,
and they only indulge in music and women's beauty!"
2 On the day Xīnsì,
the Emperor offered sacrifices to the southern suburbs.
3 In the second month,
on the day Gēngyín, which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 Originally,
Qí Xiǎnzǔ ordered the relevant officials to revise and finalize the Wèi Línzhǐ Law Code as the Qí Law Code.
See the record in "One Hundred and Sixty-Three Chapters" of the second year of Dàbǎo of Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì.
At that time, state affairs were numerous and complex,
and judgments rarely followed the letter of the law.
It was customarily called
"acting by changing the law."
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he desired to reform these abuses,
and so he supervised those who compiled the laws and decrees.
By this time, it was completed,
with twelve chapters of law.
The "Wǔdài Zhì" (History of the Five Dynasties) states: The Qí Law Code has twelve chapters: 1. Name and precedents,
2. Prohibitions and guards,
3. Marriage and households,
4. Taxation and labor,
5. Disobeying regulations,
6. Fraud and deception,
7. Fighting and litigation,
8. Robbery and theft,
9. Arrests and judgments,
10. Damage and destruction,
11. Agriculture and animal husbandry,
12. Miscellaneous laws.
There were five types of penalties: 1. Death,
the most severe being dismemberment by chariots,
next beheading,
next decapitation,
next strangulation;
2. Exile,
sent to the frontier as soldiers;
3. Imprisonment,
from five years to one year;
4. Whipping,
from one hundred to forty strokes;
5. Caning,
from thirty to ten strokes;
totaling fifteen grades.
Death has four grades,
exile one,
imprisonment five grades,
whipping five grades,
caning three grades,
totaling eighteen grades.
Today it says "totaling fifteen grades,"
and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows the text
"in total there were fifteen grades"
from the "Wǔdài Zhì."
梟 (xiāo)
is read jiānyáo (堅堯).
Officials, and the old, young, eunuchs, and mentally impaired
(the old, young, eunuchs, and mentally impaired, along with officials outside the exile category, could all ransom their penalties).
Zhèng Xuán said: "Eunuchs
are those whose essence and qi are closed and stored."
"Mentally impaired" (chī)
means not intelligent.
All paid redemption in silk instead of gold.
In the third month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
it was promulgated and put into effect,
and a general amnesty was granted.
Previous crimes were pardoned;
thereafter, those who committed offenses
would all be dealt with according to the laws and decrees.
It was also decreed that children of official families should regularly study and practice it.
"Official families" (shìmén)
refers to families with members in official positions.
It was also decreed that commoners at eighteen should receive land and pay rent and tribute;
at twenty, serve as soldiers;
at sixty, be exempt from corvée labor;
at sixty-six, return their land
and be exempt from rent and tribute.
A single adult male received eighty mu of "exposed land."
Dù Yòu said: "Land not planted with trees
is called exposed land."
調 (diào)
is read lìdiào (力弔);
the same applies to the tribute of low-grade adult males and ox tribute.
Slaves and bondservants were treated according to free people,
meaning slaves and bondservants received land according to the acreage for free people.
According to the "Wǔdài Zhì,"
a working ox received sixty mu of land,
limited to four years.
A working ox
is an ox capable of plowing;
those who herded cattle could receive its land.
Eight liang of cotton,
two shi of cultivation rent,
and five dou of righteous rent;
for slaves and bondservants, half that of free people;
for slaves and bondservants,
the government regularly employed their labor,
so their tribute was half that of free people.
One dou of cultivation rent,
and five sheng of righteous rent.
Cultivation rent was sent to the central administration,
and righteous rent was paid to the commandery to prepare for floods and droughts.
5 On the day Jǐsì,
Qí imperial palace thieves, led by Tián Zǐlǐ and several others,
together kidnapped the Grand Tutor, Péngchéng Jǐngsī Wáng Yóu, to be their leader.
Falsely claiming to be envoys,
they went directly to Yóu's residence,
entered the inner chamber,
claimed to have an imperial edict,
pulled Yóu onto a horse,
threatened him with drawn blades,
and tried to lead him to the South Palace.
Yóu shouted loudly and refused to comply,
so the thieves killed him.
6 On the day *gēngchén*,
Zhōu started ordering all officials to hold *hù* (ritual tablets).
The *Jì Yùzǎo* says: "Historians advance with ivory *hù*,
writing down their thoughts in response to commands."
The commentary explains: "These are thoughts and considerations
that are about to be reported to the sovereign.
'Response' [duì]
means responding to the sovereign.
'Command' [mìng]
means the command received.
Writing it on the *hù*
is to prevent forgetting."
It also says: "Anyone giving instructions or making gestures before the sovereign uses a *hù*;
anyone receiving commands before the sovereign uses a *hù*.
The *hù*
is used for all purposes,
hence it is adorned."
The *hù* is two *chǐ* and six *cùn* long,
three *cùn* wide in the middle,
tapering by one-sixth.
Yīng Shào said: "Formerly, when Jīng Kē pursued the Qín King,
afterward, the palace attendants carried daggers to guard against unforeseen events;
from then on, all attending officials carried knives and swords.
Gāozǔ 'ceased military pursuits and cultivated culture' (yǎnwǔ xiūwén),
and first instituted hand tablets to replace them."
The *Suí Zhì* says: "Since the Middle Ages,
only the Eight Ministers of the Department of State Affairs (Bāzuò Shàngshū) held *hù*.
The *hù*
had a white brush attached to its head
and was wrapped in a purple bag.
Other dukes and ministers [gōngqīng]
merely held hand tablets,
which were called 'writing *hù*' (bǐhù),
presumably for recording events and receiving words.
After the Western Wèi dynasty,
ivory was commonly used;
for officials of the fifth rank and below,
bamboo or wood was commonly used."
The *Ěryǎ Shìmíng* says: "A *hù*
means 'sudden' (hū),
when the sovereign issues an order or a matter is reported,
it is written on it to prevent sudden forgetting."
The *Táng Huìyào* says: "For *hù*,
the old system was: for officials of the third rank and above,
the front was curved and the back straight;
for officials of the fifth rank and above,
the front was curved and the back bent.
Since the Wǔdé period,
they were uniformly round at the top and square at the bottom."
In the eighth year of Kāiyuán,
for all *hù*: for officials of the third rank and above,
the front was bent and the back straight;
for officials of the fifth rank and above,
the front was bent and the back curved;
all used ivory.
For officials of the ninth rank and above,
bamboo or wood could be used,
with the top curved and the bottom square.
Men of the rank of *nán* and above were permitted to hold *hù* according to their rank and title.
Officials with temporary appointments (jiǎbǎn guān) also followed this rule.
7 Qí appointed Húliù Guāng as *Sītú*,
and Wǔxīng Wáng Pǔ as Grand Minister of State and Left Executive (Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè).
Pǔ was
the nephew of Guī Yàn.
On the day *jiǎshēn*,

8 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day *xīnmǎo*,
the Qí ruler sent the Concurrent Cavalier Regular Attendant (Jiān Sànqí Chángshì) Huángfǔ Liàng to establish friendly relations.
*Sàn*
is pronounced *sìdàn*.
*Qí*

In the fifth month,
on the day *rénxū*,
Xián, the son of Shìzōng, was enfeoffed as Bì Gōng.
11On the day *jiǎzǐ*,
the Qí ruler returned to Yè.
He returned from Jìnyáng.

13On the day *rénchén*,
the Qí ruler went to Jìnyáng.
14Zhōu appointed the Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) Dáxī Wǔ as Administrator of Tóngzhōu (Tóngzhōu Cìshǐ).
15In the sixth month,
the Qí ruler killed Lèlíng Wáng Bǎinián.
At that time, a white rainbow haloed the sun twice,
and it crossed but did not reach across,
and a red star appeared.
The Qí ruler wanted to use Bǎinián to suppress these omens.
It happened that Jiǎ Dézhòu, a man from Bólíng, taught Bǎinián to write,
and Bǎinián had once written several imperial edict characters.
Dézhòu sealed them and presented them to the throne.
The Emperor became enraged
and sent for Bǎinián.
Bǎinián knew he could not escape,
so he cut off a jade *jué* from his belt and left it for his wife, Lady Húliù.
He met the Emperor in the Liángfēng Hall.
The Emperor made Bǎinián write imperial edict characters
and verified that they were similar to those presented by Dézhòu.
He ordered his attendants to beat him indiscriminately,
and also commanded that he be dragged around the hall, walking and being beaten.
Wherever he passed, blood covered the ground.
When his breath was about to cease,
he was then decapitated
and thrown into a pond.
The pond water turned completely red.
His wife, grasping the *jué*, wailed and refused to eat,
and after more than a month, she also died.
The *jué* was still in her hand,
and her fist could not be opened.
Her father, Guāng, personally pried it open,
and only then did it open.
16On the day *gēngyín*,
Zhōu changed the *Yùbó* to *Nàyán*.
17Originally,
when Zhōu Tàizǔ was with Hèbá Yuè in Guānzhōng,
he sent someone to welcome Jìn Gōng Hù from Jìnyáng.
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng of Liáng Wǔdì,
Yǔwén Tài followed Hèbá Yuè into Guān.
According to Hù's reply to his mother's letter, it said:
"It has been thirty-five years
since I left your side."
Counting backward,
this year was exactly that year.
The Zhōu ruler's maternal aunt [gū]
was Yǔwén Tài's younger sister.
The Zhōngshān Palace
was the former palace of the Mùróng family.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
it had been used as a secondary palace.
Secret envoys were sent into Qí to seek them,
but no news was heard.
Qí sent envoys to Yùbì
to request opening up border markets for trade.
Hù wanted to inquire about his mother and aunt,
so he sent the Minor Grand Master of Cavalry (Sīmǎ Xià Dàfū) Yǐn Zhèng to Yùbì
to speak with them.
The Minor Grand Master of Cavalry [Sīmǎ Xià Dàfū]
was the position of Military Cavalry Commander (Jūnsīmǎ).
Wèi Xiàokuān, the Administrator of Xūnzhōu (Xūnzhōu Cìshǐ), captured people from Guāndōng,
then released them,
and through them sent a letter
expressing the intention of the Western court to establish good relations.
At this time,
because the Zhōu people had not succeeded in their previous attack on Jìnyáng,
they planned to invade Qí again with the Tujue.
The Qí ruler heard of this and
was greatly afraid,
so he agreed to send Hù's mother back west,
and also requested to establish good relations,
first sending his aunt back.
18In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the new moon *dīnghài*,
there was a solar eclipse.
19Zhōu sent Grand Pillar of State (Zhùguó) Yáng Zhōng
to join the Tujue in attacking Qí.
They reached the North River (Běihé) and returned.
The *Shuǐjīng* says: "The River flows east past the south of the old city of Wòyě,
then bends north and flows out as the South River (Nánhé).
The River then flows north,
winding west and overflowing east of the old city of Yǔhún County,
then bends east to flow as the North River (Běihé),
flowing east past the south of Gāoquē."
*Huán*
is pronounced *xuān*,
also pronounced as written.
The 20th day of the *wùzǐ* year (of the sexagenary cycle)
Zhōu appointed Qí Gōng Xiàn (齊公憲) as the Administrator of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Yǔwén Guì (宇文貴) was made Grand Minister of Instruction (Dà Sītú, 大司徒).
In the ninth month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
Wèi Gōng Zhí (衞公直) was appointed Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng, 大司空).
The meritorious deeds of those who assisted in the founding of the dynasty were posthumously recorded,
and Lǐ Bǐng (李昞), Grand Master of Cavalry (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, 開府儀同三司) and Duke of Lǒngxī (隴西公), was enfeoffed as the Duke of Táng (唐公).
This was to acknowledge the meritorious service of Bǐng's father, Hǔ (虎), in assisting the founding of the dynasty.
When the Lǐ (李) clan later obtained the empire,
the dynastic title was Táng (唐),
which originated from this.
Bǐng (昞)
is pronounced *bǐng*.
The Zhōu (周) office of the Grand Master of Charioteering (Dà Yù Zhōng Dàfū, 大馭中大夫)
was in charge of driving the jade chariot for sacrifices and for "breaking the ruts" (fàn bà, 犯軷),
belonging to the Department of Summer Officials (Xiàguān, 夏官).
Yuè (樂)
is pronounced *luò*.
Hǔ (虎) was the son of Yuè (樂);
Fèng (鳳)
was the son of Huì (惠).
Lǐ Hǔ (李虎) was first mentioned in Volume 156, in the sixth year of Dàtōng (大通) during the reign of Liáng Wǔdì (梁武帝).
Gēnhuì (若干惠) was mentioned in Volume 158, in the ninth year of Dàtóng (大同).
The 21st day of the *yǐchǒu* year,
the Qí (齊) sovereign enfeoffed his son Chuò (綽) as the Prince of Nányáng (南陽王),
and Yǎn (儼) as the Prince of Dōngpíng (東平王).
Yǎn (儼)
was the younger brother of the Crown Prince by the same mother.
The 22nd day. The Tūjué (突厥) raided Yōuzhōu (幽州) in Qí (齊),
with a force of over 100,000 men.
They entered the Great Wall,
plundered extensively, and then returned.
The 23rd day. When the Zhōu (周) imperial aunt returned (from Qí),
the Qí (齊) sovereign sent someone to write a letter for Hù's (護) mother, the Duke of Jìn (晉公),
recounting several incidents from Hù's childhood,
and also sent the brocade robe she had worn,
as proof of her identity.
It also said:
"Our clan has had a thousand-year fortune,
and has received the great benevolence of Qí (齊).
They have shown compassion for my old age and extended kindness,
allowing me to meet you.
Animals and plants,
mothers and children rely on each other.
What sin have I committed
to be separated from you?
What blessing do I now have
to hope to see you again?
Speaking of this joy and sorrow, I feel as if I have died and come back to life.
All things in the world
can be sought and obtained,
but for a mother and son in different countries,
where can one seek such a reunion?
Even if you become as noble as a king or duke,
and as rich as mountains and seas,
with an old mother
eighty years of age,
wandering thousands of *lǐ*,
facing death at any moment,
unable to see her even for a fleeting morning.
(*Zhàn* [蹔]
is the same as *zàn* [暫].)
If I am cold, I cannot have your clothes;
if I am hungry, I cannot have your food.
Though you may reach the pinnacle of glory and prosperity,
shining brightly in the world,
what good is it to me?
Before today,
you could not offer your filial support,
so there is no point in discussing what has passed.
From today onwards,
my remaining life
is entirely dependent on you.
Standing under heaven and treading on earth,
there are spirits and deities in between.
Do not say they are obscure
and thus deceive or slight them!"
When Hù (護) received the letter,
he was overcome with sorrow.
He wrote back, saying:
"The empire has fragmented,
and we have encountered disaster.
I have been separated from your presence
for thirty-five years.
(The pronunciation of *lí* [離]
is *lìzhì fān* [力智翻].)
Everyone knows of mothers and sons,
but who is like Sàbǎo (薩保)?
(Hù's [護]
courtesy name was Sàbǎo [薩保].
The pronunciation of *Sà* [薩]
is *sānggě fān* [桑葛翻].)
The son is a duke or marquis,
while the mother is a captive or slave.
In summer, I do not see my mother's summer;
in winter, I do not see my mother's winter.
I do not know if you have clothes,
nor if you are hungry or full.
It is as if you are beyond heaven and earth,
with no way to hear from you even for a moment.
Bearing this deep resentment and hardship,
throughout this life,
if there is knowledge after death,
I hope to see you in the netherworld!
I did not expect the Qí (齊) court to lift its net,
bestowing gracious words,
and permitting Māduō (摩敦) and Sìgū (四姑)
to be released with compassion.
(Hù's [護] brothers
called their mother 'Āmāduō' [阿摩敦].
Sìgū [四姑] was the aunt of the Zhōu [周] sovereign,
the fourth sister.)
(*Cháo* [朝]
is pronounced *zhíyáo fān*;
same below.)
My soul and spirits flew,
(The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* [左傳] states: Zhèng Zǐchǎn [鄭子產] said:
'When a person first begins to transform, it is called *pò* [魄].
Once the *pò* is born,
the *yáng* aspect is called *hún* [魂].
When one uses many essences, the *hún* and *pò* become strong,
hence there are *jīngshuǎng* [精爽],
leading to divine intelligence.')
I could not control myself.
The immense grace of the Qí (齊) court
has already touched me.
For those with family and state,
trustworthiness and righteousness are fundamental.
I humbly anticipate the day of your arrival,
which must be imminent.
Once I am granted to see your compassionate face,
my lifelong wish will be fulfilled forever.
To bring the dead back to life and make flesh grow on bones,
('Bringing the dead back to life' [生死],
means to make the deceased live again;
'making flesh grow on bones' [肉骨],
means to make flesh grow on withered bones.)
even bearing mountains and carrying peaks
would not be enough to repay this immense favor."
The Qí (齊) people detained Hù's (護) mother
and had her write another letter to Hù (護),
inviting Hù (護) to respond again,
with correspondence going back and forth repeatedly.
At that time, Duàn Sháo (段韶) was resisting the Tūjué (突厥) army at the frontier.
The Qí (齊) sovereign sent the Palace Attendant (Huángmén, 黃門) Xú Shìróng (徐世榮) with post-horses to deliver the Zhōu (周) letter and question Sháo (韶).
Sháo (韶) responded:
"The Zhōu (周) people are fickle
and fundamentally without trustworthiness or righteousness.
Their actions during the battle of Jìnyáng (晉陽)
clearly show this.
Hù (護) outwardly acts as Prime Minister,
but in reality, he is the ruler.
Since he is asking for peace on behalf of his mother,
he should send an envoy.
If we merely send his mother based on his letter,
I fear it will show weakness.
It is better to provisionally agree externally
and wait until the peace and alliance are firm
before sending her; it will not be too late then."
The Qí (齊) sovereign did not listen
and immediately sent her.
Hù's (護) mother arrived in Cháng'ān (長安),
but before her seat was warm,
the army for Luòyáng (洛陽) had already departed,
exactly as Duàn Sháo (段韶) had predicted.
When the Yán (閻) clan arrived in Zhōu (周),
the entire court celebrated,
and the Zhōu (周) sovereign issued a great amnesty for it.
All her provisions and offerings
were made with the utmost luxury and splendor.
During the four seasonal sacrifices (fúlā, 伏臘),
the Zhōu (周) sovereign would lead his relatives
in family rituals,
raising cups to wish her longevity.
The 24th day. After returning from Yōuzhōu (幽州), the Tūjué (突厥)
remained encamped north of the frontier.
They gathered troops from various tribes again
and sent an envoy to inform Zhōu (周)
that they wished to attack Qí (齊) together as previously agreed.
In the intercalary month,
on the *yǐsì* day,
the Tūjué (突厥) raided Yōuzhōu (幽州) in Qí (齊).
Jìn Gōng Hù 晉公護 had just recovered his mother,
and did not wish to attack Qí 齊;
fearing to break his pact with the Tūjué 突厥,
and thereby create trouble on the border,
he had no choice.
He conscripted twenty-four armies and the Qin 秦, Lǒng 隴, Bā 巴, and Shǔ 蜀 troops scattered among the Left and Right Wings,
twenty-four armies [in total].
These were the garrison troops of the Guānzhōng 關中 region, commanded by the six Zhùguó 柱國 and twelve Dà Jiāngjūn 大將軍.
Āndìng Gōng Tài 安定公泰 assisted Wèi 魏;
the Left and Right Wings each had twelve armies,
all under the command of the chancellor's office.
The Left and Right Wings [were]
the imperial guards,
also comprising the Qin 秦, Lǒng 隴, Bā 巴, and Shǔ 蜀 troops
scattered among the Left and Right Wings.
Sǎn 散,
pronounced as "sī dān" [in Old Chinese].
In all, two
hundred thousand men.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the jiǎzǐ 甲子 day,
the Zhōu 周 ruler bestowed axes and battle-axes upon Hù 護 in the ancestral temple courtyard.
On the dīngmǎo 丁卯 day,
he personally comforted the troops at Shāyuàn 沙苑.
On the guǐyǒu 癸yǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
Hù's 護 troops reached Tóngguān 潼關.
He dispatched Zhùguó Yùchí Jǐong 尉遲迥 to lead a hundred thousand elite soldiers as the vanguard,
heading towards Luòyáng 洛陽.
Dà Jiāngjūn Quán Jǐngxuān 權景宣 led the troops from Shānnán 山南 towards Xuánhù 懸瓠.
Shānnán 山南 [refers to]
the troops from Jīng 荊 and Xiāng 襄.
Wèi 尉,
pronounced as "yū wù".
Shuài 帥,
read as "lǜ 率";
the same below.
Qù 趣,
pronounced as "qī yù".
25 Zhōu Dí 周迪 again emerged from Dōngxīng 東興.
Xuānchéng Tàishǒu Qián Sù 宣城太守錢肅, garrisoned at Dōngxīng 東興,
surrendered the city to Dí 迪.
Wúzhōu Cìshǐ Chén Xiáng 吳州刺史陳詳 led troops to attack them.
(According to the Wǔdài Zhì 五代志: Páoyáng Jùn 鄱陽郡,
Liáng 梁 established Wúzhōu 吳州;
Chén 陳 abolished Wúzhōu 吳州 of Páoyáng 鄱陽,
and established Wúzhōu 吳州 in Wújùn 吳郡.)
Jiāng 將,
pronounced as "jí liàng",
also pronounced as written,
meaning "to lead".
Dí's 迪 forces revived.
Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ Xīfēng Tuōhóu Zhōu Fū 南豫州刺史西豐脫侯周敷 led his detachment to attack them.
(According to the Shìfǎ 諡法,
there is no posthumous title "Tuō" 脫.
Perhaps because Zhōu Fū 周敷 died lightly and carelessly,
it was given as a posthumous title.
According to the biography of Zhōu Fū 周敷,
Dìngchuān 定川
is a county name.)
Dí 迪 deceived Fū 敷, saying:
"In the past, I worked diligently and with one heart with my younger brother.
(The event is recorded in volume 166, Liáng Jìngdì Tàipíng Yuánnián 梁敬帝太平元年.)
Gài 紿,
pronounced as "dàng hài".
Now I wish to admit my guilt and return to court.
Through my younger brother, I reveal my innermost feelings,
and first ask to personally join in an oath."
Fū 敷 agreed.
As he was ascending the altar,
he was killed by Dí 迪.
26 Chén Bǎo Yìng 陳寶應 occupied Jìn'ān 晉安 and Jiàn'ān 建安 prefectures.
He constructed palisades by land and water
to resist Zhāng Zhāodá 章昭達.
Zhāodá 昭達 fought with him,
but was unsuccessful.
He then occupied the upper reaches [of the river],
ordering his soldiers to fell trees and build rafts,
placing battering rams upon them.
Just then, heavy rain caused the river to swell.
Zhāodá 昭達 released the rafts to ram Bǎo Yìng's 寶應 water palisades,
completely destroying them.
He then sent out troops to attack Bǎo Yìng's 寶應 infantry.
As the battle was joined,
the Emperor dispatched General Yú Xiàokǐng 余孝頃, who arrived from the sea route.
(Last year, Xiàokǐng 孝頃 was sent to supervise the troops from Kuàijī 會稽 and other prefectures to jointly attack Chén Bǎo Yìng 陳寶應 from the eastern route.)
In the eleventh month,
on the jǐchǒu 己丑 day,
Bǎo Yìng 寶應 was utterly defeated and
fled to Púkǒu 莆口.
(Púkǒu 莆口
was in the territory of Pútián 莆田 County, Quánzhōu 泉州 in the Táng 唐 dynasty.
Pútián 莆田
is now the location of Xīnghuà Jūn 興化軍.
Yú Jì's 虞寄 biography writes
"Pútián 莆田".)
Pú 莆,
pronounced as "pú".
[Bǎo Yìng 寶應 said,] "If I had followed Lord Yú's 虞公 advice early,
I would not be in this situation today."
Zhāodá 昭達 pursued and captured him,
and also captured Líu Yì 留異 and his family and associates,
sending them to Jiànkāng 建康
where they were executed.
Yì's 異 son, Zhēnchén 貞臣, was spared due to having married a princess.
Bǎo Yìng's 寶應 retainers all died.
The Emperor heard that Yú Jì 虞寄 had often advised Bǎo Yìng 寶應,
and ordered Zhāodá 昭達 to respectfully send him to Jiànkāng 建康.
Upon meeting,
he comforted him, saying:
"Guǎn Níng 管寧 is unharmed."
(At the end of the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
Guǎn Níng 管寧 sojourned in Liáodōng 遼東,
refusing Gōngsūn Dù's 公孫度 titles and appointments,
and afterwards was able to return to his hometown.
Thus, Jì 寄 was compared to him.)
Láo 勞,
pronounced as "lì dào".
The Emperor's son, Bóxìn 伯信, was enfeoffed as Héngyáng Wáng 衡陽王,
to continue the sacrifices for Xiàn Wáng Chāng 獻王昌.
27 Zhōu Jìn Gōng Hù 周晉公護 advanced his camp to Hóngnóng 弘農.
Yù
chí Jǐong 遲迥 besieged Luòyáng 洛陽. Yōngzhōu Mù Qí Gōng Xiàn 雍州牧齊公憲, Tóngzhōu Cìshǐ Dáxī Wǔ 同州刺史達奚武, and Jìngzhōu Zǒngguǎn Wáng Xióng 涇州總管王雄 camped at Mángshān 邙山.
28 On the wùxū 戊戌 day,
the Qí 齊 ruler dispatched concurrently-serving Sànqí Chángshì Líu Tì 兼散騎常侍劉逖 to come and offer tribute.
Sàn 散,
pronounced as "sī dān".
Qí 騎,
pronounced as "qí jì".
29 Initially,
Zhōu Yáng Biāo 周楊檦 was Shàozhōu Cìshǐ 邵州刺史.
(According to Wǔdài Zhì 五代志, Jiàngjùn Yuánxiàn 絳郡垣縣,
Later Wèi 後魏 established Shàojùn 邵郡 and Báishuǐ Xiàn 白水縣.
Later Zhōu 後周 established Shàozhōu 邵州,
changing Báishuǐ 白水 to Bóchéng 亳城.
Suí 隋 abolished the prefecture and commandery,
changing Bóchéng 亳城 to Yuánxiàn 垣縣.)
He fought with Qí 齊 multiple times,
and was never defeated,
thus he became arrogant.
After exiting Zhǐguān 軹關,
he alone led his troops deep into enemy territory,
and failed to take precautions.
On the jiǎchén 甲辰 day,
Qí Tàiwèi Líu Ruì 齊太尉婁叡 suddenly arrived with troops,
greatly defeating Biāo's 檦 army.
Biāo 檦 then surrendered to Qí 齊.
Quán Jǐngxuān 權景宣 besieged Xuánhù 懸瓠.
In the twelfth month,
Qí Yùzhōu Dào Xíngtái Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Tàiyuán Wáng Shìlíang 齊豫州道行臺．豫州刺史太原王士良 and Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Shìyí 永州刺史蕭世怡 both surrendered their cities to him.
Jǐngxuān 景宣 made Kāifǔ Guō Yàn 開府郭彥 defend Yùzhōu 豫州,
and Xiè Chè 謝徹 defend Yǒngzhōu 永州.
(According to Wǔdài Zhì 五代志: Rǔnán Jùn Chéngyáng Xiàn 汝南郡城陽縣,
formerly Chǔzhōu 楚州 was established,
then Later Qí 後齊 called it Yǒngzhōu 永州.)
The Zhōu 周 people built earthen mounds and dug tunnels to attack Luòyáng 洛陽,
but failed to take it for thirty days.
Jìn Gōng Hù 晉公護 ordered his generals to dig trenches to cut off the Héyáng 河陽 road,
blocking the Qí 齊 relief forces,
and then jointly attack Luòyáng 洛陽.
The generals believed that the Qí 齊 troops would certainly not dare to come out,
and would only send out scouts.
Qí 齊 dispatched Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng 蘭陵王長恭 and Dà Jiāngjūn Húlǜ Guāng 大將軍斛律光 to relieve Luòyáng 洛陽.
Fearing the strength of the Zhōu 周 army,
they did not dare to advance.
The Qí 齊 ruler summoned Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Sháo 幷州刺史段韶,
and said:
"Luòyáng 洛陽 is in dire straits.
Now I wish to send you, Prince, to relieve it.
The Tūjué 突厥 are in the north,
and still require defense and control.
What should be done?"
He replied:
"The northern barbarians encroaching on the border
are like a minor skin ailment.
Now, our western neighbor's peering and pressing
is a disease of the heart and stomach.
I request to follow the imperial decree and go south."
The Qí 齊 ruler said:
"My thoughts are also thus."
He then ordered Sháo 韶 to lead a thousand elite cavalry from Jìnyáng 晉陽.
On the dīngsì 丁巳 day,
the Qí 齊 ruler also went from Jìnyáng 晉陽 to Luòyáng 洛陽.
30 On the jǐwèi 己未 day,
Qí Tàizǎi Píngyuán Jìngyì Wáng Yān 齊太宰平原靖翼王淹 passed away.
31 Duàn Sháo (段韶) marched from Jìnyáng (晉陽).
After five days, he crossed the Yellow River.
It happened to be continuously overcast and foggy for several days.
On the day of Rénxū (壬戌),
Sháo (韶) arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽).
He led three hundred cavalry from his command
and, with the generals, ascended Mángbǎn (邙阪)
to observe the disposition of the Zhōu (周) army.
Mángbǎn (邙阪)
is the slope of Běimáng (北邙).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced as 'lǜ' (率).
When he encountered the Zhōu (周) army,
Sháo (韶) immediately galloped to alert the various camps,
gathered his cavalry,
and formed ranks to await them.
Sháo (韶) commanded the left army,
Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng (蘭陵王長恭) the central army,
and Húlǜ Guāng (斛律光) the right army.
The Zhōu (周) people did not expect their arrival
and were all terrified.
Sháo (韶) called out to the Zhōu (周) people from a distance:
"You Yǔwén Hù (宇文護) have just regained your mother,
why do you hastily come to commit aggression?"
The Zhōu (周) people replied:
"Heaven sent us here,
what is there to ask!"
Sháo (韶) said:
"The way of Heaven rewards good and punishes evil;
it must have sent you here to die!"
The Zhōu (周) people, with their infantry in front,
went up the mountain to meet the attack.
They ascended Běimáng (北邙) to intercept and fight the Qí (齊) troops.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced 'cháng'.
Waiting until their strength was exhausted,
they then dismounted to attack them.
The Zhōu (周) army was utterly defeated,
disintegrating instantly like shattered tiles.
A great number of them fell into ravines and valleys, dying.
Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng (蘭陵王長恭) with five hundred cavalry charged into the Zhōu (周) army,
and reached the foot of Jīnyǒngchéng (金墉城).
The people on the city wall did not recognize him.
Chánggōng (長恭) removed his helmet to show his face,
and only then did they send crossbowmen down to rescue him.
The Zhōu (周) troops who were at the foot of the city also lifted their siege and fled,
abandoning their camps and tents.
From Mángshān (邙山) to Gǔshuǐ (穀水),
Shuǐjīng (水經) says: Gǔshuǐ (穀水) originates from Gǔyánggǔ (穀陽谷) in Fánzhǒnglín (墦塚林), Miǎnchí (澠池) County, Hóngnóng (弘農);
it flows northeast past the north of Gǔchéng (穀城) County,
then east past the north of Hénán (河南) County,
and southeast into the Luò (洛) River.
Military supplies and equipment
filled the plains and wetlands.
Only Qí Gōng Xiàn (齊公憲), Dáxī Wǔ (達奚武), and Yōngzhōng Gōng Wáng Xióng (庸忠公王雄) remained behind,
rallying their troops to resist the battle.
Shìfǎ (諡法) says: Risking one's life to serve the superior is 'loyal' (忠).
Wáng Xióng (王雄) galloped his horse and charged Húlǜ Guāng's (斛律光) formation.
Guāng (光) retreated and fled,
and Xióng (雄) pursued him.
Guāng's (光) attendants all dispersed,
leaving only one slave and one arrow.
Xióng (雄), pressing his spear, was more than ten feet from Guāng (光).
He said to Guāng (光):
"I spare you and will not kill you;
I shall take you alive to see the Son of Heaven."
Guāng (光) shot Xióng (雄), hitting him in the forehead.
Xióng (雄) embraced his horse and rode off,
dying upon reaching his camp.
The army became even more fearful.
Qí Gōng Xiàn (齊公憲) comforted and encouraged the troops,
and their morale slightly stabilized.
By night,
he collected the troops.
Xiàn (憲) wanted to wait until dawn to fight again.
Dáxī Wǔ (達奚武) said:
"The Luòyáng (洛陽) army has scattered,
people are shocked and terrified.
If we do not return quickly tonight,
tomorrow we will not be able to.
I have been in the army for a long time
and have fully observed the situation;
you are young and inexperienced,
how can you abandon these few camps of soldiers to the tiger's mouth!"
So, they returned.
Quán Jǐngxuān (權景宣) also abandoned Yùzhōu (豫州) and fled.
On the day of Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
the Qí (齊) ruler arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽).
On the day of Jǐsì (己巳),
Duàn Sháo (段韶) was appointed Tàizǎi (太宰),
Húlǜ Guāng (斛律光) Tàiwèi (太尉),
and Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng (蘭陵王長恭) Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
These were rewards for their victorious achievements.
On the day of Rénshēn (壬申),
the Qí (齊) ruler went to Hǔláo (虎牢),
then from Huátái (滑臺) to Líyáng (黎陽),
and on the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
arrived at Yè (鄴).
Yáng Zhōng (楊忠) led his troops out to Wòyě (沃野)
to meet the Tujue.
Military provisions were insufficient,
and the various armies were worried,
with no solution in sight.
Zhōng (忠) then lured the Qīhú (稽胡) chieftains, who were all present,
(these Qīhú (稽胡) were of the same stock as the Líshí Qīhú (離石稽胡),
scattered between Yín (銀) and Xià (夏)),
Yòu (誘)
is pronounced 'yǒu'.
Qiú (酋)
is pronounced 'cíqiū'.
Zhǎng (長)
is pronounced 'zhíliǎng'.
Zuò (坐)
is pronounced 'cúwò'.
and said:
"The Grand Minister Yǔwén Hù (宇文護) has already pacified Luòyáng (洛陽),
and intends to jointly attack the disobedient Qīhú (稽胡) with the Tujue."
All those present were frightened.
Zhōng (忠) comforted and dismissed them.
Thereupon, the various Hú (胡) tribes led each other to deliver provisions,
and military supplies accumulated.
When the Zhōu (周) army concluded its campaign and returned,
Zhōng (忠) also returned.
Jìn Gōng Hù (晉公護) originally had no great military strategy.
This expedition
was also not his original intention,
hence it yielded no achievements.
He bowed his head with the generals and apologized for his faults.
The Zhōu (周) ruler comforted them and dismissed them.
32 In this year,
Shāndōng (山東) of Qí (齊) experienced great floods,
and countless people died of starvation.
33 Dàngchāng Wáng Liáng Mídìng (宕昌王梁彌定) repeatedly raided the Zhōu (周) borders.
Zhōu (周) Grand General Tián Hóng (田弘) attacked and exterminated him,
establishing Dàngzhōu (宕州) in his territory.
Dàngzhōu (宕州) is one thousand six hundred and fifty-six *lǐ* (里) southwest of Cháng'ān (長安).
Dàng (宕)
is pronounced 'tú làng'.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day of Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
Qí (齊) appointed Rènchéng Wáng Jiē (任城王湝) as Dàsīmǎ (大司馬).
2 The Qí (齊) ruler went to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
3 In the second month,
on the day of Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Zhōu (周) dispatched Chén Gōng Chún (陳公純), Xǔ Gōng Guì (許公貴), Shénwǔ Gōng Dòuyì (神武公竇毅), Nányáng Gōng Yáng Jiàn (南陽公楊荐), and others,
Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) says: Shuòzhōu (朔州) has Shénwǔ (神武) Commandery,
which governs Jiānshān (尖山) and Shùtuí (樹頹) Counties.
Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: Shùtuíshuǐ (樹頹水) flows out from the eastern mountain of Wòyáng (沃陽) County,
flows southwest,
merging on the right with Gàoshēng'yuánshuǐ (誥升爰水).
Its left side merges with Zhōnglíngchuān (中陵川).
Later Wèi (魏) established Shénwǔ (神武) Commandery in Shénwǔchuān (神武川),
governing Jiānshān (尖山) County.
Under Suí (隋), it became Shénwǔ (神武) County,
belonging to Mǎyì (馬邑) Commandery.
Jiàn (荐)
is pronounced 'zàidiān'.
along with one hundred and twenty women from the six palaces,
to the Tujue Khagan's (可汗) royal tent to bring back the princess.
Yì (毅)
was the nephew of Chì (熾).
Chì (熾) was then a Zhùguó (柱國).
After the Zhōu (周) ruler executed Yǔwén Hù (宇文護),
he made Chì (熾) Tàifù (太傅).
4 On the day of Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Zhōu (周) appointed Zhùguó Ānwǔ Gōng Lǐ Mù (柱國安武公李穆) as Dàsīkōng (大司空),
and Suídé Gōng Lù Tōng (綏德公陸通) as Dàsīkòu (大司寇).
Lǐ Mù (李穆) and Lù Tōng (陸通)
were both county dukes.
Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) says: Xiāngyáng (襄陽) Commandery formerly had Ānwǔ (安武) County,
which was merged into Nánzhāng (南漳) County by Western Wèi (西魏).
Diāoyīn (雕陰) Commandery had Suídé (綏德) County,
established by Western Wèi (西魏).
5 On the day of Rénshēn (壬申),
the Zhōu (周) ruler went to Qízhōu (岐州).
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of Jiǎyín (甲寅),
Ānchéng Wáng Xù (安成王頊) was appointed Sīkōng (司空).
Xù (頊), with the great prestige of being the emperor's brother,
wielded influence over the court and the land.
The Zhíbīng (直兵) Bào Sēngruì (鮑僧叡),
relying on Xù's (頊) power, acted unlawfully.
Since Qín (秦), all princely and ducal mansions had Zhíbīng (直兵).
From the officials of Nántái (南臺), he led a memorial to the throne and entered.
The Yùshǐtái (御史臺) was Nántái (南臺).
He made his expression solemn and sat upright.
Líng (陵) advanced and read the memorial.
At that time, Xù (頊) was standing on attendance in the hall,
looking up at the emperor,
sweating and losing color.
Líng (陵) sent a Diànzhōng Yùshǐ (殿中御史) to lead Xù (頊) down from the hall.
The Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ (殿中侍御史) resided in the hall to observe unlawful acts,
hence he was sent to lead Xù (頊) down from the hall.
The court became solemn.
7 On the day of Bǐngwǔ
Lóu Ruì, Prince of Dōng'ān and Grand General of Qí, was dismissed from office due to an incident.
8 Zǔ Tǐng,
a Compiler of Qí,
was learned and skilled
in many arts, but he was crude, unrestrained, and lacked integrity.
He once served as Gāozǔ's General of the Central and Outer Armies' Records.
Gāo Huān, Commander-in-Chief of all central and outer armies,
appointed Tǐng as the General of Records for the administration.
"Pǒluó"
refers to a type of cup.
"Pǒ"
is pronounced like "pǔ huǒ" (in fanqie).
He was also convicted of fraudulently stealing three thousand *shi* of government grain,
received two hundred strokes of the whip,
and was assigned to the armor workshops.
Tǐng, along with clerk Lǐ Shuāng and granary supervisor Chéng Zǔ, among others, created a request from Jìnzhōu for three thousand *shi* of grain.
Tǐng impersonated Records General Zhào Yànshēn to issue the order for its release.
When the matter was discovered,
he was whipped and assigned.
Tǐng, as Secretarial Director,
stole the *Huálín Biànlüè*,
and also possessed other stolen goods.
He was to be hanged,
but was instead stripped of his title and reduced to a commoner.
The *Huálín Biànlüè*
was compiled by Emperor Wǔ of Liáng with the assistance of various scholars.
A southerner brought it to Yèxià to sell.
Gāo Chéng gathered scribes,
and they copied it in one day and one night,
then returned the original.
Tǐng stole several fascicles of the *Biànlüè*,
pawned them for money to gamble with *chūpú*,
and was again punished for this offense.
During Xiǎnzǔ's time,
he again stole a volume of the *Biànlüè*,
and also fabricated appointments for over ten clerks,
all of whom had accepted bribes,
leading to his dismissal.
However, due to his talent and skills,
he was ordered to serve directly in the Central Secretariat.
When Shìzǔ was Prince of Chángguǎng,
Tǐng presented him with walnut oil.
Tǐng was good at making walnut oil
for painting.
"Your Highness has extraordinary bone structure.
Xiàozhēng dreamt that Your Highness rode a dragon to ascend to heaven."
Xiàozhēng
was Zǔ Tǐng's courtesy name.
At this time, many people went by their courtesy names.
"Shàng"
is pronounced like "shí zhǎng" (in fanqie).
"If that is so,
it will make your brother exceedingly wealthy and honored."
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Tǐng was promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant,
then transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He conspired with Hé Shìkāi in treacherous flattery.
Tǐng privately spoke to Shìkāi, saying:
"Your favor and fortune
are unparalleled since ancient times."
"Zhèngǔ"
means "since ancient times."
"Shuō"
is pronounced like "shì ruì" (in fanqie);
the later occurrences of "yí shuō" and "wēi shuō" are similar.
"Wǎn"
means "late" or "ending,"
and has the same meaning as "yànjià" (imperial demise).
Shìkāi then asked him for advice.
Tǐng said:
"You should persuade the Emperor, saying: 'The sons of Wénxiāng, Wénxuān, and Xiàozhāo
were all prevented from ascending to the throne.
Now, it is fitting to let the Crown Prince assume the great position early,
to settle the distinction between sovereign and subject.'
If this succeeds,
the Empress and the Young Lord will certainly be grateful to you.
This is a foolproof plan.
Please subtly persuade the Emperor to make him vaguely understand,
then I will submit a memorial from outside to argue the point."
Shìkāi agreed.
Coincidentally, a comet appeared.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"The comet
is an omen of removing the old and establishing the new;
there will be a change of ruler."
Tǐng then submitted a memorial, stating:
"Although Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven,
you have not yet reached the ultimate nobility.
It is appropriate to transmit the throne to the Eastern Palace,
and this also accords with the Way of Heaven."
He also presented the precedent of Wèi Xiǎnzǔ abdicating to his son.
(See volume 132, Tàishǐ 6th year of Sòng Míngdì.)
The "shàng" in "shì shàng" and "bìng shàng"
is pronounced like "shí zhǎng" (in fanqie);
the "gōng shàng" below is similar.
On the day of Bǐngzǐ (23rd),
Dùan Sháo, Grand Preceptor, was dispatched with a royal credential to present the imperial seals and ribbons,
transferring the throne to Crown Prince Wěi.
The Crown Prince immediately ascended the imperial throne at Jìnyáng Palace.
His taboo name was Wěi,
courtesy name Rénwáng,
and he was the eldest son of Emperor Wǔchéng.
"Xǐ"
is pronounced like "sī shì" (in fanqie).
"Shòu"
is pronounced "shòu."
The reign era was changed to Tiāntǒng.
An edict also made Crown Prince Húlǜ's daughter the Empress.
Thereupon, all dukes honored Shìzǔ with the title of Grand Emperor Emeritus,
and all major military and state affairs were reported to him.
Féng Zǐcóng, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, and Hú Chángcàn, Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, were appointed to assist and guide the Young Lord,
entering and exiting the forbidden palace,
specializing in presentations and reports.
Zǐcóng
was Empress Hú's brother-in-law.
Zǔ Tǐng was appointed Secretarial Director,
additionally given the title of Yítóng Sānsī (Same with the Three Ducal Ministers),
greatly favored and trusted,
and held in high esteem by both palaces.
9 On the day of Dīngchǒu (24th),
Qí appointed Hèbá Rén as Grand Tutor,
Hóumòchén Xiāng as Grand Guardian,
Rùn, Prince of Féngyì, as Minister of Works,
Ruì, Prince of Zhàojùn, as Minister of Education,
and Xiàowǎn, Prince of Hénán,
as Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day of Wùyín (25th),
Wèi Càn, Governor of Yíngzhōu, was appointed Grand Commandant,
Húlǜ Guāng as Grand General,
and Lóu Ruì, Prince of Dōng'ān, as Grand Commandant.
Wèi Càn and Lóu Ruì both being Grand Commandants
is an error in the Qí records.
According to Wèi Càn's biography,
Càn was Grand Preceptor,
which should be followed.
Lóu Ruì was enfeoffed as a commandery prince.
The *Five Dynasties Monograph* states: Yǐshuǐ County, Lángyá Commandery,
formerly had Dōng'ān Commandery established.
According to the Qí records,
Yànshēn was transferred from Right Assistant Director to Left Assistant Director.
10 In the fifth month,
the Tujue sent envoys to Qí,
beginning communication with Qí.
11 In the sixth month,
on the day of Jǐsì (6th),
the Qí ruler sent Wáng Jìgāo, concurrently Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, to arrive as an envoy.
12 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on Xīnsì (1st) which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 The Emperor dispatched Chéng Língxǐ, Area Commander, to attack Zhōu Dí by a separate route from Póyáng,
and defeated him.
Dí and over ten of his subordinates hid in a mountain cave.
As days and months passed,
his followers also gradually suffered.
Later, he sent someone to secretly go to Línchuān to buy fish and salmon.
Luò Yá, Governor of Línchuān, captured him
and ordered him to capture Dí to prove his loyalty,
then sent trusted brave warriors with him into the mountains.
That person lured Dí out to hunt,
and the brave warriors ambushed him by the roadside,
coming out to behead him.
On the day of Bǐngxū (26th),
his head was brought to Jiànkāng.
14 On the day of Gēngyín (10th),
the Zhōu ruler went to Qínzhōu;
in the eighth month,
on Bǐngzǐ (26th),
he returned to Cháng'ān.
15 On the day of Jǐmǎo (9th),
the imperial princes Bó Gù was established as Prince of Xīn'ān,
Bó Gōng as Prince of Jìn'ān,
Bó Rén as Prince of Lúlíng,
and Bó Yì as Prince of Jiāngxià.
16 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on Xīnhài (21st),
Zhōu made the city of Hángǔ Pass into the Tōngluò Defense,
and appointed Hèruò Dūn, Governor of Jīnzhōu, as Governor of Zhōngzhōu,
to guard Hángǔ.
The *Five Dynasties Monograph* states: Xīn'ān County, Hénán Commandery,
where Later Zhōu established Zhōngzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: It is east of present-day Xīn'ān County, Luòzhōu.
Dūn 恃才負氣 (relied on his talent and was full of spirit),
seeing that all his peers became Grand Generals,
but Dūn alone had not,
and moreover, in the campaign of Xiāngzhōu,
he returned with his army intact,
believing he deserved a reward,
but instead was removed from the rolls.
This incident can be found in the first and second years of the preceding volume.
Jìn Gōng Hù 護 was enraged,
recalled him,
and forced him to commit suicide.
Before his death,
he said to his son Bì:
"My ambition was to pacify Jiāngnán,
but now it is not fulfilled.
You must achieve my ambition.
I died because of my tongue;
you must not fail to reflect on this."
He then took an awl and pricked Bì's tongue until it bled, to warn him.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
the Qí Grand Emperor Emeritus arrived in Yè.
18 When Qí Shìzǔ was Prince of Chángguǎng,
he was frequently beaten by Xiǎnzǔ,
and he harbored resentment in his heart.
Whenever Xiǎnzǔ saw Zǔ Tǐng,
he always called him "thief,"
so Tǐng also resented him;
moreover, wishing to curry favor with Shìzǔ,
he persuaded Shìzǔ, saying:
"Wénxuān was violent and tyrannical,
how can he be called 'Wén' (Cultured)?
Since he did not found an enterprise,
how can he be called 'Zǔ' (Ancestor)?
If Wénxuān is an Ancestor,
what will Your Majesty be called after ten thousand years?"
The Emperor agreed.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the posthumous title of Tàizǔ Xiànwǔ Huángdì
and temple name Gāozǔ were changed,
and Xiànmíng Huánghòu was changed to Wǔmíng Huánghòu.
Officials were ordered to further discuss Wénxuān's posthumous title.
19 In the twelfth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Imperial Prince Bólǐ was enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔlíng.
20 On the day Rénxū,
the Qí Grand Emperor Emeritus went to Jìnyáng.
21 On the day Gēngwǔ,
Qí changed Emperor Wénxuān's posthumous title to Jǐngliè Huángdì,
and his temple name to Wēizōng.
According to the rules for posthumous titles: "Jǐng" means "to spread righteousness and act with firmness";
"Liè" means "to have accomplishments and pacify the people";
"Wēi" means "fierce and resolute";
"Wēi" means "having awe and being formidable";
"Wēi" means "to subdue distant lands with punishment."
Tiānkāng First Year
(Bǐngxū, 566)
The reign era was changed in the second month of this year.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 On the day Guǐwèi,
Zhōu granted a general amnesty
and changed the reign era to Tiānhé.
3 On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Qí ruler offered sacrifices at the Round Mound (Huánqiū);
on the day Guǐsì,
he performed the combined ancestral sacrifice at the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào).
Wǔdài Zhì: According to the Qí system: sacrifices at the Round Mound and Square Pool
were held once every three years,
known as Dìsì.
For the Round Mound, blue jade and bundles of silk were used.
On the first Xīn day of the first month, sacrifices were offered to the August Heaven Supreme Emperor (Hàotiān Shàngdì).
At the Grand Ancestral Temple, there were spring sacrifices,
summer Yuè sacrifices,
autumn Cháng sacrifices,
and winter Zhēng sacrifices,
all held in the first month of the season,
totaling five sacrifices including the Làyì.
A Dì sacrifice was held every three years,
and a Xiá sacrifice every five years,
these were called Yīnjì.
4 On the day Bǐngshēn,
Qí appointed Wèi Jǐn, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), as Right Palace Aide (Yòu Púshè).
5 On the day Jǐhài,
the Zhōu ruler plowed the sacrificial field (jìtián).
6 On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Qí ruler went to Jìnyáng.
7 Zhōu sent the Junior Master of Provisions (Xiǎo Zàishī) Dù Gǎo to make a diplomatic visit.
Zhōulǐ: The Zàishī
was in charge of the regulations for allocating land,
managing land affairs according to its produce,
assigning land duties and awaiting their governmental orders,
belonging to the Ministry of Land (Dìguān).
This office had two Senior Gentlemen (Shàngshì)
and four Middle Gentlemen (Zhōngshì),
but no distinction of "Grand" or "Junior."
Wǔdài Zhì: The Later Zhōu established the Zàishī
to manage the regulations for allocating land,
differentiate the number of households' fields and villages,
compile records of livestock and chariots,
examine the regulations for taxes and labor,
control the labor for repairing and expanding the capital region,
distribute the essentials of benevolence,
and review the policies for pastoral production.
8 In the second month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Qí Grand Emperor Emeritus returned to Yè.
9 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
a general amnesty was granted,
and the reign era was changed.
The reign era was changed to Tiānkāng.
10 In the third month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
Ānchéng Wáng Xù was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshūlìng).
11 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Zhōu ruler offered sacrifices at the Southern Suburbs.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
a grand sacrifice for rain was held.
12 The Emperor was unwell,
and all matters of the Imperial Chancellery were entrusted
to the Palace Aide to the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púshè) Dào Zhòngjǔ and the Minister of Five Armies (Wǔbīng Shàngshū) Kǒng Huàn to decide jointly.
Huàn
was the great-grandson of Xiùzhī.
Kǒng Xiùzhī can be found in volume 139, first year of Jiànwǔ, Qí Míngdì.
Xiù
is pronounced Xiù.

Huàn and Zhòngjǔ, along with Sīkōng, Shàngshūlìng, Governor of Yángzhōu, Prince of Ānchéng Xù, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Yuán Shū, and Palace Secretary (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Liú Shīzhī, attended to his medicine.
Shū
was the son of Jūnzhèng.
Yuán Jūnzhèng can be found in volume 163, third year of Tàiqīng, Liáng Wǔdì.
The Emperor worried that Xù would not be able to maintain his position,
and said to Xù:
"I wish to follow the example of Tàibó's deeds."
He meant to yield the throne.
Xù firmly declined.
The Emperor then said to Zhòngjǔ, Huàn, and others:
"Now the three states stand in a tripod,
and the affairs of the realm are heavy.
There must be a mature ruler.
I wish, in the near term, to follow Jìn Chéng,
and in the long term, to uphold the Yīn method."
Emperor Jìn Chéng established his younger brother by the same mother as his heir;
this incident can be found in volume 97, eighth year of Xiánkāng.
The Yīn method was that a brother succeeded a deceased elder brother.
Kǒng Huàn, shedding tears, replied:
"Your Majesty's health is unwell,
but recovery is not far off."
Quán means 'to heal';
Fù
means 'to return to the original state'.
Quán
is pronounced qián.
"Your sagely virtue daily ascends."
Máo Cháng said: Jī
means 'to ascend'.
Zhèng Xuán said: "It means to advance daily."
"You are sufficient to be a Zhōu Dàn.
If there is any intention of deposing or establishing (a ruler),
we, your humble servants,
sincerely dare not hear such an edict."
The Emperor said:
"The uprightness of ancient times
is again seen in you, minister."
Thereupon he appointed Huàn as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
Your subject Guāng (光) says: When a subject serves his ruler,
he should follow and accommodate what is good in him,
and correct and rescue him from his evils.
The Xiàojīng (孝經) records the words of the Master.
Entrusted with the heavy responsibility of being a close confidant,
and deciding the great plans of the state,
if one considers Shìzǔ's (世祖) words to be insincere,
then one should openly debate like Dòu Yīng (竇嬰)
and contend in court like Yuán Àng (袁盎).
The affair of Dòu Yīng (竇嬰) is found in Volume 16, Hàng Jǐngdì (漢景帝) year 3.
The affair of Yuán Àng (袁盎) is found in year 12.
爭 (zhēng),
is read as 諍 (zhèng).
If one considers them to be sincere,
then one should request that an edict be clearly issued,
proclaiming it throughout the realm,
so that Shìzǔ (世祖) would have the virtue of Sòng Xuān (宋宣),
and Gāozōng (高宗) would be free from the evil of Chǔ Líng (楚靈).
The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) says: Sòng Xuāngōng (宋宣公) set aside his son Yǔyí (與夷) and enthroned his younger brother Mùgōng (穆公).
When Mùgōng (穆公) died,
he set aside his son Féng (馮) and enthroned Yǔyí (與夷).
The gentleman said:
"Sòng Xuāngōng (宋宣公) can be said to have known men well.
He enthroned Mùgōng (穆公),
and his son enjoyed the benefit of it."
Chǔ Kāngwáng (楚康王) fell ill.
His younger brother Wéi (圍) entered to inquire about the king's illness,
strangled and assassinated him,
then killed his two sons Mù (幕) and Píngxià (平夏) and enthroned himself.
This was Língwáng (靈王).
If it is said that the crown prince, the legitimate heir,
cannot be moved, and one wishes to protect, assist, and secure him,
then one should be utterly loyal and devote oneself entirely,
like Xún Xī (荀息) of Jìn (晉)
and Féi Yì (肥義) of Zhào (趙).
The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) says: Jìn Xiàngōng (晉獻公) fell ill,
and entrusted his son Xīqí (奚齊) to Xún Xī (荀息).
Xī (息) said:
"Your subject will exhaust his strength,
and follow it with death."
When the Duke passed away,
Lì Kè (里克) killed Xīqí (奚齊).
Xún Xī (荀息) was about to die for him.
Someone said:
"It would be better to enthrone Zhuózǐ (卓子) and assist him."
Xún Xī (荀息) enthroned Zhuózǐ (卓子) to bury Xiàngōng (獻公).
Lì Kè (里克) killed Zhuózǐ (卓子),
and Xún Xī (荀息) died for him.
The affair of Féi Yì (肥義) is found in Volume 4, Zhōu Nánwáng (周赧王) year 20.
Then one would furtively ascertain his feelings and seek to align with them;
but after he has passed away,
then powerful ministers usurp the state and one cannot save it,
and the heir loses his position and one cannot die for him!
This is indeed the most cunning flattery,
yet Shìzǔ (世祖) called him "the upright survivor,"
entrusting him with a six-foot orphan.
Is this not preposterous?!
13 On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
the Emperor passed away.
The Emperor rose from hardship,
and understood the sufferings of the people.
He was naturally perceptive, frugal, and austere.
Every night, he would "cìguī" (刺閨) to handle external matters,
with a continuous flow of affairs.
To use an awl to pierce an object is called cì (刺);
guī (閨) is a small door in the palace.
To pierce and take out external matters from inside the guī (閨),
hence it is called
"cìguī" (刺閨).
Cì (刺),
pronounced qī cì fān (七賜翻).
He would always throw a tally onto the stone steps,
making a clanging sound,
and say:
"Even though I sleep,
I still want to be startled awake."
The Crown Prince ascended the throne,
and issued a general amnesty.
In the fifth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
the Empress Dowager was honored as the Grand Empress Dowager,
and the Empress as the Empress Dowager.
14 On the day Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
Qí (齊) appointed Wǔxīngwáng Pǔ (武興王普), who concurrently held the title of Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射), as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
15 Tuỳùhún Lónghèwáng Mòchāng (吐谷渾龍涸王莫昌) led his tribe to surrender to Zhōu (周).
Their territory was established as Fúzhōu (扶州).
The Wǔdàizhì (五代志) says: Jiāchéngxiàn (嘉誠縣) of Tóngchāngjùn (同昌郡) was established by Hòuzhōu (後周),
along with Lónghèjùn (龍涸郡) and the Fúzhōuzǒngguǎnfǔ (扶州總管府).
Tù (吐),
from tūn rùshēng (暾入聲).
Gǔ (谷),
pronounced yù (浴).
Shuài (帥),
pronounced lǜ (率).
16 On the day Gēngyín (庚寅),
Ānchéngwáng Xù (安成王頊) was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍), Sītú (司徒), Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書), and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì (都督中外諸軍事).
On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉), Xú Dù (徐度), who was Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn (中軍大將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), was appointed Sīkōng (司空);
Yuán Shū (袁樞), who was Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書), was appointed Zuǒpúyè (左僕射);
Shěn Qīn (沈欽), who was Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守), was appointed Yòupúyè (右僕射);
and Xú Líng (徐陵), who was Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
Líng (陵) believed that since the end of Liáng (梁),
appointments and selections had been largely indiscriminate.
So, he wrote a letter to the public, saying:
"Liáng Yuándì (梁元帝) inherited the chaos of Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
and Wáng Tàiwèi (王太尉) encountered the disaster and defeat of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Wáng Tàiwèi (王太尉) refers to Sēngbiàn (僧辯).
The disaster and defeat of Jīngzhōu (荊州) refers to the fall of Jiānglíng (江陵).
This led to extreme confusion.
Fāng (方) means method.
Qióng (窮) means extreme.
The Nánshǐ Xú Líng Zhuàn (南史徐陵傳) writes 'Yǒngdìng' (永定).
Yǒngdìng (永定) was the first reign era after Gāozǔ (高祖) received the abdication,
and should be followed.
Silver was hard to obtain,
while yellow tallies were easy to manage.
Officials were given ranks
in place of money and silk.
This resulted in Yuánwài (員外) and Chángshì (常侍) officers jostling shoulders on the road,
and countless Zīyì (諮議) and Cānjūn (參軍) officers in the marketplace.
How could this be the proper order of the court!
Now, with robes, caps, rites, and music,
the state is 'richer day by day and more splendid year by year.'
It means 'richer day by day' and 'more splendid year by year'.
This is an unreasonable expectation!"
The public all agreed.
17 On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Qí (齊) enfeoffed the former Emperor's son Hóng (弘) as Qí'ānwáng (齊安王),
Rén Gù (仁固) as Běipíngwáng (北平王),
Rén Yīng (仁英) as Gāopíngwáng (高平王),
and Rén Guāng (仁光) as Huáinánwáng (淮南王).
〠18 In the sixth month,
Qí (齊) sent Wéi Dàorú (韋道儒), who was concurrently Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), to visit.
Sàn (散),
pronounced sì dǎn fān (悉亶翻).
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì fān (奇寄翻).
19 On the day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Emperor Wén (文) was buried at Yǒngnínglíng (永寧陵),
with the temple name Shìzǔ (世祖).
20 In the autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Wùyín (戊寅),
Zhōu (周) built Wǔgōng (武功) and other cities to station troops.
Wǔgōng (武功) is the former Wǔgōngxiàn (武功縣) of Fúfēng (扶風) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Zhōujì (周紀) says: Wǔgōng (武功), Méi (郿), Xiégǔ (斜谷), Wǔdū (武都), Liúgǔ (留谷), and Jīnkēng (津坑) and other cities were built.
21 On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Lady Wáng (王) was established as Empress.
The King of Línhǎi (臨海) established the Empress.
22 In the eighth month,
the former Emperor of Qí (齊) went to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
23 Rǎn Lìngxián (冉令賢), Xiàng Wǔzǐwáng (向五子王) and others of the Mán (蠻) people of Zhōu's (周) Xìnzhōu (信州) rebelled in Bāxiá (巴峽).
Bāxiá (巴峽) is in Bājùn Bāxiàn (巴郡巴縣),
with gorges like Míngyuè (明月) and Guǎngdé (廣德),
