Jiǎo 皎, along with Liú Shīzhī 劉師知 and Hán Zǐgāo 韓子高, were all intimately trusted by Wén Dì 文帝.
Since the two had died,
Jiǎo 皎 naturally felt uneasy.
He comforted and reassured his subordinates,
and memorialized to request Guǎngzhōu 廣州,
to gauge the court's intentions.
The Grand Preceptor Xū 頊 feigned agreement,
but the imperial edict had not yet been issued.
Jiǎo 皎 secretly sent envoys to lead Zhōu 周 troops,
and also surrendered to Liáng 梁,
sending his son Xuánxiǎng 玄響 as a hostage.
In the fifth month,
on the Guǐsì 癸巳 day,
Xū 頊 appointed Wú Míngchè 吳明徹, the Governor of Dānyáng 丹楊, as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu 湘州.
14. On the Jiǎwǔ 甲午 day,
Qí 齊 appointed Dōngpíng Wáng Yǎn 東平王儼 as Director of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令).
15 Sītú Xù dispatched Wú Míngchè to lead a naval force of 30,000 to attack Yǐngzhōu.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
he dispatched Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Chúnyú Liàng to lead a naval force of 50,000 to follow.
He also dispatched Guànwǔ Jiāngjūn Yáng Wéntōng to take the land route from Ānchéng to Chálíng.
Liáng established the title of Guànwǔ Jiāngjūn,
which was on the same rank as Zhéchōng.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Lúlíng Jùn's Ānfù Xiàn
was formerly Ānchéng Jùn.
Chálíng Xiàn,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Chángshā Jùn.
During the Wú dynasty, it was separated and belonged to Xiāngdōng Jùn.
During the Suí dynasty, it was merged into Héngshān Jùn's Xiāngtán Xiàn.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Chálíng Xiàn belonged to Héngzhōu,
355 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Yíyáng
was formerly Yùzhāng Jùn's Yíchūn Xiàn.
Jìn Xiàowǔ Dì renamed it Yíyáng
to avoid the empress dowager's taboo name.
During the Suí dynasty, it was restored to Yíchūn Xiàn,
and it was under Yuánzhōu.
The Later Hàn dynasty established Lǐlíng Xiàn,
which belonged to Chángshā Jùn.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: It was 160 lǐ east of the commandery.
From Yíchūn to Lǐlíng was 220 lǐ.
Shǒu,
also pronounced "shì."
They conspired with Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Zhāodá and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Chéng Língxǐ to advance and attack.
In the sixth month,
on the day of Rén'yín,
Sīkōng Xú Dù was appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
to oversee all the armies in Jiànkāng,
and to proceed by land to Xiāngzhōu.
16 On the day of Xīnhài,
the Zhōu ruler honored his mother, the Chìnú clan, as Huáng Tàihòu.
According to Wèi Shōu's Guānshì Zhì: The Tuòbá tribe rose in Dàiběi
and absorbed other tribes.
They designated the separate clans within their own tribe as inner surnames;
other tribes were divided according to their regions.
In the north, there was the Chìnú clan.
17 On the day of Jǐwèi,
Qí enfeoffed Imperial Brother Rénjī as Xīhé Wáng,
Rényuē as Lèlang Wáng,
Rénjiǎn as Yǐngchuān Wáng,
Rényǎ as Ānlè Wáng,
and Rénzhí as Dānyáng Wáng.
The Kǎoyì states: The Běi Qí Shū, Imperial Annals, names him Tǒng,
but here we follow the Biographies.
Tǒng
refers to Rénzhí.
All were Jùnwáng.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Ānlè Jùn's Mìyún Xiàn
was formerly Ānlè Jùn.
18 Huá Jiǎo's envoy arrived in Cháng'ān;
the King of Liáng also submitted a memorial detailing the situation
and requested military aid.
The Zhōu people discussed sending an army to respond.
Sīkuài Cuī Yóu said:
"Last year's eastern expedition
resulted in more than half of our forces dead or wounded.
(This refers to the attack on Qí's Luòyáng, the event is found in the previous volume, Emperor Wén's Tiānjiā fifth year.)
Huì,
pronounced "wài" in ancient times.
Our wounds have not yet healed.
Now, the Chén clan protects its borders and pacifies its people,
cultivating good neighborly relations.
How can we covet their land,
accept their rebellious minister,
violate the trust of our alliance,
and raise an unrighteous army?!"
Jìnggōng Hù did not heed him.
In the intercalary sixth month,
on the day of Wùyín,
Xiāngzhōu Zǒngguǎn Wèi Gōngzhí was dispatched to supervise Zhùguó Lù Tōng, Dàjiāngjūn Tián Hóng, Quán Jǐngxūan, Yuán Dìng, and others to lead troops to assist.
19 On the day of Xīnsì,
Qí's Zuǒ Chéngxiàng, Xiányáng Wǔwáng Húlǜ Jīn, passed away
at the age of eighty.
His eldest son, Guāng, was Dàjiāngjūn.
His second son, Xiàn, and grandson, Wǔdū, were both Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and were sent out to govern regional commanderies.
Húlǜ Xiàn governed Yōuzhōu,
and Wǔdū governed Liángzhōu and Yǎnzhōu.
From his household came one empress
and two crown princes:
Jīn's eldest daughter,
Xiàozhāo married her as crown princess;
his second daughter,
Wǔchéng married her as crown princess,
and after the Hòuzhǔ received the abdication,
she was established as empress.
According to Hòuzǔ Tǐng's later statement, Guāng's sons married princesses;
this refers to Guāng's sons Wǔdū, Shìxióng, and Héngjiā, all marrying princesses.
No other family could compare for three generations.
Since Sùzōng's reign,
he was treated with especially great respect.
Whenever he had an audience,
he was always allowed to ride in a hand-pulled carriage to the steps,
or a sheep-drawn carriage would be sent to meet him.
However, Jīn was not pleased by this,
and once said to Guāng:
"Although I do not read books,
I have heard that historically, few maternal relatives have been able to preserve their clan.
If a daughter is favored,
she is envied by the nobles;
if she is not favored,
she is hated by the Son of Heaven.
Our family achieved wealth and honor solely through meritorious service;
why must we rely on a daughter's favor?!"
The historians say that Húlǜ Jīn was discerning.
20 On the day of Rénwǔ,
Qí appointed Dōngpíng Wáng Yǎn as Lù Shàngshū Shì,
appointed Zuǒ Púyè Zhào Yànshēn as Shàngshū Lìng,
and appointed Bìngshěng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Lóu Dìngyuǎn as Zuǒ Púyè,
moving him from Bìngshěng to Yèshěng Zuǒ Púyè.
Dìngyuǎn
was Zhāo's son.
Zhāo
was Empress Lóu's brother.
21 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day of Wùshēn,
Imperial Son Zhìzé was established as Crown Prince.
22 In the eighth month,
Qí appointed Rènchéng Wáng Xié as Tàishī,
Féngyì Wáng Rùn as Dàsīmǎ,
Duàn Sháo as Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
Hèbá Rén as Yòu Chéngxiàng,
Hóumòchén Xiāng as Tàizǎi,
Lóu Ruì as Tàifù,
Húlǜ Guāng as Tàibǎo,
Hán Zǔniàn as Dàjiāngjūn,
Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì as Tàiwèi,
and Dōngpíng Wáng Yǎn as Sītú.
Yǎn was favored by the former emperor and Empress Hú.
At that time, he also held the titles of Jīngjī Dà Dūdū and Lǐngjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and was concurrently Lǐng Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
According to the former practice of the Wèi dynasty: when the Zhōngchéng went out,
he would take a different road from the Imperial Crown Prince.
They would travel on separate roads,
and one's carriage would not be pulled aside to yield the way.
Cháo,
pronounced "zhāo."
The oxen would be unyoked,
and the yoke placed on the ground,
to await his passing;
if there was a delay,
and the carriage was not stopped and the yoke not immediately placed on the ground,
this delay
was a violation of the law.
Since the relocation to Yè,
this ceremony had fallen into disuse.
The former emperor wished to honor and favor Yǎn,
and ordered that the old system be fully followed.
When Yǎn first emerged from the northern palace,
about to ascend to the rank of Zhōngchéng,
all the infantry and cavalry of the capital region, the officials of the Lǐngjūn, the ceremonial entourage of the Zhōngchéng, and the ceremonial escort of the Sītú,
all followed him.
The former emperor and Empress Hú set up a tent outside the East Gate of Huálín Yuán to observe him,
and dispatched an imperial envoy to gallop towards the formation.
This was towards Yǎn's vanguard ceremonial escort.
Shǐ,
pronounced "shūlì."
Qù,
pronounced "qīyù."
The envoy declared that he was acting on imperial decree,
and a soldier with a red staff immediately smashed his saddle,
the horse was startled,
and the man fell.
The former emperor laughed heartily,
thinking it excellent,
and further ordered the carriage to stop,
and spent a long time inquiring and consoling him.
This was consoling Yǎn.
Láo,
pronounced "lìdào."
Yǎn (儼) remained in the palace.
He sat in the Hánguāng (含光) Hall attending to state affairs.
All his paternal uncles bowed to him.
The Former Emperor (上皇) occasionally traveled to Bīngzhōu (幷州);
the Jìnyáng (晉陽) Palace was in Bīngzhōu.
Each time he saw him off,
sometimes halfway,
sometimes not returning until they reached Jìnyáng.
His utensils, ornaments, clothing, and accessories
were all the same as those of the Qí (齊) sovereign,
and all his needs were supplied by the government.
Once, in the Nángōng (南宮), he saw fresh ice and early plums.
The Qí sovereign at that time resided in the Nángōng in Yè (鄴),
while Yǎn, accompanying the Former Emperor and Empress Hú (胡后), lived in the Běigōng (北宮).
He angrily said:
"My honored elder brother has them,
why do I not!"
Yǎn always referred to the Qí sovereign as "honored elder brother."
The subordinate officials and artisans would certainly be punished.
Yǎn was by nature resolute and decisive.
He once remarked to the Former Emperor:
"My honored elder brother is weak;
how can he command the左右 (zuǒyòu)!"
The Former Emperor always praised his talent
and had an intention to depose and replace the sovereign.
Empress Hú also encouraged him,
but then he stopped.
Although Yǎn and the Qí sovereign had established the distinction between ruler and subject,
they often addressed each other as brothers,
and Yǎn also harbored the intention of usurping the succession.
The historian mentioned this
to set the stage for Yǎn's downfall due to his reliance on favor.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
23 Huá Jiǎo (華皎) sent envoys to entice Zhāng Zhāodá (章昭達).
Zhāodá captured and sent them to Jiànkāng (建康).
He also enticed Chéng Língxǐ (程靈洗).
Língxǐ beheaded them.
Jiǎo considered Wǔzhōu (武州) to be his vital area.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states:
Wǔlíng (武陵) Commandery.
The Liáng (梁) established Wǔzhōu.
Zǐlóng (子隆) did not comply;
he dispatched troops to attack it,
but did not succeed.
Dài Sēngshuò (戴僧朔), the Inspector of Bāzhōu (巴州), and others were all subordinate to Jiǎo.
Emperor Wén (文帝) ordered Jiǎo to be the Grand Administrator of Xiāng (湘), Bā, and four other prefectures.
The Wǔdài Zhì states:
Bālíng (巴陵) Commandery.
The Liáng established Bāzhōu.
Originally subordinate to Jiǎo,
they then served him.
Xiāngzhōu and Chángshā (長沙) Commandery shared the same administrative seat.
Because the prefecture governed the commandery,
it is said they were originally subordinate to Jiǎo.
守 (shǒu)
is also pronounced as 手 (shǒu).
He then partially pardoned the two prefectures of Xiāng and Bā.
In the ninth month,
on the yìsì (乙巳) day,
all of Jiǎo's family members were executed.
The Liáng made Jiǎo the Sīkōng (司空),
and sent their General-in-Chief Wáng Cāo (王操) with twenty thousand troops to assist him.
The Zhōu's (周) Quán Jǐngxūan (權景宣) commanded the naval forces,
Yuán Dìng (元定) commanded the land forces,
Wèi Gōng Zhí (衞公直) was the overall commander,
and they advanced together with Jiǎo.
Chúnyú Liáng's (淳于量) army was at Xiàkǒu (夏口),
Zhí's army was at Lǔshān (魯山).
He ordered Yuán Dìng with several thousand infantry and cavalry to besiege Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Jiǎo's army was at Báiluó (白螺).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) says: The Jiāng (江) River passes north of Xiàjùn (下雋) County in Chángshā,
and the Xiāng River flows from the south to join it.
The Jiāng River then flows east past Péngchéngkǒu (彭城口),
then east past north of Rúshān (如山),
then east past south of Báiluóshān (白螺山).
螺 (luó)
is pronounced lúgē (盧戈).
雋 (jùn)
is pronounced cíyǎn (辭兗).
Xú Dù (徐度) and Yáng Wéntōng (楊文通) attacked Xiāngzhōu via the Lǐnglù (嶺路).
The Lǐnglù
is the previously mentioned footpath between Ānchéng (安成) and Yíyáng (宜陽).
Jiǎo, with the Zhōu and Liáng naval forces, sailed downstream from Bālíng with the wind.
Their military power was formidable.
They fought at Dùnkǒu (沌口).
Liáng and Míngchè (明徹) recruited small ships from their army,
offering large rewards of gold and silver,
ordering them to go out first to intercept the large ships of the Western army and endure their ramming.
After all the ramming poles on the Western army's ships were expended,
Liáng and others then rammed them with their large ships.
The Western army's ships were all shattered
and sank in the middle of the river.
Warships were equipped with ramming poles,
which were launched to ram enemy ships.
艦 (jiàn)
is pronounced hù'àn (戶黯).
Taking advantage of the wind, they set fires,
but soon the wind shifted,
and they self-immolated.
The Western army was utterly defeated.
Jiǎo and Dài Sēngshuò escaped in a single boat.
Passing Bālíng,
they dared not land.
"發 (fā)"
should probably be
"登 (dēng)".
Wèi Gōng Zhí also fled to Jiānglíng (江陵).
Yuán Dìng's isolated army
had no way to advance or retreat.
They cut through bamboo to open a path,
fighting and retreating,
hoping to reach Bālíng.
Bālíng was already occupied by Xú Dù and others.
Dù and others sent envoys to feign an alliance,
promising to allow them to return to their country.
Dìng believed them,
disarmed and went to Dù.
Dù captured him
and took all his troops captive.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) says: The Chén Shū (陳書) states,
"captured over ten thousand men and
four thousand horses."
This is also probably exaggerated,
so it is not adopted here.
Dìng died of rage and indignation.
Jiǎo's partisans, Cáo Qìng (曹慶) and over forty others, were all executed.
Only Zhāng Zhāoyù (章昭裕), the Grand Administrator of Yuèyáng (岳陽)
and Zhāodá's younger brother,
Cáo Xuān (曹宣), the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng (桂陽)
and an old minister of Gāozǔ (高祖),
and Rèn Zhōng (任忠) of Rǔyīn (汝陰), the Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽)
who had once submitted a confidential memorial,
were all pardoned.
Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) pressed his advantage to attack Hédōng (河東) of Liáng
and captured it.
Zhōu Wèi Gōng Zhí blamed the Liáng General-in-Chief Yīn Liàng (殷亮).
The Liáng sovereign knew it was not his fault,
but dared not defy him,
so he executed him.
As Zhōu and Chén (陳) had already fallen out,
Péi Kuān (裴寬), the Inspector of Miǎnzhōu (沔州) of Zhōu, reported to the General-in-Chief of Xiāngzhōu (襄州),
requesting additional garrison troops
and moving the city to Yángtíshān (羊蹄山) to avoid floods.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Zèngshān (甑山) County of Miǎnyáng (沔陽) Commandery.
The Liáng established Liáng'ān (梁安) Commandery.
The Western Wèi (西魏) changed its name to Wèi'ān (魏安) Commandery
and established Jiāngzhōu (江州).
In the third year of Emperor Fèi (廢帝),
it was renamed Miǎnzhōu.
Zèngshān has Yángtáishān (陽臺山),
thirty-five *li* south of Hànchuān (漢川).
The local dialect mistakenly calls it Yángtíshān.
Chéng Língxǐ's fleet suddenly arrived at the city.
Coincidentally, there was heavy rain,
and the water level rose sharply.
Língxǐ brought large ships to the city and launched ramming poles,
smashing the towers and battlements.
Arrows and stones were used to attack day and night for over thirty days.
Chén soldiers ascended the city,
but Kuān still led his troops to resist with short weapons.
After another two days,
he was captured.
24 On the dīngsì (丁巳) day,
the Qí Former Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
There were floods east of the mountains,
and famine.
According to Lǐ Bǎiyào's (李百藥) book: great floods east of the mountains,
people were starving.

in the tenth month,
on the jiǎshēn (甲申) day,

26 In the eleventh month,

Yǔwén Guì (宇文貴), Duke Xǔmù (許穆公) of Zhōu, returned from the Tujue (突厥)

Yǔwén Guì and Chén Gōng Chún (陳公純) and others had gone to the Tujue to escort a princess,

Guì was allowed to return first due to illness.
厥 (jué)
is pronounced jiǔwù (九勿).
還 (huán)
is pronounced cóngxuān (從宣),

卒 (zú)
is pronounced zǐxù (子恤).

30 In the twelfth month,
Hù's (護) mother, Duke Jìn (晉公) of Zhōu, died.
An imperial edict ordered him to rise
and attend to affairs.
31 Zǔ Tǐng, Secretary-General of Qí,
was on good terms with Liú Tì, Grand Master of the Yellow Gate.
Zǔ Tǐng wanted to become prime minister,
so he detailed the crimes of Zhào Yànshēn, Yuán Wényáo, and Hé Shìkāi,
and ordered Liú Tì to report them.
Liú Tì dared not comply.
When Yànshēn and the others heard of this,
they went to the Supreme Emperor first to explain themselves.
The Supreme Emperor was furious,
seized Zǔ Tǐng,
and interrogated him.
Zǔ Tǐng then exposed Shìkāi, Wényáo, Yànshēn, and others for forming cliques, abusing power, selling offices, and perverting justice.
The Supreme Emperor said,
“You are slandering me!”
Zǔ Tǐng said,
“I dare not slander Your Majesty for taking people’s daughters.”
The Supreme Emperor said,
“I took them in because of the famine,
to care for them.”
Zǔ Tǐng said,
“Why not open the granaries to provide relief,
instead of buying them into the imperial harem?”
The Supreme Emperor grew even more enraged,
struck Zǔ Tǐng’s mouth with the pommel of his sword,
and rained down whips and clubs,
intending to beat him to death.
Zǔ Tǐng cried out,
“Your Majesty, do not kill your subject!
Your subject can concoct golden elixir for Your Majesty.”
Thus, he gained a slight reprieve.
Zǔ Tǐng said,
“Your Majesty has a Fàn Zēng but cannot use him.”
These were the words of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
“You compare yourself to Fàn Zēng and take me for Xiàng Yǔ?”
Zǔ Tǐng said,
“Xiàng Yǔ, a commoner,
led a motley crowd,
and in five years achieved hegemony.
Your Majesty relies on the resources of your father and brothers
to merely reach this point.
I believe Xiàng Yǔ should not be easily underestimated.”
The Supreme Emperor became even more enraged
and ordered his mouth to be stopped with earth.
Zǔ Tǐng spoke while spitting it out,
and was then whipped two hundred times
and assigned to the armor workshops.
Soon after, he was exiled to Guāngzhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Dōnglái Jùn,
formerly Guāngzhōu.
Biéjià Zhāng Fèngfú said,
“The dungeon
is an underground dungeon.”
So Zǔ Tǐng was put into an underground dungeon,
with his cangue and fetters never leaving him.
At night,
he used turnip seeds as a lamp.
His eyes were smoked by it,
and he consequently lost his sight.
The Běncǎo states: Turnips are good for the eyes.
Now Zǔ Tǐng lost his sight because of it.
Perhaps its seeds, when ingested, clarify vision,
but when used as a lamp,
the smoke obscures the eyes and causes blindness.
The Yǎnyì states: Turnips,
today commonly called mànjīng,
wither in summer.
They are replanted in vegetable gardens
and called jīmáocài.
Just after they are picked in spring,
their seeds are harvested for oil.
If this is true,
then it is vegetable oil.
People in the southeast often use it to light the night
and have never had their eyes smoked blind.
Dù Yòu said: Wèi first established the Wǔbīng Shàngshū (Five Departments of Military Affairs),
namely Zhōngbīng, Wàibīng, Biébīng, Dūbīng, and Qíbīng.
Jìn divided Zhōngbīng and Wàibīng into Zuǒ and Yòu,
which, though making seven departments in total with the old ones,
were still called Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
not Qībīng Shàngshū.
It was not until the Later Wèi
that the Qībīng Shàngshū was first established.
Now, various authors
sometimes say that the Qībīng Shàngshū was established during the Tàikāng period of Jìn,
which is mistaken.
Beyond human reason,
it was especially egregious in the family.
One night,
he was killed by a robber,
who left behind a knife.
Upon examination,
it was the knife carried by his son, Shànzhāo.
The authorities arrested Shànzhāo
and executed him.
The historian records this as a warning.
However, judging by the circumstances,
if Shànzhāo had indeed murdered his father,
he would certainly not have left the knife to await examination.
It was likely a ruse by the robber to have his son killed.

first month,

detaining Chén Gōng Chún and others for several years without returning them.
Chún and others, who had gone to welcome the bride,

destroyed their yurts

Mùgǎn feared
this was a curse from heaven.

and Chún and others escorted her back.
In the third month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
they arrived in Cháng’ān.
The Emperor of Zhōu performed the ceremony of personally welcoming the bride.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Zhōu granted a great amnesty.
7 On the day Yǐsì,
Qí appointed Dōngpíng Wáng Yǎn as Grand General,
Nányáng Wáng Chuò as Grand Minister of Education,
Xú Xiǎnxiù, Kai Fu Yi Tong San Si, as Grand Minister of Works,
and Guǎngníng Wáng Xiàohéng as President of the Department of State Affairs.
8 On the day Wǔwǔ,
Yān Wén Gōng Yú Jǐn of Zhōu passed away.
Yú Jǐn held high merits and a prominent position,
yet he served his superior with increasing reverence.
Whenever he attended court,
he was accompanied by no more than two or three horsemen.
When there were major affairs of state,
they were often discussed with Yú Jǐn.
Yú Jǐn dedicated himself to loyal assistance
and was particularly trusted and favored among the meritorious officials,
receiving exceptionally high respect and treatment,
without any estrangement from beginning to end.
He instructed his sons
to always maintain tranquility and modesty,
and his descendants thrived,
most of whom became prominent.
9 Wú Míngchè, taking advantage of his victory, advanced to attack Jiānglíng,
referring to the victory at Dùnkǒu.
The Emperor of Liáng moved to Jìnán to avoid him.
Liú Zhāo said: Jìnán City is located more than ten li north of Jiānglíng County.
They resisted fighting day and night for ten decades.
Liáng generals Mǎ Wǔ and Jí Chè attacked Wú Míngchè
and defeated him.
Wú Míngchè retreated to defend Gōng’ān,
and the Emperor of Liáng was then able to return.
10 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Xīnsì,
Zhōu appointed Dáxī Wǔ as Grand Tutor,
Yùchí Huí as Grand Guardian,
and Qí Gōng Xiàn as Grand Marshal.
11 The Supreme Emperor of Qí went to Jìnyáng.
12 Xú Zhīcái, Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs of Qí, was skilled in medicine.
When the Supreme Emperor fell ill,
Xú Zhīcái treated him,
and he recovered.
Hé Shìkāi, Director of the Central Secretariat, wanted to gain further promotion,
so he had Xú Zhīcái appointed as Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
When the Emperor of Qí fell ill and recalled Xú Zhīcái, it was too late to treat the root cause.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Lǔ Jùn,
formerly Yǎnzhōu,
governed from Xiáqiū.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Hú Chángrén, Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, was made Left Vice President,
and Hé Shìkāi was made Right Vice President.
Hú Chángrén was
the elder brother of the Empress Dowager.
13 On the day Gēngxū,
the Emperor of Zhōu offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the day Gēngshēn,
he went to Lǐquán Palace.
Lǐquán Palace
was the old site of the Hàn Gānquán Palace,
west of Chéngyáng County, Féngyì, Hàn.
Later, Wèi established Níngyí County here.
Suí renamed it Lǐquán County.
14 On the day Rénxū,
the Supreme Emperor of Qí returned to Yè.
In the 15th autumn,
seventh month,
on the Rén-yín day,
Yáng Zhōng, Duke Huán of Suí in the Zhōu dynasty, passed away.
His son, Jiān, inherited his title.
Jiān held the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Xiǎo Gōngbó.
According to the Rites of Zhōu, the Gōngbó belonged to the Heavenly Officials (Tiānguān),
with two middle-ranking officers (zhōngshì)
and two junior officers (xiàshì).
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary states: “Bó”
means chief;
they manage the officials of the royal palace’s guards and their decrees,
carry out their ranks and order,
and organize their corvée labor.
Later, the Zhōu dynasty established Left and Right Gōngbó,
who were in charge of the prohibitions of the imperial guard;
each would take turns on duty inside,
and the Xiǎo Gōngbó was their deputy.
Jiān consulted with Bái Zhōng,
who said:
“It is difficult to be a wife between two mothers-in-law.
You should not go!”
Jiān then declined the position.
Historians, recognizing Yáng Zhōng’s discernment,
recorded his death and this incident.
Yáng Jiān first appears here.
On the bǐng-wǔ day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the wù-wǔ day,
the Zhōu ruler returned to Cháng’ān.
On the rén-xū day,
the emperor’s younger brother Bózhì was enfeoffed as King of Yǒngyáng,
and Bómóu as King of Guìyáng.
In the eighth month,
Qí requested peace from Zhōu.
Zhōu dispatched its Military Commander (Jūnsīmǎ) Lù Chéng as an envoy to Qí;
in the ninth month,
on the bǐng-shēn day,
Qí sent its Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Hú Sīwénlüè in return.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the guǐ-hài day,
the Zhōu ruler offered sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the gēng-wǔ day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the xīn-sì day,
Qí appointed Gǔangníng Wáng Xiàohéng as Lù Shàngshū Shì,
Left Grand Councilor (Zuǒ Púyè) Hú Chángrén as Shàngshū Lìng,
Right Grand Councilor (Yòu Púyè) Hé Shìkāi as Zuǒ Púyè,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān) Táng Yōng as Yòu Púyè.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of the new moon, rén-chén,
there was a solar eclipse.
Qí dispatched Li Xié, who concurrently held the title of Sanqí Chángshì, to come as an envoy.
Sǎn
is pronounced with xī dǎn.
Qí
is pronounced with qí jì.
On the jiǎ-chén day,
the Zhōu ruler went to Qíyáng.
The Five Dynasties Gazetteer states: there is Qíyáng Palace in Yōng County, Tàiyuán Commandery.
Zhōu dispatched Cuī Yàn and others, who held the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, as envoys to Qí.
Shǐxīng Wáng Bómào, seeing that Ānchéng Wáng Xù monopolized power,
was very displeased and
repeatedly uttered malicious words.
On the jiǎ-yín day,
by an edict from the Grand Empress Dowager, he falsely accused the Emperor,
saying
he “conspired with Liú Shīzhī, Huá Jiǎo, and others.”
The word
“by”
here
clarifies that the Grand Empress Dowager’s edict
was created by Xù.
Huá
is pronounced with hù huà.
“Emperor Wén’s discernment in choosing a son
is comparable to that of Emperor Yáo;
his desire to transmit to a younger brother
also matches Tàibó.
Now, he can reaffirm his past aspiration
and establish a worthy ruler.”
So, the Emperor was deposed as King of Línhǎi,
and Ānchéng Wáng entered to succeed.
Another edict was issued,
demoting Bómào to Marquis of Wēnmá;
he was the Marquis of Wēnmá County.
Shěn Yuē said: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Wēnmá County because of the Wēnmá shipyards,
belonging to Jìn’ān Commandery.
Jìn’ān
was renamed Jiàn’ān by the Suí dynasty.
Ānchéng Wáng sent bandits to waylay him on the road
and killed him in his carriage.
The Former Emperor of Qí fell ill;
Xu Zhīcái was urgently summoned by express courier,
but had not yet arrived.
On the xīn-wèi day,
his illness became critical.
He entrusted his posthumous affairs to Hé Shìkāi,
grasping his hand and saying:
“Do not betray me!”
He then passed away in Shìkāi’s hands.
The next day,
Zhīcái arrived
but was again sent back to his prefecture.
He returned to Yǎnzhōu.
Fù
is pronounced with fú yòu.
Shìkāi kept the death a secret for three days without announcing it.
The Grand Master of Palace Writers (Huángmén Shìláng) Féng Zǐcóng asked why,
and Shìkāi said:
“The deaths of Shénwǔ and Wénxiāng
were both kept secret and not announced.
Shénwǔ died,
recorded in volume 160 as the first year of Tàiqīng of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng;
Wénxiāng died,
recorded in volume 162 as the third year of Tàiqīng.
I fear that some princes and dukes may harbor disloyal intentions,
and I intend to gather them all in Liángfēng Hall
and then discuss it with you.”
Shìkāi had long harbored jealousy toward the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Lù Shàngshū Shì, Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì, as well as the General of the Imperial Guard (Lǐngjūn) Lóu Dìngyuǎn.
Zǐcóng feared that Shìkāi might forge an imperial testament to send Ruì out of the capital
and strip Dìngyuǎn of his imperial guards,
so he persuaded him, saying:
“The late great emperor had already transmitted the throne to the present emperor.
All subjects who are wealthy and noble
owe their status to the grace of the Supreme Lord and his son.
If only the noble officials within the court remain unchanged,
the princes and dukes will certainly have no different intentions.
Times change, and circumstances differ;
how can it be compared to the 'hegemonic court'?”
Gāo Huān and Gāo Chéng had not yet usurped Wèi,
but held the reins of Wèi’s government.
The ruler and ministers of Northern Qí all referred to it as the 'hegemonic court'.
Cháo
is pronounced with zhí yáo;
same below.
“The matter of ascension to the heavens
(Zhèng Xuán said: shàng means ascend;
xiá means completed.
Ascended and completed means
like an immortal departing, merely a figure of speech)
if not announced for a long time
(meaning not to show mourning or wear mourning clothes),”
Shìkāi then announced the death.
On the bǐng-zǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the wù-yín day,
the Empress Dowager Emerita was honored as the Empress Dowager.
Palace Attendant and Left Grand Councilor of the Department of State Affairs (Shìzhōng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè) Yuán Wényáo,
fearing that Féng Zǐcóng,
being the brother-in-law of Empress Dowager Hú,
would assist the Empress Dowager in interfering with court affairs,
conspired with Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì and Hé Shìkāi
to send Zǐcóng out as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Zhèngzhōu.
Emperor Shìzǔ was arrogant, extravagant, and debauched;
corvée labor was frequent and taxes were heavy,
causing suffering to officials and common people.
Historians say that Wǔchéng caused the downfall of Qí.
On the jiǎ-shēn day,
an edict stated:
“All detailed craftwork in various locations
shall be abolished.
Old and infirm palace women and government slaves in Yèxià, Jìnyáng, and Zhōngshān palaces
shall all be selected and released.”
Qí had Yè Palace, Jìnyáng Palace, and Zhōngshān Palace.
Guānkǒu refers to
the family members of criminals who were confiscated by the government and made into slaves.
“They are permitted to return home.”
Yuánzuò refers to
being implicated in a crime not as the principal offender,
but due to kinship.
In the 29th year of Zhōu, the Láo of Liángzhōu’s Hénglèng rebelled.
According to the biography of Zhào Wénbiǎo: Hénglèng
was a place name.
Its location was perilous and fortified,
spanning several hundred *lǐ*,
inhabited entirely by the Láo.
After Wénbiǎo pacified the Láo,
he established it as Péngzhōu.
恒,
pronounced *hù dēng fān*.
獠,
pronounced *lǔ hào fān*;
same below.
Zhào Wénbiǎo was the Chángshǐ of the Liángzhōu Dūgǔanfǔ.
長,
pronounced *zhī liǎng fān*.
Wénbiǎo said:
“If we attack them from all four sides,
the Láo will have no escape.
They will surely fight to the death to resist us,
making them difficult to conquer.
Now, if I show them both might and benevolence,
executing those who do evil
and pacifying those who follow good,
once good and evil are distinguished,
it will be easy to defeat them.”
He then relayed this intention throughout the army.
At that time, there were some “familiar Láo” among the troops
who were mostly acquainted with the Hénglèng people.
They reported this truthfully to them.
Those on the border who submitted were called “familiar Láo.”
Wénbiǎo’s army had already reached their territory.
Within the Láo territory, there were two routes,
one flat and one perilous.
Several Láo chieftains came to see him,
requesting to act as guides.
Wénbiǎo said:
“This route is wide and flat;
there is no need for a guide.
You may simply go ahead and reassure your kinsmen,
so they come to surrender.”
He then sent them away.
Wénbiǎo said to his generals:
“The Láo chieftains think I will advance along the wide route,
and they will surely set up an ambush to waylay me.
We must do the unexpected.”
He then led his troops in through the perilous route.
From atop a height, he looked down
and indeed saw ambushing soldiers.
Having miscalculated, the Láo
vied to lead their multitudes to surrender.
Wénbiǎo appeased and reassured them all,
and still levied their rents and taxes;
none dared to defy him.
The people of Zhōu appointed Wénbiǎo as the Chángshǐ of Péngzhōu.
Péngzhōu was originally the land of Dàngqú in the Hàn dynasty.
During Lǐ Shì’s time, it was occupied by the Láo.
Xiāo Qí established Guīhuà Jùn,
and the Liáng dynasty established Āngù Xiàn and Fúyú Jùn.
Later, the Hòuzhōu dynasty established Péngzhōu,
naming it after Péngshān.
In the first year of Tàijiàn
(*jǐchǒu*, 569)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day which was the first day of the month,
the Zhōu ruler suspended court assemblies due to the mourning for Qí Shìzǔ.
He dispatched the Sīkuài, Lǐ Lún, to offer condolences and burial contributions,
and to attend the funeral.
2. On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the King of Ānchéng ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name
and issued a general amnesty.
The Grand Empress Dowager was restored as Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager became Empress Wén.
Lady Liǔ was established as empress,
and the heir apparent, Shúbǎo, was made crown prince.
The imperial prince, Shúlíng, was enfeoffed as King of Shǐxīng,
to oversee the sacrifices to King Zhāoliè.
Emperor Wén had assigned his son, Bómào, to oversee the sacrifices to King Zhāoliè of Shǐxīng.
After the emperor killed Bómào,
Shúlíng was assigned to oversee the sacrifices.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the emperor visited the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Shěn Qīn, the Shàngshū Púyè, was appointed Zuǒ Púyè,
and Wáng Mài, the Dùzhī Shàngshū, was appointed Yòu Púyè.
Mài
was the grandson of Fèn.
3. On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the southern suburb.
4. On the *rénwǔ* day,
the imperial prince, Shúyīng, was enfeoffed as King of Yùzhāng,
and Shújiān as King of Chángshā.
5. On the *wùwǔ* day,
the emperor offered sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
6. Qí Bólíng Wénjiǎn Wáng, Jì,
who was the younger brother of Shìzǔ’s mother,
was the Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu.
He said to people:
“The turn will come to me now.”
Meaning that, in the order of brothers,
he too should become the Son of Heaven.
語,
pronounced *niú jù fān*.
He was secretly killed in the prefecture by someone sent there,
and was buried and posthumously honored with ritual courtesies.
7. In the second month,
on the *yǐhài* day,
the emperor plowed the sacrificial fields.
8. On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Qí buried Emperor Wǔchéng at Yǒngpíng Líng.
His temple name was Shìzǔ.
9. On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Qí transferred Dōngpíng Wáng Yǎn to be King of Lángyé.
10. Qí dispatched the Shìzhōng, Chìliè Chángchā, to offer a marriage proposal to Zhōu.
*Xìngzuàn*: Chìliè
is a compound surname,
originating from the western branch of the Tuòbá clan.
11. Qí appointed Sīkōng Xú Xiǎnxiù as Tàiwèi,
and Lóu Dìngyuǎn, who was concurrently Shàngshū Lìng, as Sīkōng.
At first,
Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Yòupúyè Hé Shìkāi
was intimately favored by Shìzǔ.
He entered and exited the emperor's private chambers
without any restrictions,
and thus gained the favor of Empress Hú.
When Shìzǔ passed away,
the Qí Lord, believing Shìkāi had been entrusted with a dying wish,
placed deep trust in him,
and his power and authority grew stronger.
He, Lóu Dìngyuǎn, Lù Shàngshūshì Zhào Yànshēn, Shìzhōng Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Yuán Wényáo, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Táng Yōng, Lǐngjūn Qílián Měng, Gāo Ānànágōng,
and Lǐ Yánshòu. (Lǐ Yánshòu said: Qílián
were originally of the Jī surname.
At the end of the Six States period,
they fled the chaos beyond the Great Wall
and settled in Qílián Shān.
They then took the mountain's name as their surname.
Due to the northern people's pronunciation error,
it was rendered Qílián.
Wèi Shōu's Guānshì Zhì states: The Qílián clan originated from the various western tribes.)
were at that time known as
the "Eight Nobles."
Tàiwèi Zhào Jùnwáng Ruì, Dàsīmǎ Féngyì Wáng Rùn, Āndé Wáng Yánzōng, along with Lóu Dìngyuǎn and Yuán Wényáo, all spoke to the Qí Lord,
requesting that Shìkāi be sent out to a provincial post.
It happened that Empress Dowager Hú was entertaining the court nobles in the front hall,
and Ruì openly presented Shìkāi's faults, saying:
"Shìkāi was merely the late emperor's jester,
a 'city fox and temple rat,'
accepting bribes
and defiling the palace.
We, your subjects, are bound by righteousness not to remain silent,
and risk death to speak of this."
The Empress Dowager said:
"When the late emperor was alive,
why did you, princes, not speak?
Do you now wish to deceive this orphan and widow?
Drink your wine,
and say no more!"
Ruì and the others' expressions and words became even more stern.
Yítóng Sānsī Ān Tǔgēn said:
"Your subject was originally a Hu merchant. (Ān Tǔgēn
was originally a Parthian Hu person.
In the early Tiānpíng era,
the Ròurán ruler sent an envoy to Jìnyáng.
Tǔgēn secretly reported the Ròurán's situation,
and Gāo Huān prepared accordingly.
When the Ròurán raided,
they gained nothing and returned.
Afterward, Huān made peace and formed a marriage alliance with the Ròurán,
with Tǔgēn serving as the envoy for all of these arrangements.
He later returned to Huān
and was thereupon treated with intimacy and trust.
Having received such profound grace,
how dare I fear death!
If Shìkāi is not removed,
the court and the populace will not be at peace."
The Empress Dowager said:
"We will discuss this another day.
All of you, princes, may disperse!"
Ruì and the others either threw their caps to the ground
or flicked their robes and rose.
The next day,
Ruì and the others again went to Yúnlóngmén,
ordering Wényáo to enter and present their petition.
Three times,
the Empress Dowager refused to listen.
Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Duàn Sháo had Hú Chángcàn convey the Empress Dowager's message, saying:
"The emperor's coffin is still in mourning,
and matters are too urgent.
We wish for you, princes, to reconsider!"
Ruì and the others then all bowed in thanks.
Chángcàn reported back,
and the Empress Dowager said:
"That my sister and her son's family is secure
is thanks to my brother's efforts."
Chángcàn
was the brother of Empress Dowager Hú,
hence she said this.
They were dismissed.
The Empress Dowager and the Qí Lord summoned Shìkāi and questioned him.
He replied:
"Among your subjects,
the late emperor treated me the most favorably.
Your Majesty is still in the period of deep mourning,
and the great ministers all harbor ambitions.
If I am sent away now,
it would be precisely to clip Your Majesty's wings.
It would be best to tell Ruì:
'Wényáo and I
were both entrusted and employed by the late emperor.
How can one be dismissed while the other remains?
Both can serve as provincial governors,
and for now, continue to handle matters as before.
The Shàngshū handles imperial decrees;
let him temporarily retain his current duties.
Then, send them away.'
Ruì and the others will believe I am truly leaving
and will certainly be pleased."
The Emperor and Empress Dowager agreed with this
and informed Ruì and the others as he had suggested.
Thereupon, Shìkāi was appointed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Wényáo was appointed Xīyǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xīyǎnzhōu
was at that time governed from Huátái.
Ruì and the others urged Shìkāi to depart.
The Empress Dowager wished to keep Shìkāi for more than a hundred days.
(In ancient times, the Yú sacrifice was performed on the day of burial.
After three Yú sacrifices, the mourning concluded on a strong day.
Later generations concluded mourning after a hundred days,
which remains the custom to this day.)
Within a few days,
the Empress Dowager repeatedly spoke of this.
A palace attendant, knowing the Empress Dowager's secret intention,
said to Ruì:
"Since Her Majesty's will is thus,
why should Your Highness stubbornly resist?"
Ruì said:
"My commission is not light.
The current heir is young and impulsive;
how can I allow a wicked minister to remain at his side?
If I do not protect him with my life,
how can I face heaven?"
He then went to see the Empress Dowager again
and spoke bitterly.
The Empress Dowager ordered wine to be poured and offered to Ruì.
Ruì, with a stern expression, said:
"Today we discuss important affairs of state,
not a cup of wine!"
Having spoken,
he hastily left.
Shìkāi brought beautiful women and pearl curtains to Lóu Dìngyuǎn
and offered his thanks, saying:
"The nobles wished to kill Shìkāi,
but thanks to Your Highness's power,
(Wǔchéng Dì had enfeoffed Lóu Dìngyuǎn as Línhuái Jùnwáng,
hence the address.)
I have been appointed a provincial governor.
Now I must take my leave,
and respectfully present two maidens
and one pearl curtain."
Dìngyuǎn was pleased
and said to Shìkāi:
"Do you wish to return to the court?"
Shìkāi said:
"I have long been uneasy in the court.
Now that I can leave,
I have truly achieved my original ambition,
and do not wish to return.
I only beg Your Highness's protection,
and to forever be a governor of a large province is enough."
Dìngyuǎn believed him.
When he saw him to the gate,
Shìkāi said:
"Now that I am to travel far,
I wish to bid farewell to the two palaces."
Dìngyuǎn granted this.
Shìkāi was thus able to see the Empress Dowager and the Emperor.
He then made his case, saying:
"The late emperor suddenly passed away,
and I am ashamed that I could not die with him.
Observing the intentions of the court nobles,
they wish to make Your Majesty a puppet ruler.
(Gānmíng
was the era name of Jǐnán Wáng of Qí.
The matter is recorded in scroll 168, Wén Dì, Tiānjiā first year.)
There will surely be a great change,
and how can I face the late emperor in the underworld?"
Thereupon, he wept bitterly.
The Emperor and Empress Dowager both cried
and asked:
"What is the plan?"
Shìkāi said:
"Since I have been allowed to enter,
what more is there to worry about?
I only need a few imperial edicts."
Thereupon, an edict was issued appointing Dìngyuǎn as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and charging Zhào Jùnwáng Ruì with the crime of disloyalty.
The next day,
Ruì was again about to enter to remonstrate.
His wife and children all tried to stop him,
but Ruì said:
"The affairs of the state are grave;
I would rather die serving the late emperor
than bear to see the court in distress."
When he reached the palace gate,
someone else said to him:
"Your Highness, do not enter;
there might be trouble."
Ruì replied:
"I have not betrayed Heaven above,
so I will have no regrets even if I die."
He entered
and saw the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager again spoke to him on the matter,
but Ruì held his ground even more firmly.
When he came out
and reached Yong'àng,
he encountered soldiers
who arrested him and sent him to the Quèlí Buddhist temple in Huálín Park.
Shìshì Xīyù Jì (Record of the Western Regions by Sakya): Forty Lǐ north of the Kuīcí kingdom,
there is a temple on a mountain,
named Quèlí,
which is extremely pure;
hence, a Buddhist temple was built in imitation of it.
Ruì had long presided over the court administration.
During the reign of Emperor Wénxuān,
Jǐnán acted as regent for the crown prince,
and the Grand Commander-in-chief's office was established,
which, along with the Department of State Affairs, jointly managed various matters.
Ruì was appointed acting Chief Clerk of the Grand Commander-in-chief's office.
By the time of Emperor Wǔchéng's era,
he was appointed Minister of State Affairs,
then promoted to acting Superintendent of State Affairs,
and further promoted to Grand Commandant.

Kùdí Fúlián, Gāo Shèluò, Wáng Zǐyí, Liú Pìqiáng, and Dūdu Dí Xiǎnguì were arrested,
dismembered in the rear garden,
and exposed in the main streets of the capital.
The Emperor wished to kill all the civil and military officials in Yǎn's retinue,
but Guāng said:
"These are all sons of meritorious and noble families;
if you execute them,
I fear it will cause unrest among the people."
Zhào Yànshēn also said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals blames the commander."
Thereupon, their punishments varied.
The Empress Dowager questioned Yǎn,
and Yǎn said:
"Féng Zǐcóng taught me."
The Empress Dowager was enraged,
and sent an envoy to the inner court to strangle Zǐcóng with a bowstring.
She then had the inner attendants use a supply cart to carry his body home.
Inner attendants
were eunuchs.
A supply cart
was used to carry storehouse goods.
Each meal had to be tasted by her personally.
This was out of fear of poison.
In the 17th year, in the eighth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
the Qí Lord went to Jìnyáng.
In the 18th year, in the ninth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Qí appointed Rènchéng Wáng Jiē as Tàizǎi,
and Féngyì Wáng Rùn as Tàishī.
On the 19th year, on the Jǐwèi day,
Duàn Sháo, the Qí Píngyuán Zhōngwǔ Wáng, died.
Sháo possessed strategy and resourcefulness,
and gained the utmost loyalty of his officers and soldiers.
When he was in command of the armies outside,
and consulted in the inner chambers within,
his achievements were great and his prestige high.
Yet, his nature was gentle and prudent,
embodying the qualities of a prime minister.
He was filial to his stepmother,
and his household was harmonious and solemn.
Among the meritorious and noble families of Qí,
none could equal him.
In the 20th year, Zǔ Tǐng of Qí persuaded Lù Lìngxún
to send Zhào Yànshēn out as the Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu.
The Qí Lord appointed Tǐng as Shìzhōng.
Lù Lìngxún persuaded the Emperor, saying:
"People say that King Lángyá is intelligent and courageous,
unmatched in the present age.
Observing his physiognomy,
he is probably not one to be a subject.
Since his unauthorized killing,
he has constantly harbored fear.
It is advisable to make plans for him early."
Favored retainers such as Hé Hóngzhēn also requested his execution.
The Emperor was undecided.
He secretly summoned Tǐng in a food carriage
and consulted him.
A food carriage
was used to transport meat and provisions to the Tàiguān.
"The Duke of Zhōu executed Guǎnshū.
The Duke of Zhōu had appointed Guǎnshū to oversee Yīn,
but Guǎnshū rebelled with Yīn,
so the Duke of Zhōu executed him.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ was ill,
and asked Shú Yá about the succession.
He replied:
'Qìngfù is talented.'
He asked Jì Yǒu.
Jì Yǒu said:
'Your servant is prepared to die to support Bān.'
Thereupon, he ordered Zhēn Jì to poison Shú Yá and established Bān.
Qìngfù had someone assassinate Bān.
Jì Yǒu established Duke Mǐn,
and Qìngfù again had someone assassinate him.
Jì Yǒu took Duke Xī to Zhū.
Qìngfù fled to Jǔ.
Jì Yǒu then returned
and established Duke Xī.
He sought Qìngfù from Jǔ with bribes,
and the people of Jǔ returned him.
When he reached Mì,
he sent Gōngzǐ Xīsī to plead for him,
but it was not permitted.
He wept and went.
Qìngfù heard it and said:
'That is the voice of Xīsī.'
Then he hanged himself.
Qìngfù, Shú Yá, and Jì Yǒu
were all sons of Duke Huán,
and were brothers.
However, the one who died by poison
was Shú Yá.
Indeed, there were Hàn Confucians who judged cases based on the meaning of the classics.
Someone like Zǔ Tǐng,
however, manipulated the meaning of the classics to establish his case,
which must be carefully examined."
The Emperor ordered the Right General of the Guards, Zhào Yuánkǎn, to lure Yǎn and apprehend him.
Yuánkǎn said:
"Your servant formerly served the Late Emperor,
and saw the Late Emperor's love for the King.
Now, I would rather die
than perform this act."
The Emperor sent Yuánkǎn out as the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
the Emperor addressed the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Tomorrow morning, I wish to go hunting early with Rénwēi."
Yǎn's
courtesy name was Rénwēi.
The Emperor summoned Yǎn,
but Yǎn was suspicious.
Lù Lìngxún said:
"Your elder brother calls;
why do you not go, my son!"
Yǎn went out,
and upon reaching the Yǒngxiàng,
Liú Táozhī tied his hands behind his back.
Yǎn cried out:
"I beg to see Our family, and my respected elder brother!"
Táozhī stuffed his mouth with his sleeve,
covered his head with a reversed robe, and carried him out.
Upon reaching the Dàmíng Gōng,
his face was covered in nosebleed.
He was strangled to death,
at the age of fourteen.
He was wrapped in a mat
and buried inside the palace.
The Emperor had the Empress Dowager informed,
and the Empress Dowager wept over him
for more than ten cries,
then was immediately escorted back into the palace.
His four posthumous sons
all died in confinement.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Jīngjī Fǔ was abolished
and incorporated into the Lǐngjūn.
This was because Yǎn had used the Jīngjī troops to play with weapons,
hence its abolition.
On the 21st year, on the Rénwǔ day,
Zhōu Jì Gōng Tōng died.
On the 22nd year, on the Jiǎshēn day,
the Emperor performed offerings at the Tàimiào.
The 23rd day of the *yǐwèi*
year, Zhōu sent the Right Wǔbó, Gǔ Huìkūn (谷會琨) and others, to Qí on a diplomatic mission.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: Zhōu established Left and Right Wǔbó,
who were in charge of the internal and external guard regulations,
and also commanded the six divisions of soldiers.
Two Left and Right Xiǎowǔbó (小武伯) each assisted them.
Gǔ Huì (谷會)
is a Hú (胡) compound surname.
On the 24th day, Qí Hú Tàihòu (齊胡太后) was indiscreet in her comings and goings,
and had an affair with the Shāmén Tǒng (沙門統), Tánxiàn (曇獻).
Some monks even playfully called Tánxiàn (曇獻) the "Tàishàng Huáng" (太上皇, Emperor Emeritus).
The Qí Zhǔ (齊主) heard that the Empress Dowager was not behaving properly but did not believe it.
Later, when he paid a visit to the Empress Dowager,
he saw two nuns.
He was pleased and summoned them,
but they turned out to be men.
Thereupon, the affair of Tánxiàn (曇獻) was also exposed,
and all were executed.
On the *jǐhài*
day, the Emperor returned to Yè (鄴) from Jìnyáng (晉陽), bringing the Empress Dowager with him.
When they reached Zǐmò (紫陌),
they encountered a great wind.
Shèrén (舍人) Wèi Sēngjiā (魏僧伽), who was skilled in observing winds,
reported:
"A violent rebellion is imminent."
The Emperor falsely claimed

and, drawing his bow and wrapping its tip,

He sent the eunuch Dèng Chángyóng (鄧長顒) to imprison the Empress Dowager in the Northern Palace,
and also ordered that no relatives, internal or external, should be allowed to see Hú Tàihòu (胡太后).
The Empress Dowager sometimes prepared food for the Emperor,

On the 25th day of *gēngxū*,
Qí sent the Shìzhōng (侍中), Hèlián Zǐyuè (赫連子悅), on a diplomatic mission to Zhōu.
On the 26th day, in the eleventh month,

day, the Zhōu Zhǔ (周主) went to Sǎnguān (散關).
Sǎn (散) is pronounced *xīdàn*.

On the *guǐyǒu*

On the 28th day, in the twelfth month,

On the 29th day of *rénchén*,
Shàolíng Gōng Zhāng Zhāodá (邵陵公章昭達) passed away.

Zhí (直) agreed to this,

in Lexiāng (樂鄉) County of Jìnglíng (竟陵) Commandery,

Western Wèi (西魏) established Ruòzhōu (鄀州).

The Ruòzhōu (鄀州) that Zhōu (周) now granted

Later Zhōu (後周) established Píngzhōu (平州).

first month,

The Shàngshū (尚書) office had two Púyè (僕射),
divided into Left and Right.
If one Púyè (僕射) was abolished,
then the title would simply be Púyè (僕射).
2. On the *jǐsì*
day, the Qí Zhǔ (齊主) performed a sacrifice at the Southern Suburb.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: The Later Qí (後齊) system stipulated that the Yuánqiū (圜丘) and Fāngzé (方澤) sacrifices were performed once every three years,
called *dìsì* (禘祀).
The Southern and Northern Suburb sacrifices were performed annually,
always on the first *xīn* day of the first month.
The present text records *jǐsì*,
which means it was the beginning of the fasting period.
For the Southern Suburb,
an altar was built south of the capital,
thirty-six feet in circumference,
nine feet high,
with one staircase on each of the four sides.
Three enclosures were made.
The inner enclosure was twenty-five paces from the altar.
The middle and outer enclosures were the same distance apart as the inner enclosure.
Each of the four sides had one gate.
A large camp was also built outside the outer enclosure,
two hundred seventy paces in circumference.
The camp moat was ten feet wide
and eight feet deep,
with one gate on each of the four sides.
A sacrificial pyre altar was also built in the *bǐng* (丙) position outside the middle enclosure,
twenty-seven feet in circumference,
one foot eight inches high,
with one staircase on each of the four sides.
The spirit of the Emperor Gǎndì Língwēiyǎng (感帝靈威仰) was worshipped at the altar,
with Gāozǔ Shénwǔ Huángdì (高祖神武皇帝) as the co-sacrificed deity.
The ritual used four *guī* (圭) jade tablets,
and there were ceremonial silks,
each matching the color of its direction.
For the Lord-on-High and the co-sacrificed Emperor,
one red, unblemished sacrificial animal was used for each.

In the Zhōu official system,

Shī replied:
"The Dragon constellation has just appeared;
according to ritual, a Yú sacrifice should be offered.
It is not a real dragon."
Ānàgōng angrily said:
"These Hàn people are too meddlesome,
insisting on knowing about constellations!"
So, no sacrifice was performed.
Shī left,
secretly sighing:
"Since the rites have been abandoned,
how can Qí last long!"
The Qí army selected tall and strong men to be the vanguard.
There were also the Cāngtóu, Xījiǎo, and Dàlì units,
whose vanguard was very sharp.
There were also Hú people from the Western Regions,
who were skilled archers,
never missing a shot.
All the armies particularly feared them.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
they fought at Lǘliáng.
Lǘliáng is in Péngchéng.
It is suspected that this is Shíliáng.
Wú Míngchè said to Bāshān Tàishǒu Xiāo Móhē:
"If you kill this Hú archer,
then their army will lose morale,
and your talent will be no less than Guān Yǔ's."
Móhē replied:
"Please show me his appearance;
I will take him for you."
Míngchè then summoned a surrendered person who recognized the Hú archer,
had him point him out,
and personally poured wine for Móhē to drink.
After Móhē finished drinking,
he spurred his horse and charged into the Qí army.
The Hú archer boldly stepped out about ten paces in front of the formation,
drew his bow but had not yet fired.
Móhē threw his iron spear from afar,
hitting him squarely in the forehead,
and he fell instantly.
More than ten Dàlì warriors from the Qí army came out to fight,
and Móhē also cut them down.
Thereupon, the Qí army was greatly defeated,
and Wèi Pòhú fled.
A textual variation note says: The Běi Qí Shū states that
Pòhú's defeat was in the fifth month.
Here, we follow the Qí Shū.
When Pòhú set out with the army,
the Qí people had Shìzhōng Wáng Lín accompany him.
Lín said to Pòhú:
"The Wú troops are very sharp;
you should use a long-term strategy to control them.
Be careful not to fight recklessly!"
Pòhú did not listen and was defeated.
Lín barely escaped on a single horse,
returned
to Péngchéng,
and the Qí people then sent him to Shòuyáng to recruit troops to resist the Chén army,
and again appointed Lú Qián as Yángzhōudào Xíngtái Shàngshū.
25 On the *guǐhài* day,
Huáng Fǎkè united the prefecture.
From this, we can see
that those who previously surrendered
were the garrison soldiers of Héféi.
Jù and jù are both read as *jù*.
According to the *Dìxíng Zhì* (Treatise on Geography): The Liáng dynasty established Rénzhōu,
with its seat at Chìkǎnchéng,
which was probably within Shānyáng Xiàn's borders.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
it was conquered.
26 (The emperor) administered the Míngtáng.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì* (History of the Five Dynasties): The Chén dynasty system: The Míngtáng Hall had twelve rooms,
with six central rooms,
where six thrones were placed.
The emperors of the four directions were each in their respective direction,
and the Yellow Emperor resided in the *kūnwéi* (southwest corner).
Zhì is read as *zhì*.
27 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *wùchén* day,
Qí sent Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Lù Qiān to lead 20,000 troops to relieve Qíchāng.
They emerged from Bā and Qí,
meaning from between the Bāshuǐ and Qíshuǐ.
Jiàng is read as *jiàng*.
Qí has the sound *jī*,
and also *qí*.
Xīyáng Jùn was within Huánggāng Xiàn's borders.
Jiǒng is read as *gūjiǒng*,
and also *gǔhuì*.
(Chén Qǐng) set up a diversionary force to confront them,
and personally led elite troops
along a secret path to ambush their rear,
thoroughly defeating them.
On the *jǐsì* day,
Grand General Pínběi Wú Míngchè's army reached Xiákǒu,
conquering the city on its north bank;
the defenders on the south bank abandoned the city and fled.
Xiákǒu refers to Xiáshíkǒu.
Two cities were built on either side of the banks to block the Huáiliú.
Wú Míngchè was promoted in rank for his achievements,
rising from second rank, second class, to second rank, first class.
Later, Qí established Bāzhōu in Huánggāng.
(They) also killed its garrison commander
and surrendered the city.
Qí's Bālíng Wáng Wáng Lín and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Guìxiǎn defended the outer city of Shòuyáng.
Wú Míngchè, seeing that Lín had just entered
and the morale of his troops was not yet firm,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
attacked them at night,
and the city collapsed.
The Qí troops retreated to defend Xiàngguóchéng and Jīnchéng.
Both cities were within Shòuyángchéng.
Xiàngguóchéng
was built by Liú Yù when he attacked Cháng'ān,
hence its name.
Jīnchéng
was the central city of Shòuyáng.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
the central city was commonly called Jīnchéng.
Eighth month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
Shānyángchéng surrendered.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Jiāngdū Jùn's Shānyáng Xiàn,
previously established as Shānyáng Jùn.
On the *rényín* day,
Xūyíchéng surrendered.
Xūyí Xiàn also belonged to Jiāngdū,
previously established as Xūyí Jùn.
Xūyí is pronounced *xūyí*.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn Xú Jìngbiàn conquered Hǎi'ānchéng.
According to the Chén system: Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn was of rank eight,
with a salary of six hundred *dàn*.
Hǎi'ānchéng
was to the east of Hǎilíng Xiàn,
now Hǎi'ān Zhèn.
Dōnghǎi Jùn:
The Liáng dynasty established Southern and Northern Qīngzhōu,
now Qúshān Xiàn.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Pínggù Hóu Jìngtài and others conquered Jìnzhōu.
Pínggù Xiàn,
according to Shěn Yuē's *Zhì*,
belonged to Nánkāng Jùn.
The Wú established it
and called it Píngyáng.
Jìn Wǔdì changed its name in the first year of Tàikāng.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Tóng'ān Jùn:
The Liáng dynasty established Jìnzhōu,
named after Jìnxī.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Yángpíngchéng surrendered.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Jiāngdū Jùn's Ānyí Xiàn:
The Liáng dynasty established Yángpíng Jùn.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Gāoyáng Tàishǒu Shěn Shànqìng conquered Mǎtóuchéng.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Zhōnglí Jùn's Túshān Xiàn,
anciently Dāngtú,
later Qí established Mǎtóu Jùn.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Qí'ānchéng surrendered.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Yǒng'ān Jùn's Huánggāng Xiàn:
Later Qí established Qí'ān Jùn.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Fán Yì conquered Guǎnglíng Chǔzǐchéng.
This Guǎnglíng is not the Guǎnglíng of Jiāngdū.
According to historical records: During the Tàihé reign of the Wèi dynasty,
the barbarian chief Tián Yìzōng ceded land to Wèi.
Wèi established Dōngyùzhōu for him,
with its seat at Guǎnglíngchéng.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Rǔnán Jùn's Xīnxī Xiàn:
Wèi established Dōngyùzhōu.
Thus, this Guǎnglíng is the Guǎnglíng of Xīnxī.
Also,
Liáng Wǔdì established Chǔzhōu in Chéngyáng Xiàn of Rǔnán Jùn,
with its seat at Chǔchéng,
which is Chǔzǐchéng.
According to the *Shuǐjīng* (Classic of Waterways): The Huáishuǐ first passed Chéngyáng Xiàn and then Xīnxī Xiàn,
from which we know that Guǎnglíngchéng and Chǔzǐchéng were close to each other.
28 On the *rénwǔ* day,
the Zhōu Crown Prince Yūn married the Yáng family.
She was the daughter of Grand General Suí Gōng Yáng Jiān.
This laid the groundwork for Yáng Jiān to usurp Zhōu as the Empress's father.
The Crown Prince was fond of associating with petty people.
Zuǒ Gōngzhèng Yǔwén Xiàobó spoke to the Zhōu sovereign, saying:
"The Crown Prince is looked up to by all within the four seas,
yet his virtuous reputation is unheard of.
I, as a humble palace official, indeed bear this responsibility.
Moreover, he is still young,
and his aspirations and achievements are not yet complete.
I request that upright individuals be carefully selected
to be his teachers and friends,
to guide and protect his sacred nature,
hoping that he will make daily progress and monthly advancement."
Jiù means 'to follow';
jiāng means 'to act'.
It means to engage in learning,
intending to practice it.
Zhèng Xuán said: "Daily progress and monthly advancement" means that one should diligently practice and accumulate knowledge.
"Otherwise, regret will be too late."
The Emperor composed himself and said:
"Your family has been upright for generations,
exhausting their sincerity in serving.
Observing your words,
they show your family's integrity."
Xiàobó bowed and thanked him, saying:
"It is not difficult to speak,
but difficult to accept."
The Emperor said:
"Who among upright people could surpass you!"
Thereupon, Wèichí Yùn was appointed Ròu Gōngzhèng.
Yùn
was a disciple of Jiǒng.
The Emperor once asked Wànnián Xiànchéng, Nányáng Yuè Yùn:
"What kind of person do you say the Crown Prince is?"
He replied:
"An ordinary person."
The Emperor turned to Qí Gōng Xiàn and said:
"All the officials flatter me,
calling the Crown Prince intelligent and wise.
Only Yùn's words are loyal and direct."
He then asked Yùn about the characteristics of an ordinary person.
He replied:
"Like Qí Huán Gōng:
with Guǎn Zhòng assisting him, he became a hegemon;
with Shù Diāo assisting him, he caused chaos.
He can be led to do good,
and he can be led to do evil."
The Emperor said:
"I understand."
Thereupon, he carefully selected palace officials to assist him,
and promoted Yùn to Jīngzhào Chéng.
He was promoted from Chìxiàn Chéng to Jīng Jùn Chéng.
(The Emperor's) intention was very displeased.
29 On the *guǐwèi* day,
Shěn Jūnlǐ passed away.
On the 30th day, *rénchén* (壬辰),
Rǔ Tiānnìan (魯天念), former Grand Administrator of Póyáng (鄱陽), captured Huángchéng (黃城).
According to the *Dìxíng Zhì* (地形志),
under Qíaozhōu (譙州) and Xiàcài Jùn (下蔡郡), there is Huángchéng Xiàn (黃城縣).
By this, when the Eastern Wèi (東魏) established Qíaozhōu (譙州) at Wōyáng (渦陽),
then Huángchéng (黃城) was also one of its subordinate counties.
Xiàcài (下蔡) was north of the Huái (淮),
while Huángchéng (黃城) was west of Shòuyáng (壽陽).
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The Cháishuǐ (柴水) flows east, passing west of Huángchéng (黃城),
which was the former Yìyáng Xiàn (弋陽縣).
Within the city were two smaller cities;
the western one was Huángchéng (黃城).
The Cháishuǐ (柴水) flows northeast into the Huái (淮),
known as Huáikǒu (淮口).
At noon,
Guō Mò's (郭默) city surrendered.
As the Jìn (晉) house was not strong,
and Liú (劉) and Shí (石) were powerful;
Guō Mò (郭默) had migrated south,
building a city to protect himself,
hence its name.
On the 31st day, *jǐhài* (己亥),
Zhōu Hóngzhèng (周弘正), *tèjìn* (特進) and concurrently Libationer of the Directorate of Education, was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Zhāng Diāo (張雕), Libationer of the Directorate of Education in Qí (齊),
taught the classics to the Qí (齊) sovereign as an imperial lecturer,
and the Emperor greatly esteemed him.
Diāo (雕) allied with the favored *Hú* (胡) Hán Hóngzhēn (何洪珍),
but Mù Típó (穆提婆) and Hán Chángluán (韓長鸞) disliked him.
Hóngzhēn (洪珍) recommended Diāo (雕) as a Grandee Remonstrant,
adding the title of *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司),
to report on financial affairs.
He was greatly trusted and relied upon by the Emperor,
who often called him
"Doctor."
Diāo (雕), considering his humble origins
and rise to a high ministerial position,
wished to establish achievements to repay this favor.
His discussions and proposals were forthright,
without avoidance.
He reduced unnecessary expenses in the imperial palace,
restrained the arrogant and unrestrained officials around the Emperor,
frequently criticized the favored and powerful,
and offered advice behind the imperial curtain.
The Emperor also deeply relied on him.
Diāo (雕) thus took the purification of the government as his personal responsibility,
with very high spirits,
which made the powerful and favored look askance at him.
Fēng Xiàoyǎn (封孝琰), Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs,
was the nephew of Fēng Lóngzhī (封隆之).
Fēng Lóngzhī (封隆之)
had raised troops for Gāo (高),
and was a minister who helped establish the dynasty.
Both were greatly favored by Zǔ Tíng (祖珽).
Xiàoyǎn (孝琰) once said to Tíng (珽):
"You, sir, are a cultured and distinguished chancellor,
different from others."
The Emperor's close attendants heard this
and greatly resented it.
At that time, the Qí (齊) sovereign was about to go to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Jì Shū (季舒) discussed with Zhāng Diāo (張雕),
believing that:
"Shòuyáng (壽陽) is under siege,
and the main army is out to resist it.
Messengers travel back and forth,
*shǐ* (使) means *shūlì* (疏吏) here.
They need to receive instructions.
Moreover, common people on the roads
might be frightened,
thinking that the imperial carriage is heading to Bīngzhōu (幷州)
to avoid the southern invaders.
If we do not remonstrate,
I fear the populace will be alarmed."
So he and the accompanying civil officials jointly submitted a remonstrance.
At that time, the high officials Zhào Yànshēn (趙彥深), Táng Yōng (唐邕), Duàn Xiàoyán (段孝言), etc.,
had differing opinions.
Jì Shū (季舒) argued with them,
but no decision was reached.
Chángluán (長鸞) quickly told the Emperor:
"These Han (漢) officials have jointly signed their names,
claiming to remonstrate against going to Bīngzhōu (幷州),
but in reality, they might not be rebelling.
They should be punished."
On the day *xīnchǒu* (辛丑),
the Qí (齊) sovereign summoned all those who had signed their names to gather at the Hánzhāng Diàn (含章殿),
and executed Jì Shū (季舒), Diāo (雕), Xiàoyǎn (孝琰), as well as Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Liú Tì (劉逖), Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Péi Zé (裴澤), and Guō Zūn (郭遵) in the palace courtyard.
Their families were all exiled to the northern frontier,
women were assigned to the *xīguān* (奚官),
young boys were castrated,
and their property was confiscated.
On the day *guǐmǎo* (癸卯),
he then proceeded to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) attacked Shòuyáng (壽陽),
damming the Féishuǐ (肥水) to inundate the city.
According to the *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註): The Féishuǐ (肥水) passes Shòuyáng (壽陽) city and flows into the Huái (淮).
However, diverting the water into the city,
crisscrossing within the city,
and Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) damming it to flood the city
was easy and convenient.
Six or seven tenths of the inhabitants died.
Pí Jǐnghé (皮景和) of Lángxié (琅邪), Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs for Qí (齊) Military Affairs, etc., came to relieve Shòuyáng (壽陽).
After "Lángxié" (琅邪),
the character "Wáng" (王) is probably omitted.
They were timid and dared not advance,
encamping at Huáikǒu (淮口).
Huáikǒu (淮口) is likely Yǐngkǒu (潁口).
Jǐnghé's (景和) army set out from Yǐngshàng (潁上), reached the Huái (淮), and encamped,
hence it was called Huáikǒu (淮口).
However, they had just crossed the Huái (淮).
*Rán* (然) means "thus."
Thus, they had just crossed the Huái (淮).
Thirty *lǐ* from Shòuyáng (壽陽),
they halted their army and did not advance.
All the generals were apprehensive,
saying:
"The strong city has not yet fallen,
and a large relief force is nearby.
What shall we do?"
Míngchè (明徹) said:
"Speed is essential in warfare,
but they have established camp and do not advance,
thus blunting their own edge.
I know they dare not fight,
this is clear."
On the day *yǐsì* (乙巳),
he personally donned armor and helmet,
launching a fierce assault from all four sides.
He captured it in one swift attack,
taking Wáng Lín (王琳), Wáng Guìxiǎn (王貴顯), Lú Qián (盧潛), and Fúfēng Wáng Kězhūhún Dàoyù (扶風王可朱渾道裕), and Assistant Director of the Left Lǐ Táotú (李騊駼) alive and sending them to Jiànkāng (建康).
Kězhūhún (可朱渾) is a three-character barbarian surname.
*Táo* (騊) is pronounced *tuódāo*.
*Tú* (駼) is pronounced *tóngdū*.
He seized all their camels, horses, and baggage train.
Lín (琳) had a refined and elegant appearance,
and his emotions were not evident on his face.
He had a strong memory and sharp mind;
among the thousands of his military and civil subordinates,
he knew all their names.
His punishments were not excessive,
he valued men more than wealth,
and thus won the hearts of his officers and soldiers.
Although he had lost territory and was a refugee in Yè (鄴),
the Qí (齊) people all respected his loyalty and righteousness.
When he was captured,
many of his former officers and soldiers were in Míngchè's (明徹) army.
Those who saw him sighed deeply,
unable to look up,
and competed to plead for his life
and offer provisions.
Míngchè (明徹), fearing they might cause trouble,
sent an envoy to pursue and execute him twenty *lǐ* east of Shòuyáng (壽陽).
The sound of weeping was like thunder.
An old man came with wine and dried meat to offer sacrifices,
wept with profound grief,
collected his blood, and departed.
Farmers and country folk,
whether they knew him or not,
all shed tears upon hearing of it.
Mù Típó (穆提婆) and Hán Chángluán (韓長鸞) of Qí (齊), hearing of the fall of Shòuyáng (壽陽),
continued playing *shuò* (槊) without interruption,
saying:
"It originally belonged to them,
let them take it back."
The southern and northern armies contended,
and Shòuyáng (壽陽) originally belonged to Jiāngnán (江南),
hence they said so.
The histories state that the Qí (齊) ruler and his ministers indulged in pleasure to forget their worries.
They were somewhat worried,
but Típó (提婆) and others said:
"Even if the state loses everything south of the Yellow River,
we can still form a Kuchean (龜茲) kingdom.
Moreover, life is but a fleeting stay;
we should only seek pleasure.
Why bother with sorrow?"
The favored attendants around the Emperor then jointly echoed this,
and the Emperor immediately rejoiced,
drinking heavily and dancing.
He then ordered the construction of a city and garrison at Líyáng (黎陽) by the river.
Fearing the arrival of Chén's (陳) forces,
he truly intended to draw a line at the river to protect himself.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Qí sent ten thousand soldiers to Yǐngkǒu,
the mouth where the Yǐng River enters the Huái River.
On the *xīnhài* day,
soldiers were sent to reinforce Cānglíng,
and they were again defeated.
According to the *Dìxíng Zhì* (Treatise on Geography): in Shòuchūn County, Huáinán Commandery, Yángzhōu,
there was formerly Cānglíng City of Chǔ.
According to the *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* (Commentary on the Classic of Waters): The Huái River flows eastward,
meets the Yǐngkǒu,
then flows southeast past the north of Cānglíng,
then flows northeast,
past the west of the old city of Shòuchūn County.
He was rewarded,
and appointed Minister of the Secretariat (*shàngshūlìng*).
On the *bǐngchén* day,
an imperial edict restored Shòuyáng as Yùzhōu,
following the old system of Sòng and Qí.
Míngchè was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief of Yù, Hé, and other six prefectures, Grand General of Cavalry and Chariots (*chējì dàjiāngjūn*), and Governor of Yùzhōu (*yùzhōu cìshǐ*).
The Palace Usher Xiāo Chúnfēng was sent to Shòuyáng to perform the investiture ceremony.
An altar was set up south of the city,
with twenty thousand soldiers
arrayed with banners, drums, halberds, and armor.
Míngchè ascended the altar, bowed to receive the appointment,
completed the ceremony, and retired.
His generals and soldiers honored him.
The Emperor hosted a banquet,
raised his cup, and addressed Xú Líng, saying:
"I reward you for your discernment of men."
Líng rose from his seat and said:
"The decision was made by Your Sacred Wisdom;
it is not due to my effort."
Huáng Fǎ was appointed Grand General Who Conquers the West (*zhēngxī dàjiāngjūn*) and Governor of Hézhōu (*hézhōu cìshǐ*).
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Zhàntuó captured Qíchāng City.
In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎxū* day,
Huáiyīn City surrendered.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì* (Treatise of the Five Dynasties): Jiāngdū Commandery, Shānyáng County, had Huáiyīn Commandery.
Upon its surrender,
its households were moved across the river.
On the *gēngchén* day,
General Who Manifests Might (*wēilǔ jiāngjūn*) Liú Táozhī captured Qúshān City.
According to the Chén system: General Who Manifests Might
was of the eighth rank
and received a salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
This Liú Táozhī was naturally a Chén general,
not the Liú Táozhī of Qí.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*,
Dōnghǎi Commandery had Qúshān County.
Qú
is pronounced *qú*.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Fán Yì captured Jìyīn City.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: Zhōnglí Commandery, Huàmíng County,
was formerly called Suīlíng,
and Jìyīn Commandery was established there.
Jì
is pronounced *zǐlǐ*.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Lǔ Guǎngdá attacked Jìnán Xúzhōu,
and captured it.
"濟" (Jì)
should be
The text says
"Qínán Xú"
to distinguish it from Nánxú of Jīngkǒu.
According to an examination of the *Wǔdài Shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties),
Qí's Nánxúzhōu
was originally established in Sùyù County, Xiàpī Commandery.
A detailed note is provided under "Kǎoyì" (Textual Criticism).
He garrisoned that place.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Both the Imperial Annals and the Biography of Guǎngdá in the *Chén Shū*
state "Běixúzhōu".
According to the Biography of Zǔ Tǐng in the *Běi Qí Shū*:
"Tǐng preserved Běixúzhōu city from falling."
Perhaps southerners referred to Jīngkǒu as Nánxúzhōu,
and thus called this place Běixúzhōu,
but it was actually Běi Qí's Nánxúzhōu.
According to this, the so-called Qí Nánxúzhōu
was the old Lángyé Commandery.
In the early Tàishǐ reign of Sòng,
Lángyé fell to Wèi.
In the second year of the Yǒng'ān reign of Emperor Zhuāng,
Běixúzhōu was established in Lángyé.
