Yáng Jiān, the Zǒngguǎn of Bózhōu, was appointed Shàngzhùguó and Dàsīmǎ.
Wǔdài Zhì: Qiáojùn,
during the Hòuwèi, was established as Nányánzhōu;
during the Hòuzhōu, a Zǒngguǎnfǔ was established,
later renamed Bózhōu.
Bó,
is pronounced as "páng gè fān".
19 On the day Guǐhài,
the Zhōu主 honored his birth mother, Lǐ氏, as Dìtàihòu.
His principal wife, Āshǐnà氏, had already been honored as Huángtàihòu,
and now his birth mother was honored as Dìtàihòu.
20 Eighth month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
the Zhōu主 sacrificed at the Xījiāo.
Wǔdài Zhì: The Hòuzhōu had five suburban altars,
their height and distance from the capital were according to the number of their directions.
Their square shape was all one hundred and twenty步,
and the inner enclosure was half of that.
On the day Rénshēn,
it was similar to Tóngzhōu.
Dàsītú Gōng Liàng was appointed Zǒngguǎn of Ānzhōu.
Shàngzhùguó Zhǎngsūn Lǎn was appointed Dàsītú.
Yáng Gōng Wáng Yì was appointed Dàsīkōng.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Yǒng
chāng Gōng Chūn was appointed Dàsīkòu.
21 Ninth month,
on the day Yǐsì,
the Fāngmíngtán was erected at Lóuhú.
On the day Wùshēn,
Shǐxīngwáng Shúlíng, the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, was appointed Wángguānbó,
to preside over the oath-taking of all officials.
Zhōulǐ: The Sīméng was in charge of the regulations for covenants and records.
Whenever there were doubts or gatherings and conferences in a state,
he managed the records of their covenants.
He faced north and proclaimed to the Míngshén.
After the covenant, he made a duplicate.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: "Yǒu yí" means
"not in agreement".
Míngshén are
the discerning gods,
referring to the sun, moon, mountains, and rivers.
The Jìnlǐ specifies adding a Fāngmíng on the altar,
which is how it should be followed.
"Zhào zhī" means
reading the record book to announce it.
"Èr zhī" means
writing a copy to be given to the six officials.
Chén Xiángdào said: When feudal lords had an audience with the Son of Heaven,
a palace of three hundred步 square was made,
with four gates.
The altar was twelve xún high,
four chǐ deep,
with a Fāngmíng placed on top.
The Fāngmíng in the Jìnlǐ
was made of wood,
four chǐ square.
It displayed six colors:
east was green,
south was red,
west was white,
north was black,
top was dark blue,
bottom was yellow.
It displayed six jades: top was guī,
bottom was bì,
south was zhāng,
west was hú,
east was guī,
north was huáng.
Zhèng氏 said: Fāngmíng symbolizes
the gods of the four directions, above and below.
When gathering for a covenant, the Míngshén oversee it.
The six colors
symbolize their gods.
The six jades are used to ritualize it.
The top should use a dark blue bì,
and the bottom should use a yellow cóng,
but if these are not used,
then the gods above and below are not the most honored among heaven and earth.
"Shè yù" means
carving the wood to attach them.
Wángguānbó:
In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven made a covenant with feudal lords,
he would have an elder of the Son of Heaven preside over it.
For example, at the Jiàntǔ covenant in the Chunqiū,
Wángzǐ Hǔ made a covenant with the feudal lords in the royal court,
this is what is called Wángguānbó.
At that time, Péngchéng had suffered a military defeat,
and the people of Chén, from top to bottom, were unsettled,
hence this covenant was made.
22 On the day Gēngxū,
the Zhōu主 enfeoffed his brother Yuán as Jīngwáng.
23 The Zhōu主 decreed:
"All who are to bow
shall complete the ritual with three bows."
Completing the ritual with three bows
was adopting barbarian rites.
24 On the day Jiǎyín,
the emperor proceeded to Lóuhú to swear an oath to the masses.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
envoys were dispatched to spread the oath to the four directions,
for mutual vigilance between superiors and subordinates.
25 In winter,
the Zhōu
主 returned to Cháng'ān.
Dàsīkōng Wáng Yì was appointed Zǒngguǎn of Xiāngzhōu.
Wǔdài Zhì: Xiāngyáng Jùn,
to the east of the Jiāng, Yōngzhōu was established as a temporary settlement;
the Xīwèi renamed it Xiāngzhōu.
26 On the day Wùzǐ,
Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè Lù Shàn was appointed Shàngshū Púshè.
27 Eleventh month,
the Tūjué invaded the Zhōu border,
besieged Jiǔquán,
and killed and plundered officials and common people.
Wǔdài Zhì: Fúlù Xiàn of Zhāngyè Jùn,
Jiǔquán Jùn was previously established there.
28 Twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Zhōu appointed Bìwáng Xián as Dàsīkōng.
29 On the day Jǐchǒu,
Zhōu appointed Téngwáng Yōu, the Zǒngguǎn of Héyáng, as Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
to lead troops in an invasion.
1 In spring,
first month,
on the day Guǐsì,
the Zhōu主 held court at the Lù Mén.
"Lù Mén"
should be
"Lùmén".
Lù means
"grand",
presumably the outer court of Zhōu.
Chéng Tàizhī, in his Yōnglù,
considered Táng Dàmínggōng Dānfèngmén and Tàijígōng Chéngtiānmén both as the outer courts of Táng,
presumably understanding this meaning.
Cháo is pronounced "zhí yáo fān".
From this, one can infer that the rulers and officials of Hòuzhōu
were likely wearing barbarian attire before this.
The reign era was changed to Dàchéng.
Four Fǔguān officials were established:
Dàzhǒngzǎi Yuèwáng Shèng was appointed Dàqiányí,
Zǒngguǎn of Xiāngzhōu Shǔ Gōng Yǔchí Huí was Dàyòubì,
Shēn Gōng Lǐ Mù was Dàzuǒfǔ,
and Dàsīmǎ Suí Gōng Yáng Jiān was Dàhòuchéng.
When the Lord of Zhōu first ascended the throne,
he deemed Emperor Gāozǔ's Fāmily Law [Xíngshū Yàozhì] to be too severe and abolished it.
For the implementation of Fāmily Law [Xíngshū Yàozhì] by Zhōu, see nine years prior.
Lè Yùn (樂運), Registrar of Jīngzhào (京兆) Commandery, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The 'lenient pardon for unintended disasters' [gěngzāi sìshè] mentioned in the Yú Shū [虞書] [Book of Yú]
refers to harm caused by mistakes,
for which a lenient pardon should be granted.
The Lǚ Xíng [呂刑] [Punishments of Lǚ] states: 'If there is doubt about the five punishments, there is a pardon.'
This means that if there is doubt about a punishment, one should err on the side of a lesser penalty;
if there is doubt about a penalty, one should err on the side of exemption.
Carefully examining the classics,
there is no mention of crimes regardless of their severity,
receiving a universal grand pardon [pǔtiān dàshè].
How can the Most Exalted [Dàzūn] frequently bestow extraordinary favors
to unleash the wickedness of traitors and villains!"
Dàzūn (大尊)
is equivalent to Zhìzūn (至尊) [Most Exalted].
Subsequently, the people became lax in breaking the law.
Moreover, he himself was extravagant, licentious, and prone to many faults,
disliking people's remonstrances [guījiàn].
He wished to be tyrannical and cruel,
to intimidate and subjugate his subordinates.
He then revised the Fāmily Law and Holy Edicts [Xíngjīng Shèngzhì].
Kǎoyì [考異] [Examination of Differences] states: The Zhōu Dì Jì [周帝紀] [Annals of the Zhōu Emperors] records that
the implementation of Fāmily Law and Holy Edicts [Xíngjīng Shèngzhì] was in the eighth month.
According to the biography of Yuán Yán (元巖) in the Suí Shǐ [隋史] [History of the Suí],
Lè Yùn's (樂運) remonstrance,
due to Yán's (巖) persuasion, was spared,
and after Wáng Guǐ's (王軌) death,
Yán (巖) was subsequently dismissed from office and remained at home.
Now, Yùn's (運) memorial already contains
the phrase "made the former regulations stricter" [gēng yán qián zhì],
which implies that the Fāmily Law [Xíngjīng] was implemented before Guǐ's (軌) death.
A grand offering ritual [dàjiào] was held at Zhèngwǔ Diàn (正武殿),
announced to Heaven, and performed.
Wǔdài Zhì [五代志] [Records of the Five Dynasties]: Dàojia (道家) fasting rituals: At night, under the stars,
wine, dried meat, various pastries, and currency offerings are arranged,
sacrificing successively to Tiānhuáng (天皇) [Heavenly Sovereign], Tàiyī (太一) [Grand Unity], the five planets, and the constellations.
A document is written,
incense is burned, and it is publicly read,
claiming to be presented to the Heavenly Bureau [Tiāncáo],
and this is called a Jiào (醮) [Offering Ritual].
Jiào (醮),
pronounced Zǐxiào [子肖翻].
For even minor faults,
immediate punishment and condemnation were meted out.
Furthermore,
having barely exceeded a year of mourning,
he indulged in music and entertainment.
Fish and dragon performances and various acrobatics [yúlóng bǎixì]
were constantly displayed before the palace,
Wǔdài Zhì [五代志]: During the Wǔpíng (武平) reign of Qí (齊),
there were fish and dragon displays, clowns, dwarfs, mountain chariots, giant elephants, well-drawing, melon-planting, horse-killing, donkey-skinning, and other strange and unusual acts,
over a hundred items,
known as bǎixì (百戲) [various acrobatics].
At that time, Zhèng Yì (鄭譯) was favored by the Lord of Zhōu,
who summoned the scattered entertainers of Qí (齊),
gathering them all in the capital for performances.
This was of the same genre as the Qín (秦) horn wrestling [jiǎodǐ].
He knew no rest;
he gathered many beautiful women to fill the inner palace,
increasing the number of ranks and titles,
too numerous to detail;
he indulged in banquets and revelry,
sometimes not emerging for ten days.
All officials wishing to present matters
had to do so through the eunuchs.
Thereupon, Lè Yùn (樂運) went to the court hall, carrying a coffin [yúchěn],
and presented the emperor's eight faults:
The first,
he believed that
"the Most Exalted [Dàzūn] has recently made many decisions unilaterally,
without consulting the various chancellors,
or sharing them with the multitude."
The second,
"seeking beautiful women to fill the inner palace,
forbidding women of rank Yítóng [Yítóng] and above from marrying,
causing resentment among both the noble and the humble."
The third,
"the Most Exalted [Dàzūn], once entering the inner palace,
does not emerge for several days;
necessary reports and requests are mostly submitted through the eunuchs."
The fourth,
"issuing an edict to leniently punish,
but before half a year had passed,
making the former regulations stricter again."
The fifth,
"Emperor Gāozǔ carved away ornamentation to embrace simplicity,
but before a year had passed since his passing,
you have suddenly pursued extreme extravagance."
The sixth,
"imposing corvée labor and taxes on the common people,
to support actors and horn wrestlers [jiǎodǐ]."
The seventh,
"punishing those whose memorials contained character errors,
thus blocking the path for submitting memorials."
The eighth,
"celestial phenomena [xuánxiàng] serve as warnings,
yet you fail to consult about good governance."
Xuánxiàng (玄象)
means Tiānxiàng (天象) [celestial phenomena].
The sun, moon, and stars
form images in the sky.
Zōu (諏),
pronounced Zǐyú [子于翻],
also Zǐhóu [子侯翻].
"If these eight matters are not reformed,
I fear the Zhōu ancestral temple will no longer receive blood sacrifices."
Sacrifices of animals are called xuèshí (血食) [blood sacrifices].
He was about to be executed.
The court officials were terrified,
and no one dared to intercede.
Yuán Yán (元巖) of Luòyáng (洛陽), Grand Master of the Household [Nèishǐ Zhōng Dàfū], sighed,
"Zāng Hóng (臧洪) died together with others,
and people still wished for it."
Chén Róng (陳容) wished to die together with Zāng Hóng (臧洪);
this event is recorded in Volume 61, during the third year of Xīngpíng (興平) of Emperor Xiàndì (獻帝) of Hàn.
He likened Lè Yùn's (樂運) loyal remonstrance to Bǐgān (比干).
"I shall die with him!"
He then went to the palace gate to request an audience,
saying:
"Lè Yùn (樂運), disregarding his own death,
seeks to make a name for himself.
Your Majesty would do better to commend him and dismiss him,
to broaden your sagely magnanimity."
The emperor was somewhat enlightened.
The next day,
he summoned Yùn (運),
and said:
"Last night, I pondered over your memorial,
and indeed, you are a loyal subject."
He bestowed imperial food upon him and dismissed him.
2 On the day Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
Zhōu established imperial son Chǎn (闡) as Prince of Lǔ (魯).
According to Lǐ Yánshòu's (李延壽) Běi Shǐ [北史] [History of the Northern Dynasties]: Emperor Jìngdì's (靜帝) taboo name was Yǎn (衍),
later changed to Chǎn (闡).
In light of this,
then the Zhōu's establishment of imperial son Yǎn (衍) as Prince of Dào (道) nine years ago
must have been Emperor Gāozǔ's (高祖) son?
On the day Jiǎchén (甲辰),
the Lord of Zhōu made an eastern tour;
he appointed Yǔwén Shàn (宇文善), Duke of Xǔ (許), as Grand Minister of Rites [Dàzōngbó].
On the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
the Lord of Zhōu arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽);
he established Prince Chǎn (闡) of Lǔ (魯) as the Crown Prince.
Chǎn (闡),
pronounced Chāngshàn [昌善翻].
3 In the second month,
on the day Guǐhài (癸亥),
the Emperor personally plowed the sacrificial field [jiètián].
4 Zhōu issued an edict,
designating Luòyáng (洛陽) as the Eastern Capital [Dōngjīng];
it dispatched troops from the various prefectures east of the mountains to repair the Luòyáng (洛陽) palace,
with a constant workforce of forty thousand people.
The six prefectural offices [liùfǔ] of Xiāngzhōu (相州) were relocated to Luòyáng (洛陽).
For the establishment of the six prefectural offices [liùfǔ] in Xiāngzhōu (相州) by Zhōu, see nine years prior.
Xiāng (相),
pronounced Xīliàng [息亮翻].
5 Wáng Guǐ (王軌), Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu (徐州) for Zhōu,
hearing that Zhèng Yì (鄭譯) was in power,
knew that disaster awaited him.
He said to his trusted confidants:
"In the former court,
I indeed presented vital strategies for the state.
What is happening today,
can be clearly foreseen.
This prefecture controls the Huáinán (淮南) region,
bordering strong enemies.
If I wished to make plans for myself,
it would be as easy as turning over my palm.
Strong enemies [qiángkòu],
refers to Chén (陳).
Yì (易),
pronounced Yǐshì [以豉翻].
I cannot betray my principles,
especially since I have received the late emperor's profound kindness.
How can I, because I have offended the current ruler,
suddenly forget it!
I can only await death here,
hoping that after a thousand years,
people will know my true intention!"
The Lord of Zhōu (周主) calmly asked Yì (譯):
"Who caused the staff marks on my legs?"
He replied:
"The matter was caused by Wūwán Guǐ (烏丸軌)."
The incident of receiving the staff is found in the eighth year of the previous volume.
Wáng Guǐ (王軌) was likely granted the surname Wūwán (烏丸),
hence he is referred to as such.
Cóng (從),
pronounced qiān róng (千容).
Why did Yǔwén Xiàobó (宇文孝伯) say such a thing?
Was he trying to save himself from death?
Yet, he ultimately could not escape it.
The incident of stroking his beard is found in the same place as above.
Yuán Yán (元巖) refused to sign the imperial edict.
Yùzhèng Zhōngdàfū (御正中大夫) Yán Zhīyí (顏之儀) remonstrated vehemently.
In the first year of Wǔchéng (武成),
four Yùzhèng (御正) were established.
Yán (巖) stepped forward and continued,
removing his cap and kowtowing,
bowing three times and advancing three times.
The Emperor said:
"Do you intend to side with Wūwán Guǐ (烏丸軌)?"
Yán (巖) replied:
"Your servant does not side with Guǐ (軌);
I only fear that indiscriminate executions will lose the trust of the world."
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered eunuchs to strike him in the face.
Bó (搏),
means to strike with the hand.
Yán (巖) was also dismissed and returned home.
Both those near and far, known and unknown,
all shed tears for Guǐ (軌).
Zhīyí (之儀)
was the younger brother of Zhītuī (之推).
Yán Zhītuī (顏之推) had first served in Qí (齊),
and after Qí (齊) fell, he entered Zhōu (周).
When the Lord of Zhōu (周主) was太子 (tàizǐ),
Shàng Zhùguó (上柱國) Wèichí Yùn (尉遲運) was the Gōngzhèng (宮正).
This refers to the太子宫正 (tàizǐ gōngzhèng).
Wèi (尉),
pronounced yū wù (紆勿).
He was not employed;
furthermore, he, Wáng Guǐ (王軌), Yǔwén Xiàobó (宇文孝伯), and Yǔwén Shénjǔ (宇文神舉) were all favored by Gāozǔ (高祖).
The太子 (tàizǐ) suspected them of jointly disparaging him.
When Guǐ (軌) died,
Yùn (運) was afraid,
and privately said to Xiàobó (孝伯):
"We are certainly not immune to disaster. What should we do about it?"
Xiàobó (孝伯) said:
"Now there is an old mother above the hall,
and below the ground is Wǔdì (武帝).
Wǔdì (武帝)
is Gāozǔ (高祖).
How can we know where we want to go?
Zhī (之),
means to go.
We originally pursued fame and righteousness;
if our remonstrances are not heeded,
how can we escape death!
Zhì (質),
read as written.
Yān (焉),
pronounced yú gān (於乾).
It is best to keep a distance for now."
Thereupon, Yùn (運) sought to be sent out as Qínzhōu Zǒngguǎn (秦州總管).
Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery
was the old Qínzhōu (秦州).
Another day,
the Emperor, feigning an issue concerning Qíwáng Xiàn (齊王憲), reprimanded Xiàobó (孝伯) saying:
"You knew Qíwáng (齊王) was plotting rebellion,
why did you not speak?"
He replied:
"Your servant knew Qíwáng (齊王) was loyal to the state (shèjì, 社稷),
and was slandered by vile scoundrels.
Anything I said would certainly not be heeded,
which is why I did not speak.
Moreover, the late emperor entrusted your humble servant,
only instructing me to assist and guide Your Majesty.
Now, my remonstrances are not followed,
I have truly failed in my trust.
To be punished for this,
I willingly accept."
The Emperor was greatly ashamed,
bowed his head and said nothing,
ordered him to be led out,
and granted him death at home.
Jiāng (將),
means to lead,
or to escort.
At that time, Yǔwén Shénjǔ (宇文神舉) was Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史).
The Emperor sent an envoy to his prefecture to poison him to death.
Wèichí Yùn (尉遲運), upon reaching Qínzhōu (秦州),
also died of grief.
6. Zhōu (周) disbanded the armies that were campaigning in the south.
7. The Tūjué (突厥) Kèhán (可汗) Tuóbō (佗鉢) requested peace with Zhōu (周).
The Lord of Zhōu (周主) made the daughter of Zhàowáng Zhāo (趙王招) into Qīnjīn Gōngzhǔ (千金公主)
and married her to him,
and also ordered him to seize and deliver Gāo Shàoyì (高紹義);
Tuóbō (佗鉢) did not comply.
8. On the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
Zhōu Xuāndì (周宣帝) abdicated the throne to太子 (tàizǐ) Chǎn (闡),
issued a general amnesty,
changed the reign title to Dàxiàng (大象),
and styled himself Tiānyuán Huángdì (天元皇帝).
His residence was called
"Tiāntái" (天臺).
His crown had twenty-four streamers,
and the number of his carriages, clothing, flags, and drums were all double those of previous kings.
The Emperor called the Zhèngyáng Gōng (正陽宮),
and established officials such as Nàyán (納言), Yùzhèng (御正), and various Wèi (衞) officials.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng (保定),
Zōngbó (宗伯) was changed to Nàyán (納言).
This Nàyán (納言) is similar to the Nàyán (納言) official of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
serving as the head of the Ménxià Shěng (門下省).

The various Wèi (衞) officials included Zuǒ-Yòu Gōngbó (左-右宮伯), Xiǎo Gōngbó (小宮伯), Zuǒ-Yòu Zhōngshì (左-右中侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Shì (左-右侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Qiánshì (左-右前侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Hòushì (左-右後侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Qíshì (左-右騎侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Zōngshì (左-右宗侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Shùshì (左-右庶侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Xūnshì (左-右勳侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Wǔbó (左-右武伯), Xiǎo Wǔbó (小武伯), Zuǒ-Yòu Wǔbēn (左-右武賁), Zuǒ-Yòu Lǚbēn (左-右旅賁), Zuǒ-Yòu Shèshēng (左-右射聲), Zuǒ-Yòu Xiāoqí (左-右驍騎), Zuǒ-Yòu Yǔlín (左-右羽林), and Zuǒ-Yòu Yóují (左-右游擊).
The Empress Dowager was honored as Tiānyuán Huáng Tàihòu (天元皇太后).
Tiān Yuán, after abdicating the throne,
became increasingly extravagant and arrogant.
He was determined to exalt himself,
having no scruples or fears.
The ceremonial rites of the state
were altered at his whim.
Whenever he faced his ministers, he would refer to himself as "Heaven,"
and use zūn, yí, guī, and zàn vessels for eating and drinking.
The Rites of Zhōu mention six zūn and six yí.
A zūn has a léi, and an yí has a zhōu.
Zhèng Xuán said: Yí
is also a zūn.
Yùchàng is called yí.
Yí
means "law,"
indicating it is the standard for zūn.
Zhèng Zhòng said: A vessel made at the head of a guī,
which can be used to scoop yùchàng for libation sacrifices,
is called a zàn.
Zàn,
pronounced 'cáng hàn'.
He would observe a three-day fast
and purify himself for one day.
Since he compared himself to the Lord on High,
he did not want to associate with ministers as equals.
He always wore a ribbon himself
and a Tōngtiān Guān,
adorned with a golden cicada.
When he saw his attending ministers with golden cicadas on their official caps or kings and dukes wearing ribbons,
he ordered them all to remove them.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: In ancient times, rulers and ministers wore jade pendants,
and ribbons were used to string and hold the pendants.
Furthermore, they wore fú both above and below,
like a knee-cover.
After the Five Hegemons,
warfare was ceaseless.
Pendants were not weapons,
and fú were not war regalia.
Thus, they removed their pendants and fú,
retaining only the ties for their sù.
When fú and pèi were abolished,
Qín then used colorful cords to connect to the sù,
and these were also called shòu.
According to the Zhōu system: The emperor's sash and ribbon
could be cyan,
green,
vermilion,
yellow,
white,
black,
dark red,
crimson,
purple,
dark gray,
jade green,
or light green,
totaling twelve colors.
Princes and the Three Dukes had nine colors,
from yellow downwards;
for kings, dukes, and below,
the colors decreased incrementally.
The Tōngtiān Guān,
according to ancient regulations, was nine cun high,
stood straight up at the crown,
sloped slightly backward,
then went straight down.
It had an iron scroll-beam
and a zhan tong in the front.
The front of the cap was adorned with a golden bóshān shù.
Those with golden attached cicadas
were the wǔ biàn worn by Shìzhōng and Chángshì.
Historians all mention Tiān Yuán's arbitrary self-exaltation.
Shòu,
pronounced 'shòu'.
Guān tōng zhī guān,
pronounced 'gǔ wán'.
Lìng,
pronounced 'lì dīng'.
Qù,
pronounced 'qiāng lǚ'.
The appellations of "Tiān"
(Heaven),
"Gāo"
(High),
"Shàng"
(Supreme),
and "Dà"
(Great) were all changed
if found in official titles.
Those whose surname was Gāo
were changed to "Jiāng" .
They were descendants of Qí Tàigōng,
who were granted a fief at Gāo,
and thus adopted it as their clan name.
Their original surname was Jiāng,
so they were made to revert to their original surname.
"Zhǎng Zǔ" .
He also ordered all carts in the realm to have wheels made of solid wood.
He forbade women throughout the empire from applying powder and rouge.
Powder was for applying to the face,
and rouge for filling the forehead and painting eyebrows.
All had yellow eyebrows and dark makeup.
Whenever he summoned attending ministers for discussions,
he only desired to initiate creations and reforms,
never speaking of governance.
His amusements were inconsistent,
and his comings and goings without regulation.
The feathered honor guard,
departing in the morning and returning at night,
and the accompanying officials
were all unable to endure the demands.
From the high ministers down,
they were often subjected to flogging.
Each time someone was beaten,
it was set at one hundred and twenty strokes,
called the "Heavenly Rod."
Later, this was increased to two hundred and forty.
Court ladies and inner officials were also treated similarly.
Empresses, fēi, bīn, and yù,
even if favored,
were often flogged on their backs.
Consequently, there was terror both inside and outside the court;
people felt insecure.
Everyone sought merely to escape punishment,
and no one had firm resolve.
They "stood with overlapping feet and held their breath,"
meaning they stood with their feet pressed together,
holding their breath in suppressed anxiety, not daring to breathe.
Chóng,
pronounced 'zhí lóng'.
Lěi,
pronounced 'lì wěi'.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Zhōu appointed Yuèwáng Shèng as Tàibǎo,
Yùchí Huí as Dà Qiányí,
and Dàiwáng Dá as Dà Yòubì.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the stone classics from Yèchéng were moved to Luòyáng.
An edict stated:
"The seven grand governors of Héyáng, Yōu, Xiàng, Yù, Bó, Qīng, and Xú
shall all receive orders from the Six Bureaus of Dōngjīng."
In the third month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Tiān Yuán returned to Cháng'ān,
displaying a grand military array,
personally donning armor and helmet.
He entered through the Qīngmén,
with Jìngdì preparing the fǎjià to follow him.
Qīngmén was the third gate counting from the east, south of the Hàn Cháng'ān city wall.
Its color was green,
hence its name, Qīngmén.
Fǎjià was a carriage second only to the dàjià.
Cóng,
pronounced 'cái yòng'.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day, Rénxū,
Lady Zhū was made Tiān Yuán Dìhòu.
The empress,
a native of Wú,
came from a humble and lowly background.
She gave birth to Jìngdì,
and was more than ten years older than Tiān Yuán.
Being of low status and unfavored,
she was specially honored
because of Jìngdì.
On the day Yǐsì,
the Zhōu sovereign performed sacrifices at the Tàimiào.
On the day Rénwǔ,
a grand ritual offering was held at Zhèngwǔ Diàn.
In the fifth month,
Xiāngguó Jùn was established as Zhào Guó,
Jìnán Jùn as Chén Guó,
Wǔdāng and Ānfù two commanderies as Yuè Guó,
Shàngdǎng Jùn as Dài Guó,
Xīnyě Jùn as Téng Guó,
each with ten thousand households.
Each fief had its own actual territory.
"Ānfù"
should be "Ānfú."
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Wǔdāng Xiàn in Xīyáng Jùn,
formerly Wǔdāng Jùn.
Also,
Ānfú Xiàn was established as Ānfú Jùn.
Xīnyě Xiàn in Nányáng Jùn,
formerly known as Jíyáng,
was established as Xīnyě Jùn.
Jì,
pronounced 'zǐ lǐ'.
Suí Gōng Yáng Jiān privately said to the Grand General, Ruǒnán Gōng Qìng:
"Tiānyuán truly has no accumulated virtue;
observing his appearance,
his lifespan will also not be long.
Furthermore,
the various princes are weak;
each has been ordered to return to his state,
and there has been no plan to deeply root and solidify the foundation.
With feathers and wings clipped,
how can they fly far!"
Looking at Yáng Jiān's words here,
how could he have harbored intentions of usurpation!
However, for Jiān, in a suspicious and cruel court, to utter such words,
his escape from harm was indeed fortunate.
(He) was Shénjǔ's younger brother.
10 The Tujue invaded Zhōu's Bīngzhōu.
In the sixth month,
Zhōu dispatched the people of the eastern side of the mountains to repair the Great Wall.
This was repairing the Great Wall built by Qí.
Qí built the Great Wall;
see Volume 166, Liáng Jìngdì, Tàipíng First Year.
11 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Gēngyín,
Zhōu appointed Yáng Jiān as Grand Former Doubt,
and Pillar of the State Sīmǎ Xiāonán as Grand Latter Successor.
12 On the day Xīnmǎo,
the "great coin" six-zhū coin was first put into circulation.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Liáng Wǔdì minted coins
with a prominent rim and a hole,
inscribed "Wǔ Zhū";
and also separately minted coins
without the prominent rim and hole,
which were called "female coins";
both types circulated concurrently.
The common people sometimes privately traded with old coins,
which had various denominations such as "Zhíbǎi Wǔ Zhū," "Wǔ Zhū Nǚqián," "Tàipíng Bǎiqián," "Dìngpíng Yībǎi," "Wǔ Zhū Zhìqián," and "Wǔ Zhū Duìwén,"
and whose weights were inconsistent.
The Son of Heaven repeatedly issued edicts
that all coins other than the two newly minted types
were not permitted for use,
yet private use only increased.
By the Pǔtōng era,
a discussion arose to abolish all bronze coins
and instead mint iron coins.
People found iron cheap and easy to obtain,
and all privately minted them.
After Dàtóng,
iron coins were piled up like mountains everywhere.
The value of a string of coins varied by location;
by the last years,
the number of coins in a string decreased,
with thirty-five coins making a string.
At the beginning of Chén, after a period of chaos and loss,
iron coins were no longer in circulation.
Initially,
at the end of Liáng, there were also "two-pillar coins" and "goose-eye coins";
the two-pillar coins were heavy and the goose-eye coins were light,
and they were used mixed together,
having the same value.
Private individuals often melted down coins,
and also mixed in tin and iron,
and traded with grain and silk as currency.
By Emperor Wén's Tiānjiā Fifth Year,
new Wǔ Zhū coins were minted,
initially valued at ten goose-eye coins.
At this time, the "great coin" six-zhū coin was again minted,
with one valued at ten Wǔ Zhū coins;
later, it returned to being valued as one,
and people generally did not find it convenient.
Not long after,
the emperor passed away,
and the six-zhū coin was abolished, and the Wǔ Zhū coin was put back into circulation.
13 On the day Bǐngshēn,
Zhōu made Sīmǎ Xiāonán's daughter Empress of the Zhèngyáng Palace.
She was Jìngdì's empress.
Nán is pronounced Dàn fān.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Zhōu honored Tiānyuán Dì's Empress Dowager Lǐ as Tiānhuáng Tàihòu.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Tiānyuán's Empress Zhū was redesignated Tiānhuánghòu,
Yuán Shì was established as Tiānyòu Huánghòu,
and Chén Shì as Tiānzuǒ Huánghòu,
making a total of four empresses.
Yuán Shì was the daughter of the Kaīfǔ Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn Shèng;
Chén Shì was the daughter of the Grand General Shāntí.
Chén Shāntí was the retainer of Ěrzhū Zhào,
see Volume 156, Liáng Wǔdì, Zhōngdàtōng Fifth Year.
In the eighth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Tiānyuán went to Tóngzhōu.
14 On the day Dīngmǎo,
the emperor reviewed military exercises at Dàzhuàngguān.
He ordered Dudū Rèn Zhōng to lead 100,000 infantry and cavalry to array at Xuánwǔ Hú,
and Dudū Chén Jǐng to lead 500 storied warships out of Guāpù Jiāng,
then returned in triumph.
15 On the day Rénshēn,
Zhōu Tiānyuán returned to Cháng'ān.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Chén Shāntí and Yuán Shèng were both appointed Shàngzhùguó.
These two individuals
were both fathers of empresses.
Shèng is pronounced Chéng zhèng fān.
16 On the day Wùyín,
the emperor returned to the palace.
Yùzhāng Nèishǐ Nánkāng Wáng Fāngtài,
having completed his term in the commandery,
set fire which spread and burned down residences,
then engaged in violent plunder,
rounding up wealthy individuals,
and extorting money and valuables.
Lù means to seize.
Fāngtài was supposed to follow orders [to return to the capital],
but claimed his mother was ill and did not go,
instead covertly going among the people to commit adultery with others' wives,
and was apprehended by the prefecture.
Zhōu refers to Yángzhōu.
Shāng Jìnsī means to injure the officers of the prohibition bureau.
Zhàng refers to weapons.
Jìnsī are those who manage prohibitions and prevent wrongdoing.
Shuài is read as Lǜ.
The emperor was greatly enraged,
imprisoned Fāngtài,
stripped him of his office,
and abolished his noble title and fief;
soon after, he was reinstated.
17 On the day Rénwǔ,
Zhōu appointed Shàngzhùguó Bì Wáng Xián as Tàishī,
and Xún Gōng Hán Yè as Dà Zuǒfǔ.
In the ninth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Fēng Wáng Zhēn was appointed Dàzǒngzǎi.
Yún Gōng Xiào
Kuān was appointed Xíngjūn Yuánshuài,
leading Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn Gōngliàng and Chéng Gōng Liáng Shìyàn to invade Huáinán.
Additionally, Yùzhèng Dù Gǎo and Lǐbù Xuē Shū were dispatched to come as envoys.
18 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Rénxū,
Zhōu Tiānyuán visited Dàohuì Yuàn,
where a grand religious offering was held,
with Gāozǔ accompanying the offering.
He initially restored Buddhist statues and statues of the Heavenly Venerable.
Zhōu destroyed scriptures and statues; see previous volume, Sixth Year.
Various entertainments were grandly displayed,
allowing the gentry and commoners of Cháng'ān to watch freely.
19 On the day Jiǎxū,
Shàngshū Púyè Lù Sàn was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
20 In the eleventh month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
a great amnesty was declared.
21 Zhōu Wéi Xiàokuān divided his forces, sending Gōngliàng to attack Huángchéng from Ānlù,
and Liáng Shìyàn to attack Guǎnglíng.
They advanced in two routes to attack Huáinán.
This Guǎnglíng was in Xīnxī.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Shìyàn reached Féikǒu.
Féi Shuǐ's mouth where it enters the Huái River.
22 On the day Yǐwèi,
Zhōu Tiānyuán went to Wēntāng.
This was the Wēntāng at Líshān,
located northwest of Líshān.
The Shídào Zhì states: There are three hot springs;
one of them is the royal hall's stone well,
built by Hòu Zhōu Yǔwén Hù.
23 On the day Wùxū,
the Zhōu army advanced to besiege Shòuyáng.
24 Zhōu Tiānyuán went to Tóngzhōu.
25 An imperial edict appointed Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Nányánzhōu Cìshǐ Chúnyú Liàng as Shàngliú Shuǐjūn Dūdū,
Zhōnglǐngjūn Fán Yì as Dūdū Běitǎo Zhūjūnjìshì,
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Rèn Zhōng as Dūdū Běitǎo Qiánjūnjìshì,
and former Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ Gāo Wénzòu to lead 3,000 infantry and cavalry towards Yángpíng Jùn.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Jiàn'ān Jùn,
Chén established Fēngzhōu.
Jiāngdū Jùn's Ānyí Xiàn,
Liáng established Yángpíng Jùn.
Gāo is a surname,
descendants of Gāo Yáo.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn mentions Yuè Dàfū Gāo Rú.
Shuài is read as Lǜ;
same below.
Qí is pronounced Qí jì fān;
same below.
Qù is pronounced Qī yù fān;
same below.
26th year, Rén-yín (壬寅).
Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) returned to Cháng’ān (長安).
27th year, Guǐ-mǎo (癸卯).
Rèn Zhōng (任忠) led 7,000 cavalry and infantry to Qínjùn (秦郡).
On Bǐng-wǔ (丙午),
Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (仁威將軍) Lǔ Guǎngdá (魯廣達) led his troops into Huái (淮).
Liáng (梁) established the titles of Wǔdé Jiāngjūn (五德將軍):
Zhì (智), Rén (仁), Yǒng (勇), Xìn (信), and Yán (嚴);
Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn (五威將軍),
replacing the old Zhēnglǔ (征虜) title;
and Wǔwǔ Jiāngjūn (五武將軍),
replacing the old Guānjūn (冠軍) title.
Fán Yì (樊毅) led a navy of 20,000 from Dōngguān (東關) into Jiāohú (焦湖).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Cháohú (巢湖)
is also called Jiāohú (焦湖).
Fán Yì’s (樊毅) navy intended to proceed from this lake to Héféi (合肥).
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced as liàng (亮),
and also as its own character,
meaning to lead.
Jiāo (焦)
is pronounced zǐ-xiǎo (子小).
Wǔyì Jiāngjūn (武毅將軍) was also established by Liáng (梁),
ranking below the two classes of Wǔdé (五德).
On Wù-shēn (戊申),
Wéi Xiàokuān (韋孝寬) captured Shòuyáng (壽陽),
Gōng Liàng (公亮) captured Huángchéng (黃城),
and Liáng Shìyàn (梁士彥) captured Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
On Xīn-hài (辛亥),
Hǔozhōu (霍州) was also taken.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: Xiāo Qí (蕭齊) established Hǔozhōu (霍州),
with its seat in Qián (灊) County, Tiānzhùshān (天柱山).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Hǔoshān (霍山) County of Lújiāng (廬江) Commandery,
Liáng (梁) established Hǔozhōu (霍州).
On Guǐ-chǒu (癸丑),
Shǐxīngwáng Shūlíng (始興王叔陵), the Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州), was appointed Dàdūdū (大都督),
commanding all land and naval forces.
28th year, Dīng-sì (丁巳).
Zhōu (周) minted the Yǒngtōng Wànguó (永通萬國) coin,
with one coin worth a thousand,
circulating alongside the Wǔxíng Dàbù (五行大布).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Zhōu (周) decreed: Wǔxíng Dàbù (五行大布) was to be used concurrently with the three types of Wǔzhū (五銖) coins.
29th year, 12th month.
On Wù-wǔ (戊午),
due to repeated occurrences of ominous phenomena, Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元)
abandoned his imperial guards
and went to Tiānxīng Gōng (天興宮).
All officials submitted memorials
urging him to resume his normal routine.
On Jiǎ-zǐ (甲子),
he returned to the palace,
held court in Zhèngwǔ Diàn (正武殿),
and gathered all officials, palace ladies, and external noblewomen.
External noblewomen
were the wives of officials of the fifth rank and above.
For the first time, the "Qǐhán Hú Xì" (乞寒胡戲) was performed.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Qǐhán (乞寒)
was originally music from the western regions, from outside tributary states.
The Xīn Tángshū (新唐書) states: According to the custom of Kāngguó (康國),
in the eleventh month,
they beat drums and danced for Qǐhán (乞寒),
finding joy in splashing water on each other;
this performance spread to China.
30th year, Yǐ-chǒu (乙丑).
The three prefectures of Nán Yǎn (南兗), Běi Yǎn (北兗), and Jìn (晉)
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) does not record the seat of Běi Yǎnzhōu (北兗州).
In Tóng’ān (同安) Commandery,
Liáng (梁) established Yùzhōu (豫州),
later renamed Jìnzhōu (晉州),
later Qí (齊) renamed it Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and Chén (陳) restored it to Jìnzhōu (晉州).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: Chénjì (陳紀)
has "nine commanderies" (九郡)
written as
"nine prefectures" (九州),
which is likely a mischaracter.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Jiāngdū (江都) County’s Yǒngfú (永福) County
was formerly called Pèi (沛).
Liáng (梁) established Jìngchéng (涇城) and Dōngyáng (東陽) Commanderies and Jìngzhōu (涇州).
Chén (陳) abolished the prefecture
and merged the two commanderies into Pèijùn (沛郡).
Quánjiāo (全椒) County,
Liáng (梁) established Běi Qiáojùn (北譙郡).
Nánliángjùn (南梁郡) has existed since the Sòng Zhì (宋志),
but its actual location is unknown.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (天監) of Liáng (梁),
Fèng Dàogēn (馮道根), as Administrator of Nánliáng (南梁), garrisoned Fùlíng (阜陵),
so it likely became an actual territory from then on.
Qiáozhōu (譙州) was seated in Wōyáng (渦陽),
in Shānsāng (山桑) County of Qiáojùn (譙郡).
Běi Xúzhōu (北徐州) was established in Lángyé (琅邪) Commandery.
31st year. Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) went to Luòyáng (洛陽),
personally driving relay horses,
covering three hundred *lǐ* a day.
His four empresses and several hundred civil and military guards
all rode in post-chariots to follow.
He also ordered the four empresses to drive their chariots abreast,
方駕 (fāngjià) means driving abreast.
and if anyone fell behind,
he would reprimand them,
causing people and horses to stumble and fall,
lining the road.
32nd year, Guǐ-yǒu (癸酉).
Píngběi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍) Shěn Kè (沈恪) and Diànwēi Jiāngjūn (電威將軍) Péi Zǐliè (裴子烈) were sent to garrison Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州).
Kāiyuǎn Jiāngjūn (開遠將軍) Xú Dàonú (徐道奴) was sent to garrison Zhàkǒu (柵口).
Diànwēi (電威) and Kāiyuǎn Jiāngjūn (開遠將軍)
were both of the seventh rank,
with a stipend of six hundred *shí*.
Zhàkǒu (柵口)
refers to Zhàjiāngkǒu (柵江口).
On Wù-yín (戊寅),
Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍) Fán Yì (樊毅) was appointed Dūdū (都督) of the military affairs of Jīng (荊), Yǐng (郢), Bā (巴), and Wǔ (武) prefectures, both land and naval.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: In Gōng’ān (公安) County of Nánjùn (南郡),
Chén (陳) established Jīngzhōu (荊州). In Jiāngxià (江夏) Commandery, Yǐngzhōu (郢州) was established.
In Bālíng (巴陵) Commandery, Bāzhōu (巴州) was established.
In Wǔlíng (武陵) Commandery, Wǔzhōu (武州) was established.
33rd year, Jǐ-mǎo (己卯).
Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) returned to Cháng’ān (長安).
34th year. Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn (貞毅將軍) Zhōu Fǎshàng (周法尚) of Rǔnán (汝南).
Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn (貞毅將軍)
ranked below the Wǔdé Jiāngjūn (五德將軍).
Shújiān (叔堅) slandered him to the emperor,
saying he intended to rebel.
The emperor arrested his elder brother, Fǎsēng (法僧), the Governor of Dìngzhōu (定州).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: In Máchéng (麻城) County of Yǒng’ān (永安) Commandery,
Chén (陳) established Dìngzhōu (定州).
The territory at that time had already been lost to Zhōu (周).
Fǎshàng (法尚) fled to Zhōu (周).
Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) appointed him
Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn (儀同大將軍) and Governor of Shùnzhōu (順州).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: In Shùnyì (順義) County of Hàndōng (漢東) Commandery,
Xī Wèi (西魏) established Shùnzhōu (順州).
Fǎshàng (法尚) sent his Bùqǔ Dū (部曲督) Hán Lǎng (韓朗) to feign surrender to Měng (猛),
saying:
"Fǎshàng’s (法尚) troops are unwilling to surrender to the north.
Everyone is secretly discussing
deserting and returning.
If your army comes,
we will naturally turn our weapons against them."
Měng (猛) believed this,
and led his troops to advance rapidly.
Fǎshàng (法尚) feigned fear,
entrenched himself at a bend in the river.
江曲 (jiāngqǔ) means a bend in the river.
He set an ambush,
and Měng (猛) barely escaped with his life,
nearly eight thousand men were lost.
Collated by Zhāng Xīchēn (章錫琛) with punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐)
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) under imperial decree
Hòuxuétiāntái (後學天台)
Tàijiàn (太建) 12th year
(Gēng-zǐ (庚子), 580 CE)
1st month.
Spring.
Guǐ-sì (癸巳).
Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元) offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.

Délín said:
"I am willing to serve the public with my life."
Jiān was greatly pleased.
Initially,
Liú Fǎng and Zhèng Yì proposed making Jiān Dà Zhǒngzǎi,
Yì himself would temporarily take charge of Dà Sīmǎ,
and Fǎng also sought the position of Xiǎo Zhǒngzǎi.
The Later Zhōu established the Xiǎo Zhǒngzǎi,
who was a Shàng Dàfū,
of the sixth rank.
According to the Ěryǎ: Zhǒng,
means "great."
Zhèng Xuán said: Zhǒng,
is above "great."
It is not appropriate to add the character "xiǎo" (small) above Zhǒngzǎi,
therefore the Zhōu Guān only refers to Xiǎo Zǎi.
Fǎng,
pronounced fēn wǎng.
Zhǒng,
pronounced zhī lǒng.
"How do you wish to be placed?"
Délín said:
"It is appropriate for you to be Dà Chéngxiàng, Jiǎ Huáng Yuè, and Dū Dú Zhōng Wài Zhū Jūn Shì;
otherwise,
there will be no way to awe the masses."
According to Fǎng and Yì's words,
although Dà Zhǒngzǎi was the head of the six officials,
he was still equal to the various dukes.
What Délín said,
however, was what Yǔwén Tài used to assist the Wèi dynasty.
"Bù ěr" (otherwise),
is synonymous with "bù rú cǐ" (not like this).
Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng.
Yā,
pronounced yú jiǎ.
He immediately acted upon this.
The Zhèng Yáng Palace was made the Prime Minister's residence.
At that time, public sentiment was not unified;
it means that the Zhōu court officials had not yet fully pledged their loyalty to Jiān.
When he was about to go to the Eastern Palace,
the Zhèng Yáng Palace was originally the Eastern Palace.
Jiān secretly ordered Bēn to arrange the armed guards.
Zhàng wèi,
refers to soldiers holding weapons and guarding at night.
Lú Bēn, as Sī Wǔ Shàng Shì, commanded them.
Yáng Jiān secretly ordered Bēn,
what was the purpose of this action?
He said:
"Those who desire wealth and honor should follow me."
Observing Jiān's words here,
his long-held ambition is clear.
When some wanted to leave or stay,
Bēn arrived with disciplined troops,
and no one dared to move.
When he exited the Chóng Yáng Gate,
the Chóng Yáng Gate was the eastern gate of the Zhōu palace city.
The gatekeepers refused to admit him.
Bēn reasoned with them,
but they did not move;
he glared and shouted at them,
and the gatekeepers then retreated,
allowing Jiān to enter.
Bēn then took charge of the Prime Minister's residence's night guard.
Lú Bēn thus became Yáng Jiān's personal subordinate.
He was the disciple of Biàn.
Lú Biàn,
was the one who, with Sū Chuò, established the official system of the Later Zhōu.
Liú Fǎng was Sīmǎ,
and Lǐ Délín was a Fǔ Shǔ.
The Prime Minister's residence had Juàn and Shǔ.
The Nèi Shǐ Xià Dàfū Bóhǎi Gāo Gǒng
(According to the Suí Shū: Gāo Gǒng claimed to be from Tiáo, Bóhǎi).
Gǒng,
pronounced gǔ jiǒng.
He was skilled in military affairs
and possessed many strategies.
Jiān wished to bring him into the residence;
he was to be brought into the Prime Minister's residence as an official.
Yáng Huì was Jiān's nephew (clan son).
When Jiān first assumed control of Zhōu's government,
he wished to recruit talented individuals of the time,
so he sent Huì to convey his intentions.
After Jiān received the abdication,
he enfeoffed Guān Wáng
and changed his name to Xióng.
Gǒng said joyfully:
"I am willing to be at your command.
Even if your endeavor fails,
Gǒng will not shrink from the extermination of his clan."
Thereupon, he was made the Prime Minister's residence's Sī Lù.
Sī Lù,
oversees all affairs of the residence.
Lìng,
pronounced lì dīng.
Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng.
At that time, Hàn Wáng Zàn 漢王贊 resided in the forbidden palace,
and often sat in the same tent as Jìng Dì 靜帝.
Liú Fǎng 劉昉 adorned beautiful courtesans and presented them to Zàn,
who was greatly pleased by them.
Fǎng thereupon persuaded Zàn, saying:
“Your Royal Highness,
you are the late emperor’s brother,
to whom the hopes of the time are directed.
The child is young and immature;
how can he bear the great affairs of state!
Now the late emperor has just passed away,
and people’s feelings are still unsettled.
Your Highness should return to your residence for now,
and after affairs have settled,
enter to become the Son of Heaven.
This is a perfectly safe plan.”
Zàn was young,
and his nature and intellect were mediocre;
he believed it to be true,
and so he followed the advice.
Jiān 堅 reformed Xuān Dì’s 宣帝 harsh and cruel policies,
making them more lenient and magnanimous,
simplifying the old laws,
and creating an essential penal code,
which he presented and implemented;
he personally practiced frugality,
and all within and without the court were pleased with him.
Jiǎ Yì 賈誼 said: “Those who are cold find comfort in coarse clothes,
and those who are hungry relish dregs and husks;
the widespread suffering throughout the land
is the new lord’s opportunity.”
The ancients who gained the empire
must first have obtained the hearts of the people,
and even cunning heroes employing strategies and tactics
could not operate outside of this principle.
Gēng 更,
pronunciation gōng-héng-fān.
At night, Jiān 堅 summoned Tài Shǐ Zhōng Dàfū Ù Yǔ Jìcái 太史中大夫庾季才.
The Grand Astrologer (Tài Shǐ) was in charge of astronomy and calendrical calculations.
According to the Zhōu 周 system, the Tài Shǐ Zhōng Dàfū,
belonged to the Ministry of Spring (Chūn Guān 春官),
and held the fifth rank (wǔ mìng 五命).
“I, being mediocre and empty,
Yōng 庸 (mediocre),
means having no ability oneself;
Xū 虛 (empty),
means having nothing in one’s mind;
these are humble terms.
What do you think of the heavenly timing and human affairs?”
Jìcái replied:
“The way of Heaven is subtle and profound,
difficult to discern by mere intention.
I humbly infer from human affairs,
that the omens and portents are already fixed.
Fú 符,
means prophecy,
evidence,
and verification.
Zhào 兆,
means the crack patterns on a tortoise shell,
and also the portents and signs of human affairs.
How could Your Grace again engage in the affairs of Jīshān 箕山 and Yǐngshuǐ 潁水!”
Sīmǎ Zhēn 司馬貞 said: Yáo 堯 yielded the empire to Xǔ Yóu 許由,
who then fled to Jīshān,
and washed his ears in the Yǐngshuǐ River.
Fù 復,
pronunciation fú-yòu-fān,
also pronounced as written.
[Jiān] said:
“It is indeed as you say.”
Dúgū Fūrén 獨孤夫人 also said to Jiān:
“The great matter is already done;
it is the posture of riding a tiger,
one must not dismount,
strive onward!”
Dúgū Fūrén
was Jiān’s wife.
If one dismounts from a tiger,
one will surely be devoured.
Jiān 堅 considered Xiàngzhōu Zǒngguǎn Yùchí Jiǒng’s 相州總管尉遲迥 position and prestige to be exceedingly great,
and feared he might have other plans.
He sent Jiǒng’s son, Wèi Ān Gōng Dūn 魏安公惇, with an imperial edict to summon him to the funeral.
Wèi Ān Jùn Gōng 魏安郡公.
In the Wǔ Dài Zhì 五代志,
Wǔwēi Jùn Chāngsōng Xiàn 武威郡昌松縣 had a Wèi Ān Jùn 魏安郡 in the Later Wèi.
Further notes will be found later.
On the day Rénzǐ 壬子,
Wéi Xiàokuān 韋孝寬 was appointed Xiàngzhōu Zǒngguǎn 相州總管 with the title Shàng Zhùguó 上柱國;
also, Chìliè Chángyì 叱列長义 was appointed Xiàngzhōu Cìshǐ 相州刺史 with the title Xiǎo Sītú 小司徒.
Chìliè 叱列,
was a foreign compound surname,
originating from the western branch of the Tuòbá 拓跋 clan,
later becoming a prominent family (qīlǐ) in Zhōu.
Xiàokuān continued to advance.
Yè 鄴,
was the administrative seat of the Xiàngzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
At that time, Chén Wáng Chún 陳王純 was garrisoned in Qízhōu 齊州.
Chún had gone to his feudal state in Jìnán 濟南.
Jìnán Jùn 濟南郡 was Qízhōu.
Qízhōu was also Jìnán Jùn.
The Ménzhèng 門正,
was in charge of the regulations for opening and closing gates and for those entering and leaving.
[Jiān] sent someone to summon Chún.
When Chún arrived,
Péng 彭 asked to dismiss the attendants,
and spoke secretly,
then seized and chained him,
and loudly declared:
“Chén Wáng has committed a crime,
and has been summoned to court by imperial edict!
No one is to move!”
His followers were astonished and departed.
Péng
was Kǎi’s 楷 grandson.
Cuī Kǎi’s 崔楷 death in office is mentioned in volume 151, Liáng Wǔ Dì Dàtōng Yuán Nián 梁武帝大通元年.
In the sixth month,
the five princes all arrived in Cháng’ān 長安.
On the 12th day, Gēngshēn 庚申,
Zhōu 周 once again allowed the two religions of Buddhism and Daoism to be practiced.
Zhōu’s prohibition of the two religions is mentioned in volume 171, the sixth year.
Fù 復,
pronunciation fú-yòu-fān,
also pronounced as written.
The edict simplified entry into religious orders.
Jiǎn 簡,
means to differentiate.
Zhōu Wèichí Jiǒng 周尉遲迥, knowing that the Chancellor Jiān 堅 was about to act unfavorably toward the imperial house,
plotted to raise an army to attack him.
Wéi Xiàokuān 韋孝寬 arrived in Cháogē 朝歌.
Wǔ Dài Zhì: Jí Jùn Wèi Xiàn 汲郡衞縣,
formerly called Cháogē.
Zhōu Shū 周書: Hèlán 賀蘭,
their ancestors rose together with Wèi 魏,
there was Héfú 紇伏,
who was Hèlán Mòhéfú 賀蘭莫何弗,
and they took this as their surname.
Xiàokuān kept Guì 貴 to talk with him to ascertain the situation,
suspecting there was trouble,
so he feigned illness and traveled slowly;
he also sent someone to Xiàngzhōu 相州 to seek medicine,
secretly using this to observe the situation.
Xiàokuān’s elder brother’s son, Yì 藝,
was Wèijùn Shǒu 魏郡守.
Jiǒng sent Yì to welcome Xiàokuān.
Xiàokuān asked about Jiǒng’s actions,
but Yì was allied with Jiǒng
and did not answer truthfully.
The Wèijùn Shǒu and the Xiàngzhōu Zǒngguǎn Fǔ were administered together in Yè 鄴,
and their duties were connected.
Moreover, Jiǒng was loyal to the imperial house,
so it was fitting that Yì would be allied with his superior.
Shǒu 守,
pronunciation shǒu-yòu-fān.
[Xiàokuān] was about to execute him,
Yì was afraid,
and revealed all of Jiǒng’s plans to Xiàokuān.
Xiàokuān took Yì and fled west.
Each time they reached a post station (tíngyì 亭驛),
Tíng 亭,
refers to a postal pavilion,
which is where post stations are located.
Chuánmǎ 傳馬,
refers to post horses.
Chuán 傳,
pronunciation zhāng-liàn-fān.
Yìsī 驛司,
refers to the official in charge of the post station.
[Xiàokuān] would say, “Shǔ Gōng 蜀公 is about to arrive,
so prepare wine and food quickly.”
Wèichí Jiǒng was enfeoffed as Shǔ Gōng,
hence this appellation.
When the pursuers arrived at the post station,
they always found a grand feast,
and no horses,
so they delayed and could not advance.
Xiàokuān and Yì thus managed to escape.
The historian says Wéi Xiàokuān’s ingenuity surpassed others.
Jiān again ordered Hòu Zhèng Pòliùhán Póu to go to Huí to convey the imperial edict.
Pòliùhán
is a three-character barbarian surname.
Yù
means "to compare,"
"to tell,"
and "to enlighten."
Zhǐ
means "intention" or "aim."
Póu,
read "báo hóu."
The Xìng Yuàn (Genealogy of Surnames) states: The Jìn family was originally descended from Tángshū Yú,
taking their state as their clan name.
Cháng,
read "zhī liǎng."
Chǎng,
read "chǒu liǎng."
When Huí heard of this,
he killed Chǎng and Póu.
He gathered the civil and military officials, gentry, and common people.
"Civil and military"
refers to the civil and military officials and subordinates of the Zǒngguǎnfǔ and various prefectures and commanderies.
Lìng,
read "lì dīng."
He addressed them, saying:
"Yáng Jiān is relying on the power of his empress's father,
holding the young emperor hostage to wield arbitrary power.
His disloyal acts
are manifest for all to see.
I am the state's maternal nephew.
Wèichí Huí was the maternal nephew of Yǔwén Tài.
The late emperor placed me here,
intending to entrust me with the nation's safety and peril.
Now I wish to rally righteous volunteers with you gentlemen,
to assist the state and protect the people.
What do you think?"
All the people complied.
Huí then declared himself Dà Zǒngguǎn [Grand Commander],
and established official bureaus by imperial decree.
He called himself Dà Zǒngguǎn
wishing to oversee all the prefectures.
The Zǒngguǎn established official bureaus,
but being separated from the powerful minister,
he was unable to report to the Son of Heaven,
hence it is called "by imperial decree."
He left his youngest son in the capital.
Zhào Wáng Zhāo Guó was in Xiāngguó.
Xiāngguó belonged to the Xiāngzhōu Zǒngguǎnfǔ.
Cháo,
read "zhí yáo."
Shào,
read "shī zhào."
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Jiān dispatched troops from Guānzhōng,
appointing Wéi Xiàokuān as Xíngjūn Yuánshuài [Campaign Commander].

Chéng Gōng Liáng Shìyàn, Yuè'ān Gōng Yuán Xié, Huàzhèng Gōng Yǔwén Xīn, Púyáng Gōng Wǔchuān Yǔwén Shù, Wǔxiāng Gōng Cuī Hóngdù, Qīnghé Gōng Yáng Sù, Lǒngxī Gōng Lǐ Xún, and others were all appointed Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn [Campaign Generals]
to suppress Huí.
Liáng Shìyàn was a Guógōng [Duke of the State].
Chéng
is an ancient state name.
From Yuán Xié downwards, all were Jùngōng [Commandery Dukes].
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Qianshéng County in Běihǎi Commandery
formerly established Yuè'ān Commandery.
The Dìxíng Zhì states: Xiàzhōu has Huàzhèng Commandery.
Referring to the Wǔdài Zhì,
it should be in the area of Yánlǜ County, Xiàzhōu.
Juancheng County in Dōngpíng Commandery
formerly established Púyáng Commandery.
The Shù Zhuàn states: Shù
was from Wǔchuān, Dàijùn.
The Zhì states: Shànyáng County in Mǎyì Commandery has Dàijùn.
Xiāng County in Shàngdǎng Commandery,
Shí Lè established Wǔxiāng Commandery.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: The Zhōu dynasty changed Huàyīn County in Féngyì to Wǔxiāng Commandery.
Wǔchéng County in Qīnghé Commandery
formerly established Qīnghé Commandery.
Lǒngxī is an ancient commandery,
and the Later Wèi administered Xiāngwǔ Shǒuyáng County.
Yuè,
pronounced "luò."
Pú,
read "bó mù."
[Yuán Xié was] Kǎi's grandson;
Xún
was Mù's elder brother's son.
Lǐ Mù was then the Cìshǐ of Bìngzhōu.
Initially, Xuāndì sent Jìbù Zhōngdàfū Yáng Shàngxī to console Shāndōng.
The Later Zhōu established the Jìbù,
which was likely in charge of account books and records,
like the Sīshū in the Zhōu government.
Dù Yòu said: The Jìbù belonged to the Tiānguān.
Hearing of Xuāndì's death,
[Shàngxī] mourned with Wèichí Huí.
Shàngxī went out
and told his attendants:
"Shǔgōng cries without sorrow and looks uneasy;
he must have other plans.
If I don't leave,
I fear I will be caught in the disaster."
So he fled by a shortcut overnight.
A shortcut
means not taking the main road,
but quickly finding a direct path to travel.
Huí realized this,
pursued him but did not catch him,
so Shàngxī returned to Cháng'ān.
Jiān dispatched Shàngxī to lead three thousand Zōngbīng [clan soldiers] to garrison Tóngguān.
Yáng Shàngxī
was from Hóngnóng.
The Yáng clan of Hóngnóng Huàyīn
was a prominent family from the Eastern Hàn to the Later Wèi.
When Wèi was divided into Eastern and Western,
Hóngnóng again became a battleground,
hence the Yáng family had Zōngbīng.
Yōngzhōu Mù Bì Lál Wáng Xián
conspired with the Five Kings to kill Jiān.
The plot was leaked.
Xiè
is the same as Xiè.
Along with his three sons,
[Jiān] suppressed the plot of the Five Kings without investigation.
How could Jiān truly not investigate?
There was unrest in Shāndōng,
and internal plots were resurfacing,
so he merely aimed to pacify those with wavering loyalties.
Gōng Chūn was Dà Sītú [Grand Minister of Education].
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Zhùguó Liáng Ruì was appointed Yìzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
Ruì
was Yù's son.
See Liáng Yù in Volume 156, sixth year of Dàtōng during Liáng Wǔdì's reign.
The Zhōu dynasty sent Rǔnán Gōng Shénqìng and Sīwèi Shàngshì Zhǎngsūn Shèng.
Rǔnán
is an ancient commandery name.
Shèng,
read "chéng zhèng."
Shèng
was Yòu's great-grandson.
According to Suí Zhǎngsūn Shèng Zhuàn and Táng Zǎixiàng Shìxì Biǎo,
Shèng
was the fifth-generation grandson of Zhǎngsūn Zhì.
Zhì's courtesy name
was Yòuqīng.
He had a son Yù;
Yù had a son Shàoyuǎn;
Shàoyuǎn had a son Lǎn;
Lǎn had a son Chǎng;
Chǎng had a son Chì;
Chì had a son Shèng.
Thus, he was not a great-grandson.
If "Zhì" is written,
the character "Qīng"
is also missing
after "Yòu".
[The Zhōu dynasty] also sent Jiànwēi Hóu Hèruò Yì.
Jiànwēi County Marquis.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Jiànwēi County belonged to Wǔdū Commandery.
Ruò,
read "rén zhě."
Kě,
enters tone from "kān."
Hàn,
pronounced "hán."
Tuópō pretended to hunt with Shàoyì in the southern border,
and ordered Yì to capture him.
Yì
was Dūn's younger brother.
Hèruò Dūn
was Bì's father.
In the seventh month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Shàoyì arrived in Cháng'ān and was exiled to Shǔ.
After a long time,
he died of illness in Shǔ.
Yùchí Qín (尉遲勤), Grand Governor (zǒngguǎn) of Qīngzhōu (青州) for the Northern Zhōu (周) dynasty,
was Yuán Jiǒng (迥)'s disciple.
When he first received a letter from Yuán Jiǒng,
he submitted it to the throne,
and soon after, he also followed Yuán Jiǒng.
The territories under Yuán Jiǒng's command included Xiāng (相), Wèi (衞), Lí (黎), Míng (洺), Bèi (貝), Zhào (趙), Jì (冀), Yíng (瀛), and Cāng (滄).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Jí Jùn (汲郡)
had Yìzhōu (義州) established during the Eastern Wèi (東魏),
which was changed to Wèizhōu (衞州) by the Later Zhōu (後周).
Líyáng Xiàn (黎陽縣)
was Líyáng Jùn (黎陽郡) during the Later Wèi (後魏),
and Lízhōu (黎州) was established later.
Wǔ'ān Jùn (武安郡)
had Míngzhōu (洺州) established by the Later Zhōu.
Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡)
had Bèizhōu (貝州) established by the Later Zhōu.
Dàlù Xiàn (大陸縣) in Zhào Jùn (趙郡),
formerly called Guǎng'ā (廣阿),
had Yīnzhōu (殷州) established,
which was later renamed Zhàozhōu (趙州).
Xìndū Jùn (信都郡)
formerly had Jìzhōu (冀州) established.
Héjiān Xiàn (河間縣) in Héjiān Jùn (河間郡)
formerly had Yíngzhōu (瀛州) established.
Ráo'ān Xiàn (饒安縣) in Bóhǎi Jùn (勃海郡)
formerly had Cāngzhōu (滄州) established.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Zhōu Shū (周書) biography of Yuán Jiǒng (迥) also mentions Máozhōu (毛州).
According to research, after Yuán Jiǒng's demise,
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Suí (隋) first established Máozhōu.
The biography of Yuán Jiǒng is incorrect.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Běihǎi Jùn (北海郡) had Qīngzhōu (青州) established.
Qí Jùn (齊郡)
was formerly called Qízhōu (齊州).
Gāomì Jùn (高密郡)
formerly had Jiāozhōu (膠州) established.
Dōnglái Jùn (東萊郡)
formerly had Guāngzhōu (光州) established.
Yíshuǐ Xiàn (沂水縣) in Lángyá Jùn (琅邪郡)
formerly had Nánqīngzhōu (南青州) established,
which was later renamed Jǔzhōu (莒州) by the Later Zhōu.
The multitude numbered in the tens of thousands.
Shào Gōng Zhòu (邵公冑), the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Xíngzhōu (滎州).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Sìshuǐ Xiàn (汜水縣) in Xíngyáng Jùn (滎陽郡)
was the ancient Hǔláo (虎牢).
The Eastern Wèi (東魏) established Dōngzhōng Fǔ (東中府),
the Eastern Wèi established Běiyùzhōu (北豫州),
and the Later Zhōu established Xíngzhōu.
Shào Gōng Zhòu (邵公冑)
was of the Zhōu imperial clan,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Shàojùn (邵郡公).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Yìyáng Jùn (義陽郡),
on the Jiangzuǒ (江左), had Sīzhōu (司州) established,
which was renamed Yǐngzhōu (郢州) by the Later Wèi,
and later renamed Shēnzhōu (申州) by the Later Zhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Lángyá Jùn (琅邪郡)
had Nánxúzhōu (南徐州) established by the Later Wèi,
changed to Dōngxúzhōu (東徐州) by Liáng (梁),
changed to Dōngchǔzhōu (東楚州) by the Eastern Wèi,
changed to Ānzhōu (安州) by Chén (陳),
and changed to Sīzhōu (泗州) by the Later Zhōu.
Could it be that historians recorded them using their old provincial names?
Fèi (費) also,
a barbarian compound surname,
probably refers to the Fèiyě (費也) clan.
Fèi (費),
pronounced fú fèi.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志),
the Later Zhōu also had no Tóngzhōu (潼州),

Furthermore, the provisions for "deliberation" (yì), "petition" (qǐng), "reduction" (jiǎn), "redemption" (shú), and "official compensation" (guāndāng) were established to benefit officials and scholars.

All who could redeem themselves did so with copper instead of silk.
One jīn of copper for redemption was a fù (load),
ten fù constituted a diàn.
Ten strokes of caning required one jīn of copper;
up to one hundred strokes of flogging required ten jīn.
One year of penal servitude required twenty jīn of copper for redemption;
each additional grade added ten jīn of copper,
so three years would be sixty jīn.
Exile of one thousand lǐ required eighty jīn of copper for redemption;
each additional grade added ten jīn of copper,
so two thousand lǐ would be one hundred jīn.
Both forms of capital punishment could be redeemed with one hundred twenty jīn of copper.
For private crimes,
if one's official position compensated for penal servitude:
for officials of the fifth rank and above,
one official position compensated for two years of penal servitude;
for officials of the ninth rank and above,
one official position compensated for one year of penal servitude.
For those eligible for exile,
all three exile grades were treated the same as three years of penal servitude.
If public crimes were committed,
each penal servitude sentence was increased by one year;

Emperor Wén ordered Jìn Wáng Guǎng to support him with troops.
Jìn Wáng Guǎng was then governor of Bīng province (Bīng Shěng),
and all the northern borders were under his jurisdiction,
hence he was ordered to support Shābōluè with troops.
He was bestowed with carriages, clothing, drums, and wind instruments (gǔchuī).
Shābōluè then attacked Ābō in the west,
defeating him.
He used the power of the Súi army to achieve victory.
The imperial army (guānjūn) attacked Ābá,
defeating him,
and all the spoils were given to Shābōluè.
Shābōluè was greatly pleased,
and thus made a covenant,
with the desert (qì) as the boundary.
Qì
is pronounced qī jì.
"There cannot be two suns in the sky,
nor two kings on the earth."
This saying originated from Mèngzǐ.
Shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng;
the same applies below.
"How dare we obstruct with arms or rely on treacherous terrain,
illicitly seizing titles!
Now, moved by admiration for the pure customs,
we commit our hearts to the righteous Way,
bending our knees and kowtowing,
forever to be a vassal. "
He sent his son Kùhézhēn to pay respects at court.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The Súi Tūjué Biography writes
"Kūhézhēn,"
now following the Imperial Annals.
Cháo
is pronounced zhí yáo.
In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
Kùhézhēn arrived at Cháng'ān.
The Súi Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Though Shābōluè was formerly in harmony,
'Formerly'
means 'in the past,'
referring to past events.
Now, becoming lord and subject,
we are one body."
He then ordered a solemn announcement to the ancestral temples and altars of heaven and earth (jiāo miào),
and a widespread promulgation to all, far and near;
all edicts bestowed upon Shābōluè
did not address him by name.
He hosted Kùhézhēn in the inner palace.
The Tūjué had previously oppressed the various Huá states,
and Zhōu and Qí had humbled themselves to ally with them.
Now, Shābōluè presented a memorial declaring himself a subject,
and sent his son to pay respects.
The Súi Emperor announced this to the jiāo miào,
publicized it to his officials and common people,
magnifying the event;
hosting him in the inner palace
showed intimacy.
The rewards and commendations were very generous.
Shābōluè was greatly pleased,
and from then on, his annual tributes were uninterrupted.
13. In the ninth month,
General Zhàn Wénchè invaded Súi's Hézhōu.
Fèi Bǎoshǒu, Yítóng Sānsī of Súi, attacked and captured him.
14. On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Lǐ Ruò and other Súi envoys came for a visit.
15. In winter,
on the day Rénchén in the tenth month,
Súi appointed Yáng Sù, a Shàngzhùguó, as the Commander-in-Chief of Xìnzhōu.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Bādōng Commandery,
Liáng established Xìnzhōu.
Súi stationed Yáng Sù at Yǒng'ān,
intending to use him to lead a navy to attack Chén.
16. Previously, Fù Zài of Běidì
had served the Emperor (Shàng) as a commoner in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
When the Emperor ascended the throne, Fù Zài was promoted to Mìshūjiān, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, and concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was arrogant due to his talent,
and many people resented him.
Shī Wénqìng and Shěn Kèqīng together slandered Fù Zài, accusing him of accepting gold from Gāolì envoys.
The Emperor arrested Fù Zài and imprisoned him.
Zhàiyú (縡於) submitted a memorial from prison, saying:
"A ruler of men
reverently serves the Supreme Lord,
loves the common people as his children,
curtails his desires,
keeps flattery and deceit at a distance,
puts on his clothes before dawn,
and forgets food until late in the day.
Thus, his benevolence covers the entire realm,
and blessings flow to his descendants.
Your Majesty, of late, has been excessively indulged in wine and women,
not revering the great deities of the suburban and ancestral temples,
but instead exclusively flattering licentious and muddled spirits,
saying that these favor Zhāng Guì (張貴),
and making female shamans dance and conduct lewd sacrifices in the palace.
Eunuchs wield power,
detesting loyalty and uprightness as if they were enemies,
viewing the common people as grass and mustard seeds.
The empresses and concubines in the inner palace trail luxurious silks,
while the poor lack even pulse and grain.
The common people are displaced and scattered,
and corpses cover the fields.
Bribery and corruption are rampant,
and the treasury is depleted.
Heaven is angered, and the people resentful,
with the masses rebelling and close relatives alienated.
Your minister fears that the kingly aura of the Southeast will end from this point."
When the memorial was presented,
the emperor was greatly enraged.
After a while,
his anger slightly subsided,
and he sent an envoy to Zhàiyú (縡於), saying:
"I wish to pardon you.
Can you reform your errors?"
He replied:
"My heart is like my face.
If my face can be changed,
then my heart can be changed."
The emperor became even more furious,
and ordered the eunuch Lǐ Shànqìng (李善慶) to thoroughly investigate the matter,
whereupon Zhàiyú (縡於) was granted death in prison.
The emperor, whenever it was time for suburban sacrifices,
often claimed illness and did not attend,
which is why Zhàiyú (縡於) mentioned it.
This year,
Liáng (梁) Grand General Qī Xīn (戚昕) attacked Gōng'ān (公安) with a naval force,
but failed and returned.
Gōng'ān (公安) was
the administrative seat of Chén (陳)'s Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Xīn (昕),
pronounced as xǔ jīn.
Huán (還),
pronounced xuán,
also as written.
The Suí (隋) ruler summoned Zhāng Zhǔ (梁主)'s paternal uncle, Grand Commandant Wúwáng Cén (吳王岑), to court,
appointed him Grand General,
enfeoffed him as Huáiyì Gōng (懷義公),
and then detained him, not allowing him to return;
he also re-established the Jīnglíng Zǒngguǎn (江陵總管) to oversee him.
The Suí (隋) abolished the Jiānglíng Zǒngguǎn (江陵總管),
as seen in the previous volume under Chén Gāozōng (陳高宗) Tàijiàn (太建) fourteenth year.
Fù (復),
pronounced fú yòu.
Jiān (監),
pronounced gōng xián.
Liáng (梁) Grand General Xǔ Shìwǔ (許世武) secretly invited Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Yíhuáng Hóu Huìjì (宜黃侯慧紀) to take the city;
Yíhuáng (宜黃) was
an ancient county,
established by Wú (吳),
belonging to Línchuān Jùn (臨川郡),
and merged and abolished by Suí (隋).
The Liáng (梁) ruler killed him.
Huìjì (慧紀) was
a grand-nephew of Gāozǔ (高祖).
The Suí (隋) ruler ordered Sīnóng Shàogīng Cuī Zhòngfāng (司農少卿崔仲方) to conscript thirty thousand men
to build the Great Wall in Shuòfāng (朔方) and Língwǔ (靈武),
extending east to the Hé (河) (Yellow River)
and west to Suīzhōu (綏州).
The Five Dynasties Gazetteer: Diāo Yīn Jùn (雕陰郡),
established Suīzhōu (綏州) by Western Wèi (魏).
This was to block the Hu (胡) bandits.
Liáng (梁) changed its reign title to Guǎngyùn (廣運).
On the day Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
the Dǎngxiàng Qiāng (党項羌) requested to surrender to Suí (隋).
The Suíshū (隋書) states: The Dǎngxiàng Qiāng (党項羌)
are descendants of the Sānmiáo (三苗),
claiming to be of the macaque species.
They bordered Línfú (臨洮) and Xīpíng (西平) to the east,
and Yèhù (葉護) to the west,
spanning several thousand li from north to south,
with each surname forming a separate tribe.
Dǎng (党),
pronounced dǐ lǎng.
Jiàng (降),
pronounced hù jiāng.
On the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
Suí (隋) promulgated its calendar to the Tūjué (突厥).
Promulgating the calendar meant submitting to the legitimate reign.
In the second month,
Suí (隋) first ordered the senior assistants to the Cìshǐ (刺史) to come to court for evaluation each year-end.
Shàngzuǒ (上佐)
refers to the Zhǎngshǐ (長史) and Sīmǎ (司馬).
Gèng (更),
pronounced gōng héng.
Shàng (上),
pronounced shí zhǎng.
On the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
Suí (隋) again ordered Cuī Zhòngfāng (崔仲方) to conscript one hundred and fifty thousand men
to build several tens of cities
east of Shuòfāng (朔方)
along the border's strategic points.
Shuòfāng Jùn (朔方郡)
was Xiàzhōu (夏州).
Fù (復),
pronounced fú yòu.
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
the emperor's younger brother Shūmó (叔謨) was enfeoffed as Bādōng Wáng (巴東王),
Shūxiǎn (叔顯) as Línjiāng Wáng (臨江王),
Shūtǎn (叔坦) as Xīnhuì Wáng (新會王),
and Shūlóng (叔隆) as Xīnníng Wáng (新寧王).
The Five Dynasties Gazetteer: Wūjiāng Xiàn (烏江縣) of Lìyáng Jùn (歷陽郡),
Chén (陳) established Línjiāng Jùn (臨江郡);
Xīnhuì Xiàn (新會縣) of Nánhǎi Jùn (南海郡),
formerly established Xīnhuì Jùn (新會郡);
Xīnxīng Xiàn (新興縣) of Xìn'ān Jùn (信安郡),
Liáng (梁) established Xīnníng Jùn (新寧郡).
On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Suí (隋) issued a general amnesty.
In the third month,
on the day Jǐwèi (己未),
Gāo Dé (高德), a man from Luòyáng (洛陽), submitted a memorial
requesting the Suí (隋) ruler to become Taishang Huang (太上皇)
and transfer the throne to the Crown Prince.
The emperor said:
"I have received the mandate of Heaven,
and nurture the common people.
I toil diligently until late in the day,
still fearing I may not be adequate.
How could I imitate recent emperors
who passed the throne to their sons
to seek their own ease and pleasure!"
This refers to not imitating Qí Wǔchéng (齊武成) and Zhōu Tiānyuán (周天元).
Lè (樂),
pronounced luò.
In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Zhōu Pán (周磻) and others were dispatched as envoys to Suí (隋).
In the fifth month,
on the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
the emperor's son Zhuāng (莊) was enfeoffed as Kuàijī Wáng (會稽王).
In autumn,
eighth month,
Suí (隋) dispatched Sànjì Chángshì (散騎常侍) Péi Háo (裴豪) and others to come as envoys.
Sàn (散),
pronounced xī dǎn.
Jì (騎),
pronounced qí jì.
On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Suí (隋) Shēnmíng Gōng Lǐ Mù (申明公李穆) passed away.
Suí (隋) bestowed the posthumous title Míng (明) upon Lǐ Mù (李穆) because he was able to perceive subtle signs and preserve himself.
Zú (卒),
pronounced zǐ xù.
In the intercalary month,
on the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Suí (隋) Crown Prince Yǒng (勇) garrisoned Luòyáng (洛陽).
Suí (隋) Shàngzhùguó Chéng Gōng Liáng Shìyàn (上柱國郕公梁士彥) suppressed Wèichí Jiǒng (尉遲迥),
as detailed in volume 174, Gāozōng (高宗) Tàijiàn (太建) twelfth year.
Wèi (尉),
pronounced yū wù.
He was replaced as Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (相州刺史) by Jiǒng (迥);
the Suí (隋) ruler, wary of him,
recalled him to Cháng'ān (長安).
Shàngzhùguó Gōng Yǔwén Xīn (上柱國公宇文忻) had been close to the Suí (隋) ruler in his youth,
was skilled in military strategy,
and possessed great prestige;
the Suí (隋) ruler was also wary of him,
and dismissed him from office due to a reprimand.
Xīn (忻) was Right Língjūn Dà Jiāngjūn (右領軍大將軍).
Zhùguó Shū Gōng Liú Fǎng (柱國舒公劉昉) were all estranged,
living idly,
harboring considerable resentment,
frequently visiting each other,
and secretly plotting rebellion.
Xīn (忻) wanted to make Shìyàn (士彥) raise troops in Púzhōu (蒲州).
Púzhōu (蒲州)
was the strategic point of Púbǎn (蒲坂)
and Héjīn (河津),
located over three hundred *lǐ* (里) from Cháng'ān (長安).
Shìyàn’s (士彥) nephew Péi Tōng (裴通) was privy to the plot and reported it.
The Emperor concealed the matter,
appointing Shìyàn (士彥) as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jìnzhōu (晉州).
Jìnzhōu (晉州)
(Píngyáng (平陽))
was a place of military importance.
When the Zhōu (周) and Qí (齊) armies contended,
it was considered a vital stronghold.
Shìyàn (士彥) was delighted,
and said to Fǎng (昉) and others:
"It is Heaven's will!"
He then requested Yí Tóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Xuē Mó'ér (薛摩兒) to be his Chángshǐ (長史).
The Emperor also permitted it.
Later, while attending court with the high officials,
the Emperor ordered his attendants to seize Shìyàn (士彥), Xīn (忻), and Fǎng (昉) from the ranks,
and interrogated them.
At first, they refused to confess.
When Xuē Mó'ér (薛摩兒) was captured and brought in,
he was commanded to face them in court,
where they were confronted with the facts in the palace courtyard.
Shìyàn (士彥) turned pale,
looked at Mó'ér (摩兒) and said,
"You are killing me!"
On the *bǐngzǐ* (丙子) day,
Shìyàn (士彥), Xīn (忻), and Fǎng (昉) were all executed.
Their nephews and brothers were spared death but stripped of their titles.
In the ninth month,
on the *xīnsì* (辛巳) day,
the Suí (隋) ruler, in plain clothes, went to the archery hall
and ordered all officials to shoot at the possessions of the three families as a warning.
These three men had been old acquaintances of the Suí (隋) ruler,
and had performed meritorious service in supporting him,
but they conspired to commit treason.
Therefore, he wore plain clothes and used them as a warning to all officials.
In the 15th winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,
the Suí (隋) appointed Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書) Yáng Shàngxī (楊尚希) as Lǐbù Shàngshū (禮部尚書).
The Suí (隋) ruler held court every morning,
and did not tire until late in the day.
Shàngxī (尚希) admonished him, saying:
"King Wén (文) of Zhōu (周) shortened his life through anxious toil,
while King Wǔ (武) prolonged his life through peace and joy.
Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the *Lǐjì* (禮記) contains these words.
pronounced *zǔ lì fān*.
pronounced *luò*.
Assign responsibility to the chief ministers.
Trivial and busy affairs
are not what a ruler should personally attend to."
The Emperor approved of his words but was unable to follow them.
On the 16th *guǐchǒu* (癸丑) day,
the Suí (隋) established the Shānnán Dào Xíngtái (山南道行臺) in Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
Xiāngzhōu (襄州) administered Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
the land of which was south of the southern mountains of Cháng'ān (長安).
Jùn Cuī Shì (俊崔氏) gave birth to a boy,
and the Suí (隋) ruler was pleased,
bestowing gifts upon all officials.
Lǐ Wénbó (李文博) of Bólíng (博陵), a Zhí Mìshū Nèishěng Bóshì (直祕書內省博士),
had always been poor.
The Cao Wèi (曹魏) dynasty's books were stored in the Mìshū (祕書),
in the inner and outer three pavilions.
At this time, the Mìshū (祕書) already had an inner and outer division.
The Suí (隋) dynasty opened channels for submitting books,
summoned skilled calligraphers from all over the realm to mend and complete damaged and missing parts,
creating two copies, one main and one secondary,
stored in the palace.
The rest were used to fill the inner and outer pavilions of the Mìshū (祕書).
Hence, the office of Zhí Mìshū Nèishěng (直祕書內省) was established.
Bólíng Jùn (博陵郡)
was Dìngzhōu (定州).
Wénbó (文博) said:
"The establishment of rewards and punishments
depends on merit and demerit.
Now, if the king has a son,
what has that to do with all the officials,
that they should receive undeserved rewards!"
Those who heard him were ashamed.
On the 17th *guǐhài* (癸亥) day,
Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Jiāng Zǒng (江總) was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
and Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Xiè Zhóu (謝伷) was made Púyè (僕射).
In the 18th eleventh month,
on the *jǐmǎo* (己卯) day,
there was a general amnesty.
The 19th Toghon (吐谷渾) Khagan Kuālǚ (夸呂) had been on the throne for a hundred years.
"Kuālǚ" (夸呂),
in the *Suí Shū Tǔyùhún Zhuàn* (隋書吐谷渾傳) is written as
"Lǚkuā" (呂夸).
Later, the crown prince was afraid
and conspired to seize Kuālǚ (夸呂) and surrender;
he requested troops from the Suí (隋) border officials.
Qínzhōu Zǒngguǎn (秦州總管) Hékán Wáng (河間王) Hóng (弘) offered to send troops to assist him.
Qínzhōu (秦州)
was Tiānshuǐ Jùn (天水郡).
Hékán Wáng (河間王) Hóng (弘) was a cousin of the Suí (隋) ruler.
The crown prince's plot was discovered
and he was killed by Kuālǚ (夸呂).
His youngest son, Wéiwáng Hē (嵬王訶), was then made crown prince.
Diézhōu Cìshǐ (疊州刺史) Dù Càn (杜粲)
In *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志): Líntáo Jùn (臨洮郡) Diéchuān Xiàn (疊川縣),
the Hòu Zhōu (後周) established Diézhōu (疊州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: because the mountains in that area were often overlapping.
The Suí (隋) ruler also refused.
That year,
Wéiwáng Hē (嵬王訶) again feared execution
and planned to lead his tribes, fifteen thousand households, to surrender to the Suí (隋).
He sent envoys to the imperial court
to request troops to escort them.
The Suí (隋) ruler said:
"The customs of the Hún (渾) bandits
are especially different from human morality.
This means their customs deviate from human morality
and are different from those of China.
The son is also unfilial.
I instruct people with virtue,
how can I help them in such wickedness and rebellion!"
So he said to the envoy:
"If a father has faults,
the son should remonstrate.
How can one secretly plot illegal acts
and earn the name of unfilial!
All under Heaven are my subjects,
and if each does good deeds,
it will please my heart.
Since Wéiwáng (嵬王) wishes to submit to me,
I will only teach Wéiwáng (嵬王) the principles of being a subject and a son.
It is not appropriate to send distant troops
to assist in wicked deeds!"
The Suí (隋) ruler can be said to have spoken like a true sovereign. Zhēnmíng Yuánnián (禎明元年)
( *dīngwèi* (丁未), 587)
1st spring,
first month,
on the *wùyín* (戊寅) day,
there was a general amnesty,
and the era name was changed.
2nd *guǐsì* (癸巳) day,
the Suí (隋) ruler offered sacrifices at the Tàimiào (太廟).
3rd *yǐwèi* (乙未) day,
the Suí (隋) decreed that each prefecture should annually present three scholars.
4th second month,
on the *dīngsì* (丁巳) day,
the Suí (隋) ruler performed the morning sacrifice to the sun in the eastern suburbs.
*Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志): According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven offers morning sacrifice to the sun in the eastern suburbs at the vernal equinox,
and evening sacrifice to the moon in the western suburbs at the autumnal equinox.
Han (漢) law did not wait for the two equinoxes;
it regularly offered sacrifices to the Tàizhì (泰畤) in the eastern and western suburbs.
In the morning, one would leave the bamboo palace,
bow to the east towards the sun,
and in the evening bow to the west towards the moon.
Emperor Wén (文) of Wèi (魏) criticized this as being too tedious and irreverent, like household matters,
and instead performed the morning sacrifice to the sun outside the eastern gate in the first month.
Previous historians also considered this to be out of season.
Then, in the first year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Míng (明), on the *dīnghài* (丁亥) day of the second month,
the morning sacrifice was performed to the sun in the eastern suburbs.
On the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day of the eighth month,
the evening sacrifice was performed to the moon in the western suburbs,
which finally conformed to ancient practice.
The Hòu Zhōu (後周) performed the morning sacrifice to the sun outside the eastern gate of the capital at the vernal equinox,
setting up an altar like that for suburban sacrifices,
using a single sacrificial animal,
green silk,
and a green *guī* (圭) with a base.
The Emperor rode in a green carriage,
and the sacrificial officials all wore green crowns,
while attendants wore green caps.
The burnt offering was like that at the Yuánqiū (圓丘).
At the autumnal equinox, the evening sacrifice to the moon was performed outside the western gate of the capital,
with an altar set up in a depression.
The burnt offering
and rites were similar to the morning sacrifice to the sun.
In the early Kàihuáng (開皇) era of Suí (隋),
an altar was set up outside the Chūnmíng (春明) Gate in the east of the capital,
and the morning sacrifice to the sun was performed every vernal equinox.
Another altar was set up in a depression outside the Kāiyuǎn (開遠) Gate in the west of the capital,
and the evening sacrifice to the moon was performed every autumnal equinox.
The sacrificial animals and silk were the same as those of Zhōu (周).
*Cháo* (朝),
pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
5th envoys including Jiān Sànqí Chángshì (兼散騎常侍) Wáng Hēng (王亨) were sent to the Suí (隋) for a mission.
*Sàn* (散),
pronounced *xī dān fān*.
pronounced *qí jì fān*.
6 The Suí dynasty dispatched over 100,000 able-bodied men to repair the Great Wall,
and they were dismissed after twenty days.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Shānyáng Dú Canal was opened in Yángzhōu to facilitate transport.
The seat of Yángzhōu was Guǎnglíng,
and Shānyáng county was under its jurisdiction.
According to the Chūnqiū,
the state of Wú built Hán and
dug canals to connect the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
The Shānyáng Dú Canal had long connected to Guǎnglíng;
the Suí merely widened and deepened it,
intending to attack Chén.
7 Shābōlüè Kèhán of the Tūjué sent his son to pay tribute to the Suí,
and then requested permission to hunt between Héng and Dài.
The Tuòbá clan first established their capital at Píngchéng,

The Suí emperor asked Gāo Jǐng for a strategy to take Chén.

"The land north of the Jiāng is cold,
