and Hán Qínhǔ was ordered to lead an army
to cross the river at Héngjiāng渡
and attack Gūshú.
Wúzhōu was administered from Guǎnglíng,
and Hèruò Bì was ordered to cross the river from Guāzhōu
and attack Jīngkǒu.
若,
pronounced Rénzhě.
Dōnghǎi Jùn
was Hǎizhōu.
Qīngzhōu was administered from Yìdū.
This probably means that Yàn Róng was ordered to lead the Qīngzhōu army to cross the sea from Qúshān to attack Nánshā.
燕,
pronounced Yīnjiān.
The army numbered 518,000,
all under the command of Jìn Wáng Guǎng.
Extending east to the vast sea,
and west to Bā and Shǔ,
their banners, flags, and ships
stretched for thousands of _lǐ_.
Gāo Jǐng, the Left Minister, was made Jìn Wáng Guǎng's Marshal's Chief Clerk;
Wáng Sháo, the Right Minister, was made司馬.
All military matters were decided by them;
the allocation and management of resources
proceeded without hindrance.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the Suí Emperor personally saw off the generals and soldiers;
on the day Yǐhài,
he arrived at Dìngchéng.
The record of the expedition states: Dìngchéng is thirty _lǐ_ from Tóngguān,
with one city on each side of the road.
6 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Imperial Younger Brother Shúróng was made King of Xīnchāng,
and Shúkuāng was made King of Tàiyuán.
7 The Suí Emperor went to Hédōng;
Hédōng
was Púzhōu.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
he returned to Cháng'ān.
8 Mòhé Kèhán of the Tūjué attacked a neighboring country to the west,
was struck by an arrow in the midst of battle, and died.
His countrymen enthroned Yōngyúlǘ,
who was titled Xiéjiāshīduōnádūlán Kèhán.
This laid the groundwork for the Tūjué's renewed rebellion.
頡,
pronounced Hùjié.
伽,
pronounced Qiújiā.
9 When the Suí army arrived at the river,
Gāo Jǐng said to Xuē Dàohéng, the Ministry of Personnel Director of the Xíngtái:
"With this grand expedition,
can Jiāngdōng definitely be conquered?"
Dàohéng replied:
"It can be conquered.
I once heard Guō Pú say:
Guō Pú,
a Jìn man,
was skilled in numerology.
'...and then it will unite with China again.'
Now this cycle is nearing its end,
this is the first reason.
Emperor Yuán of Jìn crossed south,
and was enthroned in Jiànkāng in the year Dīngchǒu.
This year
is the year Wùshēn,
a total of 272 years.
Shúbǎo is profligate and arrogant,
this is the second reason.
The safety or danger of a state lies in whom it entrusts power.
They have made Jiāng Zǒng prime minister,
who only indulges in poetry and wine.
They have promoted the villain Shī Wénqìng
and entrusted him with political affairs.
Xiāo Móhé and Rènmánnú are great generals,
but they are merely individual talents,
this is the third reason.
Rènmánnú
is Rèn Zhōng.
They lack virtue and are small.
Their armored soldiers number no more than 100,000.
From Wūxiá in the west
to the vast sea in the east,
if divided, their power will be dispersed and weak;
if gathered, they will defend one place and lose another,
this is the fourth reason.
The momentum to sweep them away
is beyond doubt."
Jǐng said joyfully:
"Your words on the reasons for success and failure
are truly enlightening.
I originally valued you for your talent and learning,
but I did not expect your strategy to be so profound."
爾
means "thus" or "like this."
Qín Wáng Jùn supervised the various armies stationed at Hànkǒu,
acting as the commander of the upper reaches.
An imperial edict ordered Sànqí Chángshì Zhōu Luóhóu to be the Grand Supervisor of all military affairs along the Bāxiá River to resist them.
散,
pronounced Sǐdǎn.
騎,
pronounced Qíjì.
Yáng Sù led his fleet down the Three Gorges,
and the army reached Liútóutān.
General Qī Xīn, with over a hundred _qīnglóng_ ships,
defended Lángwěitān.
The terrain was treacherous and steep,
causing the Suí people concern.
The _Shuǐjīng Zhù_ says: The Jiāng River passes Liútóutān,
then flows east past the north of ancient Yíchāng County,
and then east past Lángwěitān.
This area is still to the west of Huángniúxiá.
Dù Yòu's _Tōngdiǎn_ says: Lángwěitān
is now within the borders of Yīdū County, Yílíng Commandery.
艘,
pronounced Sūzāo.
峭,
pronounced Qīxiào.
"The great plan for victory or defeat
rests on this one move.
If we launch our boats in broad daylight,
they will see our strengths and weaknesses.
The current is swift and strong,
beyond human control,
so we will lose our advantage.
It is better to surprise them at night."
Yáng Sù personally led several thousand _huánglóng_ ships,
advancing silently,
and dispatched Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Wáng Chángxí to lead infantry to attack Qī Xīn's separate stockades from the south bank.
Grand General Liú Rén'ēn led armored cavalry from the north bank towards Báishā,
arriving at dawn,
and attacked them.
Qī Xīn was defeated and fled.
All his troops were captured,
treated well and released,
without a single hair being touched.
Yáng Sù led the naval forces eastward.
Their boats and sterns covered the river,
and their banners and armor shone in the sun.
Yáng Sù sat in a large flat-decked ship,
with a majestic appearance.
The Chén people looked upon him
and were all terrified,
saying:
"Qīnghé Gōng is truly the River God!"
The garrisons at Jiāngbīn reported successively
that the Suí army was approaching,
but Shī Wénqìng and Shěn Kèqīng both suppressed the reports and did not speak of them.
Initially,
the Emperor feared Xiāo Yán and Xiāo Huán,
members of the Liáng imperial clan,
who had come over with their followers;
thus, he felt apprehensive about them.
Therefore, he dispersed their forces,
appointing Yán as the Intendant of Dōngyángzhōu,
and Huán as the Intendant of Wúzhōu.
He ordered Commander Rèn Zhōng to guard Wúxīng Jùn,
to serve as a strategic buffer for the two prefectures.
He ordered Nánpíng Wáng Yí to guard Jiāngzhōu,
and Yǒngjiā Wáng Yàn to guard Nánxúzhōu.
Jiāngzhōu was administered from Xúnyáng,
and Nánxúzhōu from Jīngkǒu;
both were important strategic towns along the Jiāng.
Yí,
pronounced like ‘yú lì’ in reverse.
He commanded all ships and boats from the defenses along the Jiāng to return to the capital with the two princes,
to demonstrate their might to those who came from Liáng.
As a result, there was not a single *dǒu* boat on the Jiāng,
and the troops from the upper-river prefectures were all blocked by Yáng Sù’s army,
unable to arrive.
The Intendant of Xiāngzhōu, Jìnxī Wáng Shūwén,
whose administration was in Chángshā,
was greatly loved by the people.
The Emperor, seeing that he occupied the upper reaches of the river,
secretly resented him.
He judged that he had shown little favor to his close ministers,
feared they would not serve him,
and found no one reliable.
So, he promoted Shī Wénqìng to Dūdū and Intendant of Xiāngzhōu,
allocated him two thousand elite soldiers,
intending for him to move west.
He then recalled Shūwén to the court.
Wénqìng was very pleased with this arrangement,
but feared that once he left,
those in charge would exploit his weaknesses.
Therefore, he advanced his partisan Shěn Kèqīng to replace himself.
Before their departure,
the two jointly managed confidential matters.
Commander of the Guards Fán Yì said to Púyè Yuán Xiàn:
"Jīngkǒu and Cǎishí are both vital locations.
Each requires five thousand elite soldiers,
and two hundred 'gold-wing' boats,
to patrol up and down the Jiāng
for defense."
Jīncì,
a type of boat.
He then discussed with civilian and military ministers
and requested that Yì’s plan be adopted.
Not long after,
Hán Qínhǔ crossed at Cǎishí,
and Hèruò Bì captured Jīngkǒu.
The two routes advanced simultaneously,
and Chén perished.
There are places that must be defended;
this does not require a wise person to know.
To abandon his duty of reporting his administration (Shùzhí),
Mèngzǐ said: When feudal lords appear before the Son of Heaven, it is called *shùzhí*.
Here, *shùzhí* refers to taking up a post in a border region.
Zhī,
to go.
Rèn,
duty.
Zhī rèn,
to go and assume one's duty.
Wénqìng and Kèqīng were at that time jointly managing confidential matters.
If Wénqìng were to leave,
Kèqīng would have sole control.
"If there are proposals,
they need not be presented in person;
simply write a memorial,
and it will be officially submitted."
This means if court officials have something to present,
they do not need to meet Emperor Chén to say it in person;
just send it in writing,
and it will be conveyed.
Wéi,
pronounced like 'yú wěi' in reverse;
the lower 'nèi wèi' is the same.
The two brought the memorial and reported.
The Emperor said:
"This is a common matter.
The generals and commanders at the border are sufficient to handle it.
If we send out troops and boats,
I fear it will cause alarm."
When the Suí army advanced to the Jiāng,
spies frequently arrived.
Xiàn and others earnestly requested,
even repeatedly.
Wénqìng said:
"The New Year's grand assembly is approaching.
On the day of the Southern Sacrifice,
the crown prince will have many followers.
Chén followed the Liáng system
of performing sacrifices to Heaven and Earth at the Southern and Northern suburbs in the first *xīn* day of the first month every other year,
using one special ox.
The next year, this ritual was to be performed in the first month,
hence Shī Wénqìng said so.
Cóng,
pronounced like 'cái yòng' in reverse.
The matter will then be neglected and abandoned."
The Emperor said:
"Let's deploy troops for now.
If there's no trouble in the north,
we can then use the navy for the sacrifice.
Why not?"
He also said:
"If we do this, the news will reach neighboring countries,
and they will think our country is weak."
Later, he also bribed Jiāng Zǒng,
and Zǒng spoke on his behalf inside the court,
meaning that after various opinions were presented,
Wénqìng again bribed Jiāng Zǒng
to help him.
Shuì,
pronounced like 'shū ruì' in reverse.
Zhòng,
as written.
So he ordered the matter to be handed over for external detailed discussion.
Zǒng again suppressed Xiàn and others,
which caused the deliberation to be prolonged and unresolved.
The Emperor casually said to his attending ministers:
"The imperial aura is here.
The Qí army came three times,
and the Zhōu army came twice,
and none failed to be crushed and defeated.
The Qí army came three times,
referring to when Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē, with the Qí army, attacked Jiànkāng in the first year of Liáng Jìng Dì's Shàotài era,
occupying Shítou.
In the first year of Tàipíng,
they again attacked and broke Cǎishí,
and with Qí's Xiāo Guǐ, invaded
and pressed upon Jiànkāng.
In the first year of Shìzǔ Tiānjiā,
Qí generals Liú Bóqiú and Mùróng Shìdé assisted Wáng Lín in capturing Wúhú;
all were defeated.
The Zhōu army came twice,
referring to when Dúgū Shèng and Hèruò Dūn entered Xiāngchuān in the first year of Tiānjiā,
and in the first year of Línhǎi Wáng Guāngdà,
Yǔwén Zhí and Yuán Dìng assisted Huá Jiǎo;
all were defeated.
Cóng,
pronounced like 'qiān róng' in reverse.
Dūguān Shàngshū Kǒng Fàn said:
"The Cháng Jiāng is a natural barrier;
anciently, it was considered the boundary separating north and south.
When Wèi Wén Dì attacked Wú,
he approached the Jiāng,
saw the surging waves of the river,
and exclaimed:
'Indeed, Heaven established this to separate north and south!'
Qiàn,
pronounced like 'qī yàn' in reverse.
Border generals merely seek to gain merit
and falsely claim the situation is urgent.
I always lament my low rank.
If the barbarians cross the Jiāng,
I will surely become Tàiwèigōng!"
Kǒng Fàn considered himself skilled in both civil and military matters,
hence he boasted about establishing merit.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
the Three Ducal Ministers were commonly referred to as Tàiwèigōng, Sītúgōng, and Sīkōnggōng.
Fàn said:
"These are my horses;
why should they die?"
He meant that if the horses crossed the Jiāng,
they would certainly not be able to return north and would all become his property,
which was also a boast.
Therefore, no thorough preparations were made;
performances, drinking, and poetry continued without interruption.
10 That
Tuòyùhún píwáng Tuòbá Mùmí.
The Tuòyùhún themselves also had the Tuòbá surname.
Pí,
pronounced bēi.
Tǔ,
from tūn in the entering tone.
Gǔ,
pronounced yù.
The Suí Zhǔ said:
"Under all heaven,
all are Our subjects.
In Our nurturing,
benevolence and filial piety are all upheld.
The Hún bandit is deluded and mad,
his wives and children are filled with fear,
and all wish to submit,
to save themselves from peril and destruction.
However, a husband who rebels and a son who turns against his father
cannot be accepted.
Yet, their original intention is precisely to avoid death.
If We now refuse them,
it would again be inhumane.
If there is any further news,
merely console and pacify them,
allowing them to extract themselves.
There is no need to send out troops to receive them.
If his brother-in-law and nephew wish to come,
let them follow their own will;
there is no need to persuade or entice them."
The so-called
"rebellious husband and disloyal son"
and
"brother-in-law and nephew"
certainly all had specific names at the time,
but the histories do not record them in detail.
*Suí Shū* writes
"míngwáng Tuòbá Mùmí";
"píwáng"
is also a term used in *Hàn Shū*.
Bèi,
read as pūmèi.
Yòu,
read as yángjiǔ.
11 The King of Hénán, Yízīpóu, died.
The Suí Zhǔ ordered his younger brother, Shùguī, to inherit and govern his people.
Yízīpóu's submission to Suí can be seen in the previous volume under Gāozōng, Tàijiàn Thirteenth Year.
Póu,
read as pūhóu.
Zú,
read as zǐxù.
